19878-the-passaic-flood-of-1903:
The Passaic Flood of 1903 is a federal water-supply paper by Marshall Ora Leighton. It was transmitted to the Geological Survey for publication in that series. The Passaic River drains a crowded corner of New Jersey. Its 1903 flood ranked among the worst then recorded there. Leighton's report measures the water and maps the damage. Government science treated floods as data problems first.

Leighton became a leading American hydrologist. His flood studies set methods for gauging and records. Mill towns along the Passaic suffered repeated inundations. A careful post-flood survey served engineers and insurers alike. The report preserves rainfall, flow, and loss figures. It is a primary source for New Jersey flood history.
20130-magazine-or-animadversions-on-the-:
Magazine, or Animadversions on the English Spelling, dates from 1703, a very early spelling tract. Animadversions means critical remarks, and spelling is the target here. English spelling was still unsettled in Queen Anne's time. Writers of tracts argued for simpler, more regular ways to spell words.

The modern edition lists scholars from Columbia, Chicago, Princeton, and other schools. Their names show how later editors framed this old text for study. Readers get a glimpse of English before spelling froze into place. It suits those who love the history of words and print.
alchimia-nova-das-ist-die-guldene-kunst-: Alchimia nova, 1603. The new alchemy. This book preserves that work. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years. Tomorrow's readers will find it.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol1-1803:
Amadis of Gaul is the great Spanish romance of chivalry that set the pattern for a whole age of fiction. Robert Southey, the English poet, translated it, and the first volume appeared in 1803. Its hero Amadis became the model knight for readers across Europe.

Amadis loves the lady Oriana and proves himself against giants, enchanters, and rival knights. Battles, shipwrecks, and magic fill this opening volume. The book bewitched Renaissance readers, and Cervantes honored it even while mocking its imitators. Southey's version brought the Spanish epic to English readers in full. Volume one launches the quest in high style.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol2-1803:
Robert Southey's translation of Amadis of Gaul ran to four volumes in 1803, and this is the second. The Spanish romance follows the peerless knight Amadis, the standard by which later heroes were judged. His deeds for his lady Oriana drive the whole vast tale.

Volume two carries Amadis through wars fought for Oriana's hand and fresh dangers in strange lands. Enchantments test his faith, and new knights enter the lists beside him. The pace is pure romance, with marvel piled on marvel. Readers of Cervantes will know this world well, since Don Quixote's library was full of such books. The epic here rides at full gallop.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol3-1803:
The third volume of Southey's Amadis of Gaul came out in 1803 with the rest of his translation. Amadis, the Spanish knight whose fame spread over Europe, faces his hardest trials of constancy here. His lady Oriana remains the center of all his deeds.

Sorcerers lay cunning traps, and magic isles rise out of the sea to test him. Amadis must hold his faith through long separation and false reports. The wonders come thick in this book, the richest in marvels of the four. Southey, himself a poet of romance, keeps the old Spanish fire alive in English. The volume brings the epic near its climax.
amadis-of-gaul-southey-vol4-1803:
Southey's Amadis of Gaul ends with this fourth volume, published in 1803. The Spanish romance had shaped European ideas of knighthood for three hundred years before Southey Englished it. Here the long tale of Amadis and Oriana reaches its close.

Final battles settle the wars that run through all four volumes. The last enchantments break, and old wrongs come right at last. The lovers win their hard reward after years of trial. With this volume ends the romance that taught Europe how to dream of knights. Its shadow falls across Don Quixote and across every chivalric tale written after it.
anselm-proslogium-monologium-cur-deus-ho:
Sidney Norton Deane published his translation of St Anselm's major works in 1903. Anselm, archbishop of Canterbury in the 1100s, wrote the Proslogium and Monologium as prayers that reason through faith. Deane gathered those works with Cur Deus Homo in one English volume.

The Proslogium holds Anselm's famous argument that God, as the greatest conceivable being, must exist. Gaunilon, a monk, replied on behalf of the fool who denies God, and Anselm answered him. Cur Deus Homo explains why God became man, in the satisfaction theory of the atonement. These texts founded scholastic philosophy, the effort to prove the faith by reason, and they still anchor courses on medieval thought.
anthropography-or-bible-phrenology-of-th: Anthropography or Bible Phrenology, 1903. The nations' phrenology. This book preserves that work. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. Writers of history may cite it later in their work.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-03:
Volume three of Burton's Arabian Nights, issued in 1885, carries Shahrazad's tales deeper into the cycle. By now the frame is familiar: night after night of story buys the teller her life. The tales turn through courts, markets, deserts, and islands of wonder in Burton's unabridged English.

Sea voyages and marvels grow more frequent as the volume proceeds. Burton refused to soften the Arabic text's frank passages, which kept his edition to private subscribers at first. His terminal essay and notes, spread through the set, made it a storehouse of lore. Later editors borrowed his learning even when they cut his text. The third volume sustains the pace set by the first two.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
The third supplemental volume of Burton's Nights, published from 1886, carries the overflow of the Arabic tradition further. Burton worked from manuscripts in several collections to catch tales the main cycle missed. Some are variants of known stories; others stand alone, rougher and stranger than the famous ones.

His method does not change: full text, kept verse, and notes that explain rite, dress, and law. The supplement as a whole shows how open the Nights remained, growing by copyists' hands for centuries. Burton wanted English readers to see that growth, not a polished extract. Volume three sits midway in the supplement's six books. It rewards readers who finished the main set and still want more.
arnaldi-de-villanova-philosophi-medici-e: Arnaldi de Villanova Omnia, 1603. The Villanova complete works. This book preserves that collection. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
arnim-svf-vol2-1903:
Chrysippus of Soli, the third head of the Stoic school, wrote hundreds of books, and none of them survive whole. Hans von Arnim devoted the second volume of his fragment collection, printed in 1903, to what remains of Chrysippus on logic and physics. The passages appear in Greek and Latin, as the sources kept them.

Here are the Stoic views on truth, signs, causes, fate, and the makeup of the cosmos, rebuilt from quotes in later authors. Chrysippus was the thinker who turned Stoicism into a tight system. This volume holds most of what can still be known of that system, and it stays a working tool for scholars of ancient thought.
arnim-svf-vol3-1903:
The third volume of Hans von Arnim's Stoic fragment collection, printed in 1903, turns from logic and physics to ethics. It gathers what survives of Chrysippus on how a person should live, and adds fragments from the Stoics who came after him. The texts stand in Greek and Latin, drawn from the authors who quoted them.

Readers find the roots of Stoic moral teaching here: virtue as the only true good, and the passions treated as errors in judgment. Duty is sorted by what fits nature and one's role in life. Because Chrysippus wrote the fullest defense of these views, his fragments form the core of Stoic ethics as later ages took it up.
arxiv-2510-00103:
Alberto Torralba and a large team of co-authors published this 2025 astronomy paper on a class of objects called Little Red Dots. These compact red sources may mark a key phase in the growth of giant black holes. The team studied one bright example with deep spectra from the James Webb Space Telescope. They wanted to learn what kind of gas surrounds such an object.

The spectra revealed a forest of faint iron lines coming from a warm, dense outer layer. That same layer scatters hydrogen light and gives the broad hydrogen lines their wide wings. The layer is mostly opaque to hydrogen light, which shapes the object's sharp Balmer break. A simple glowing-slab model matches much of the spectrum well. The picture that emerges is of a black hole wrapped in a warm cocoon of excited gas.
arxiv-2510-00203:
Robert Hayek, Joaquin Chung, and Rajkumar Kettimuthu wrote this 2025 review paper on software for quantum networks. Quantum networks promise secure communication, distributed sensing, and linked quantum computers. Moving from lab demos to dependable service takes software matched to quantum hardware's odd constraints. The authors survey what exists for designing such networks and for running them.

The review organizes tools into three planes: infrastructure, logical, and control or service. Design simulators such as SeQUeNCe, QuISP, and NetSquid get detailed coverage. Operating functions, from entanglement handling to resource management, are sorted into a proposed taxonomy. A stubborn gap separates protocol papers from working simulator or testbed code. The gap is worst for changing topologies and day-to-day network management. The authors close with open challenges and a roadmap toward large hybrid quantum networks.
arxiv-2510-00403:
Huan Yu, Qi Xia, and Jun Fang published this 2025 astrophysics paper simulating particle acceleration at relativistic shocks. Their plasma mixes electrons and positrons with a small share of protons, about five percent by number. Particle-in-cell simulations follow the shock that forms when this flow reflects off a wall. Such shocks power the glowing jets and bursts seen across the universe.

Downstream, positrons reached energies comparable to the protons themselves. Their spectrum grew a hard nonthermal tail, while electrons stayed stuck at lower energies. The authors blame waves driven by the protons, whose polarization favors positron acceleration. Density and magnetic field behind the shock fluctuated strongly in the runs. The lesson is that a pinch of protons reshapes who gets accelerated in pair plasmas. That composition effect should inform models of pulsar wind nebulae and gamma-ray bursts.
arxiv-2510-00703:
Bussolan and six co-authors release MultiPhysio-HRC in this 2025 arXiv paper, a multimodal dataset of physiology recorded during industrial human-robot collaboration. Robots that share factory work should sense stress and cognitive load so they can adapt, yet training such perception needs labelled data. Volunteers performed controlled cognitive tasks, virtual reality experiences, and industrial disassembly work, both manually and with robotic assistance. Sensors captured brain, heart, skin, breathing, and muscle signals.

The release includes voice recordings and facial action units, which widen the signal mix beyond body sensors. Validated psychological questionnaires supplied ground-truth labels for the participants' mental states. Baseline models for stress and cognitive load classification showed the signals carry information, though accuracy stayed hard to push high. The authors argue that gap invites better multimodal fusion methods. The dataset is public, aimed at affective computing and safer, human-aware factory robots.
arxiv-2510-01203:
Kadiyala and Mirzaeinia forecast minute-by-minute stock prices by blending market data with news sentiment scored by ten different language models. Short-term prices whip around on headlines, so raw price history alone misses the story. The team aligned a month of Apple news articles with one-minute trading data.

Each article received sentiment scores from every model, later merged with prices and technical indicators. Two modern architectures, Mamba and Reformer, trained on the enriched stream. Mamba predicted more accurately and ran faster across the sentiment sources. Pairing it with the strongest sentiment models sharpened short-term adaptability most. Ten sentiment judges disagree, and that disagreement itself carries signal. Hyperparameters were tuned systematically rather than guessed. A three-day evaluation window tested the freshest behavior. Lower error and higher speed rarely arrive together. Minute-level trading is the harshest classroom for forecasters of all kinds.
arxiv-2510-01303:
Sonthalia, Murray, and Montúfar explain why the gradients that train small neural networks are simpler than they look. Learning theory usually assumes tidy, isotropic data, which real datasets violate cheerfully. The team studies two-layer networks under a spiked, anisotropic data model instead.

The input-weight gradient turns out to be approximately low rank in both major scaling regimes. Two rank-one components dominate, one tracking the bulk data and one tracking the spike. Data properties, scaling, and activation choice set the balance between them. Common regularizers, from weight decay to Jacobian penalties, tune the components selectively. Mean-field and neural-tangent scalings both obey the same low-rank story. Input noise joins the list of knobs that modulate the balance. Synthetic and real data both confirmed the theoretical split. Feature learning gains a concrete mechanism from the decomposition. Two terms carry the gradient.
arxiv-2510-01403:
Nyland and co-authors image a tiny double-lobed radio source that a piggyback survey noticed flickering at low frequency. The instrument collects data during other astronomers' observations, turning spare capacity into a transient watch. One source varied by about a fifth over roughly a year, earning closer inspection.

Very-long-baseline imaging resolved two lobes spanning only tens of parsecs, a compact symmetric object. Its spectrum peaks in the hundreds of megahertz under either of two standard absorption models. Variable boosting by relativistic motion was ruled out as the flicker's cause. Interstellar scintillation and intrinsic changes remain the live explanations. Three hundred forty megahertz is the survey's home frequency. Photometric redshift places the source deep in the distant universe. Free-free and synchrotron self-absorption both fit the turnover. Milliarcsecond scales are where the double structure lives. Commensal observing turns idle antennas into discovery machines.
arxiv-2510-01503:
Evans and Norris couple the geometry of an irradiated surface to where the ions actually deposit their energy, inside continuum models of nanopattern formation. Ion bombardment sculpts astonishingly regular ripples on semiconductors, yet no unified model explains every detail. The collision cascade matters twice: it moves material quickly, and it creates defects enabling slow viscous flow.

Their asymptotic approximations track the deposition profile and the buried amorphous boundary together. Predictions for ripple wavelength, onset angle, and roughening prove surprisingly sensitive to coupling details. Both the early linear and later nonlinear growth regimes receive matched approximations. Surface amplitude and slope define the two regimes being bridged. The amorphous layer's thickness mediates the viscous response. Sputtering handles the fast transport the cascade initiates. Patterning onset angle is exquisitely sensitive to deposition shape. Details of coupling stop being details at all.
arxiv-2510-01803:
Stival and five co-authors study how Italians judge their environment's effect on health in this 2025 statistics paper. Their data come from PASSI, Italy's nationwide health surveillance system. Survey answers are merged with town-level data on income, pollution, and geography. The team models which personal and local factors push perceptions toward positive or neutral views.

Their tool is a penalized ordered regression model with partly parallel effects. It lets some factors act uniformly across response levels while others vary, and it regularizes unstable estimates. Results showed strong differences across Italian territories, so local character shapes perception heavily. Individual traits interacted with those local influences rather than acting alone. Higher fine-particle pollution levels were linked to poorer views of the local setting. The authors read that link as evidence that residents notice real hazards, which can guide policy planning.
arxiv-2510-02203:
Wang, Shishkin, and Soker check whether stripped stars still carry the seeds of a jet-driven explosion in this 2025 astrophysics paper. The jittering-jets mechanism explodes massive stars through jets launched by convectively stirred accretion. Earlier work studied hydrogen-rich progenitors, leaving stripped-envelope supernovae unexamined. The authors evolved models from twelve to forty solar masses with the MESA code.

Every model, whatever its envelope state, held at least one strong convective zone in the inner core. Those zones carry the angular momentum jittering jets need. The key layer sits inside the mass coordinate matching a neutron star's maximum mass. Its angular momentum parameter clears the threshold the mechanism demands. Hydrogen-rich, hydrogen-stripped, and helium-stripped variants all qualify. The result extends the jittering-jets picture to the stripped-envelope events that dominate many surveys. Core convection, it seems, almost guarantees the explosion machinery can start.
arxiv-2510-02303:
Hayatsu and co-authors revisit a deep sky survey whose two prize detections vanished. Their 2025 astronomy paper examines the ALMA Deep Field in SSA22. The survey hunted faint far-infrared emitters from the young universe. Two bright candidates appeared above six sigma. Follow-up observations found nothing at those spots. The team injected fake sources into the raw data. Those mock tests measured how real sources should appear. They also probed a possible technical fault with the ALMA operations team. Comparing real and mock data cubes showed noise behaved normally.

The authors then rebuilt the luminosity count for carbon emission at redshift six. Their method tracks both contamination and completeness in full. Honest upper limits replace the false detections. Deep surveys everywhere face the same trap. A careful audit trail protects their catalogs.
arxiv-2510-02503:
Katale and co-authors model stealthy cyberattacks against gas pipeline control systems. Their 2025 engineering paper builds a physics informed simulation testbed. Pipelines run on sensor networks watched by SCADA systems. An extended Kalman filter rebuilds full network state from partial readings. Model predictive control then sets valves and compressors safely. The attacker enters as one level of a bilevel problem. False data injections aim to cut throughput quietly. The injections must stay under bad data detectors. A mathematical reformulation turns the game into one solvable program.

Two case networks, with fifteen and twenty four nodes, test the setup. Sensor level attacks stayed statistically hard to spot. Throughput damage still landed despite the stealth constraint. Defenders can rehearse against such optimized attackers safely. Real grids cannot serve as practice targets. Physics aware testbeds reveal where monitoring is thin.
arxiv-2510-02803:
Liao and a large team test self-driving systems in road work zones. Work zones have odd layouts, cones, and shifting lanes. Car makers now add vision-language models to help cars plan paths. The team ran the first broad study of these models in work zones. Mainstream models failed to draw a correct path in most cases. The failure rate reached about two thirds of the trials.

The authors mined the failures for shared patterns. Human checks confirmed eight common failure types. They then built REACT-Drive to fix the problem. It turns past failures into rules and planning code. A retrieval step pulls in rules that match each new scene. On a public data set, path error fell to about a third of the baseline level. Tests in a real car covered fifteen work zone scenes. The system also answered faster than fine-tuned rivals.
arxiv-2510-02903:
von Bassewitz and co-authors model how single cells change over time. A stem cell slowly turns into a tissue cell. Genes switch each other on and off in a tangled web. Current top models need costly transport preprocessing. They also fail to name the gene links they use. The team's Cell-MNN puts a simple differential equation at its core.

The equation runs in a hidden space inside an encoder-decoder design. Near each cell state, the dynamics act almost linear. That form lets the model state gene links in plain terms. Training runs end to end with almost no preprocessing. Benchmark scores matched the best rival models. Scaling to big data sets and joint training went better than rivals. The learned gene links agreed with a curated database called TRRUST. The model may guide future gene-edit tests.
arxiv-2510-03003:
Sharma and co-authors predict ship shaft power from sparse daily reports. Shaft power drives fuel use, so fleets track it closely. Rich sensor streams predict it well but cost a lot to gather. Most ships file only noon reports, one summary per day. The team bridges the gap with transfer learning. A model first learns from dense sensor data on one vessel. Daily reports from other vessels then fine-tune it.

Trials used sister ships, a near twin, and a distinct vessel. Transfer cut the percentage error in every case. Sister ships gained the most from the shared start. Even the distinct vessel improved by a clear margin. A model trained on reports alone served as the baseline. The gap between report and sensor models shrank a lot. Fleets can thus reuse one instrumented ship's lessons widely. That helps fuel planning across ships that lack rich sensors.
arxiv-2510-03503:
Muster and Froufe-Pérez present a 2025 arXiv paper on making suspended particles interact only in groups, never in pairs. Colloids usually push and pull on each other two at a time, and effects stay hard to isolate. The authors shine random light fields on the particles to create forces. By tuning the color mix of that light, they aim to cancel pair forces while holding total light energy fixed. A model of electric and magnetic dipole response guides the tuning.

Their optimization found spectra that effectively cancel pair interactions across a range of distances. Under those conditions, a colloid would feel only many body forces. The claim holds under general assumptions in their analysis. Many body systems would let physicists study group effects that pair based theories blur, from self assembly to fluids. Lab builders get a recipe for light recipes that sculpt interactions in a way.
arxiv-2510-03703:
Bokade and Bhaghyesh present a 2025 arXiv paper predicting the masses and decays of baryons made of three charm or three bottom quarks. These particles, the Omega ccc and Omega bbb, have not been observed, so theory must guide the search. The authors treat each baryon as a quark bound to a diquark and solve a model with a potential. They compute the spectra of radial excitations. Transition rates follow from the wave functions.

The ground state mass predictions land with other estimates, at four point seven gigaelectronvolts for the charm baryon and fourteen point two for the bottom one. States excited inside the diquark sit lower in mass than states excited between quark and diquark. That ordering highlights how diquark structure matters. Bottom decay widths come out a thousand times smaller than charm ones. Decays to the ground state are suppressed, so experiments should watch for cascade paths.
arxiv-2510-03903:
Atabuzzaman, Zhang, and Thomas present this 2025 arXiv paper on naming the exact species or model in a photo, with no training examples. Fine-grained classification is hard because rival classes look nearly alike, like similar bird species or car models. Large vision-language models answer general questions well, but asking them for a class name works poorly here. The authors recast the task as careful question answering instead.

Their method asks the model multiple-choice questions in rounds, narrowing the options step by step. An attention intervention steers the model toward the image regions that matter most. They also wrote richer class descriptions than datasets usually supply. Across five benchmarks and several model families, the iterative method beat earlier zero-shot approaches by wide margins. The attention trick helped smaller models the most. The authors note current models still miss many fine distinctions, so the task remains open.
arxiv-2510-04003:
Nguyen and Thiet present this 2025 arXiv paper on reading ancient Sino-Vietnamese manuscripts with optical character recognition. Vietnam's historical records were written in classical Chinese characters, called Han-Nom, and digitizing them would open them to search and translation. Standard OCR tools fail on degraded scans, non-standard glyphs, and handwriting in these old sources. The authors fine-tune a modern OCR system on real manuscript material instead.

They retrained the recognition module of PaddleOCRv5 on a curated set of ancient Vietnamese Chinese texts. The full pipeline covers image preparation, data conversion, training, evaluation, and visualization. After fine-tuning, exact recognition accuracy rose from under two-fifths to one-half of test cases. Gains were strongest on noisy, low-quality images, exactly where historians need help most. Better OCR for Han-Nom texts supports translation, semantic alignment, and historical linguistics research.
arxiv-2510-04103:
Zhang, Liu, and Jia present this 2025 arXiv paper asking which six-quark particles quark confinement could ever allow. Exotic multiquark states beyond ordinary mesons and baryons are now experimental reality, but compact hexaquarks remain elusive. The authors use the MIT bag model, which confines quarks inside a finite region with perturbative interactions. Confinement energy must stay negative for a bag to hold together, and that condition sets a critical radius.

They derive a critical bag radius that matches the known string-breaking distance of about one point two to one point four femtometers. Applying the framework to six-, seven-, and eight-quark systems, they find most heavy-light flavor combinations fail the test. Two configurations built from light quarks and bottom antiquarks emerge as candidates for narrow states. The authors recommend that the LHCb experiment search for those specific hexaquarks.
arxiv-2510-04303:
Tailor presents this 2025 arXiv paper on detecting covert collusion among language model agents that coordinate through hidden signals. Agents in pricing, auctions, and peer review can embed messages in word choice or message length while appearing compliant. Audits rely on heuristics without false-positive guarantees and rarely transfer between tasks. The paper attacks the problem on three fronts: theory, benchmark, and detector.

A channel-capacity analysis quantifies how paraphrasing, rate limiting, and role permutation shrink the covert channel. The ColludeBench suite covers pricing, first-price auctions, and peer review with covert schemes. A pipeline fuses mutual information across runs, permutation invariance, watermark variance, and acceptance bias, tuned to a one-in-a-thousand false-positive budget. Ten thousand honest runs and an e-value martingale validate the calibration. The combined test reached state-of-the-art detection power and caught fairness-driven colluders that mutual information alone missed.
arxiv-2510-04403:
Masakazu Teragaito wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on special knots and the surgeries performed on them. A Dehn surgery cuts and reglues space around a knot, and some results are prized L spaces. Knots with no symmetry are rare in the standard census tables. Among the census knots, exactly nine asymmetric L space knots are known. Computer work had shown that each one admits two surgeries of a special alternating kind.

Teragaito set out to confirm those eighteen surgeries by hand, without leaning on the computer search. His tool is the Montesinos trick, a classic method that turns a surgery question into a question about links. Step by step, he checks each knot and each slope from the known table. The branching sets that appear are knots or links of the required alternating type. The paper thus gives a human proof of that result. Knot theorists gain a verified list.
arxiv-2510-04603:
Johan Linåker and Sachiko Muto wrote this 2025 paper on open source software in digital government. Open source code underlies almost all modern software, and governments gain reuse, openness, and sovereignty from it. Yet maturity indexes that grade governments barely measure open source aid. The team studied policy and practice in sixteen countries picked for their digital maturity. They read policy documents and interviewed government staff in each country.

Policies that support reuse of open source code proved widespread across the sixteen. They cover both taking code in and sharing code out with others. Central public bodies usually run those policies, with stated goals of interoperability, sovereignty, transparency, and cost savings. Open source program offices at several levels of government supply training, shared resources, and project care. Security appears in the policies as both a risk and a strength. The authors distill indicators across fourteen areas for future maturity indexes.
arxiv-2510-05103:
Anna Nymann Heisel and Niels Lauritzen publish a short correction to recent algebra research in this 2025 arXiv note. Hashemi and Kapur had proposed an algorithm for converting Gröbner bases between monomial orders. Their method truncates polynomials and lifts partial results step by step. Such conversions are routine workhorses in computational algebra.

Doubts about the published proof pushed the authors to hunt for a counterexample. Computer experiments over the rationals found the first cracks. The note then gives a tiny example over the two-element field, small enough to check by hand. On that example the algorithm fails to produce a valid Gröbner basis. The correction matters because others might build on the faulty method.
arxiv-2510-05303:
Bojan Kuzma, Chi-Kwong Li, and Edward Poon classify transformations that preserve special matrix behavior in this 2025 arXiv paper. They study linear maps on square matrices, over both complex and real numbers. The maps send every unitary matrix to a scalar multiple of a unitary matrix. Such preserver problems ask how rigid that condition forces the map to be.

For dimension three and up, the answer is fully rigid. Every bijective example is built from fixed unitary factors, a scaling, and possibly a transpose. The authors then apply that structure to matrix pairs with extremal norm behavior. Maps preserving pairs whose product norm equals the product of norms take an even simpler conjugation form. The two-by-two case needs separate treatment and gets its own section.
arxiv-2510-05503:
Wang and colleagues predict how a rare particle, the Bc(2S) meson, will decay. This meson is an excited state made of a bottom quark and a charm quark. It should appear in large numbers at the high-luminosity LHC collider. Both the ground state and this excited state are now listed by the Particle Data Group. Its weak decays into two lighter particles have not yet been measured.

Using QCD factorization, the team computes decay rates for channels driven by either heavy quark. The most favored decays, into a Bs meson plus a light partner, may reach measurable levels. Decays that produce charmonium states are far rarer, thanks to strong suppression factors. Those rare channels will likely stay beyond the reach of near-future detectors. Search teams can plan around these numbers. The paper serves as a ready reference for experimental searches at the collider.
arxiv-2510-05703:
Du and colleagues align language models under explicit safety constraints. The goal is maximum reward with harmful-content cost below a fixed threshold. Earlier methods train separate reward and cost models at heavy expense. Their 2025 primal-dual DPO approach skips that machinery entirely.

First, standard DPO on reward preferences supplies reward information. A rearranged Lagrangian objective then fine-tunes on cost preferences. The theory bounds both suboptimality and constraint violation of the final policy. An online extension adds exploration bonuses for uncovered prompt-response space. That version drops the dependence on preference data coverage. Memory and compute costs fall significantly versus safe RLHF pipelines. No prior knowledge of the optimal solution is required either. Forbidden tokens from laws or course rules fit the same constrained frame. Experiments on the PKU-SafeRLHF dataset confirm the method works.
arxiv-2510-05803:
Bailie and Gong reinterpret a data-sharing framework through the lens of contextual integrity. National statistical offices use the Five Safes to judge disclosure risk before sharing data. The framework splits risk into five dimensions, from safe people to safe outputs. Their symposium paper, from 2023, maps it onto Nissenbaum's contextual integrity theory.

The five parameters of contextual integrity align one-to-one with the five safes. That mapping shows the Five Safes as contextual integrity specialized to statistical dissemination. The authors then place differential privacy inside this broader frame. Differential privacy becomes one tool within a holistic risk toolkit, not the whole story. The frame also guides how offices should design privacy implementations. Disclosure control is a wicked problem with stakeholders in direct conflict. Data users want finer detail while contributors expect confidentiality and anonymity. Regulation and social norms, not just mathematics, shape correct deployment.
arxiv-2510-06003:
Ray examines compact stars under a modified theory of gravity in a 2025 astrophysics paper. The theory, called f(Q,T) gravity, links the geometry of spacetime with the trace of the matter energy tensor. Ray studies stars whose internal pressure differs by direction, a property known as anisotropy. Such stars include neutron stars and pulsars seen by telescopes.

Ray solves the modified field equations for a chosen form of the theory and checks the solutions against standard stability conditions. The model stays free of singularities and can account for pulsars heavier than twice the mass of the Sun. It also covers objects in the mass gap, such as the lighter partner in the merger event GW190814. Predicted radii run from about 10.5 to 14.5 kilometers, and the range for the pulsar PSR J0740+6620 agrees with published estimates.
arxiv-2510-06103:
Xi and four co-authors propose a new spin observable for electron scattering in a 2025 particle physics paper. In semi-inclusive deep inelastic scattering, an electron knocks a quark from a nucleon, and the debris forms hadrons. The authors track two Lambda hyperons from one event, one near the struck quark and one near the remnant.

Comparing the two hyperons' helicities measures how spin passes through both regions at once. Remarkably, the measurement works even when neither beam nor target is polarized. The correlation isolates a polarized fragmentation function and a polarized fracture function that are otherwise hard to reach. With perturbative matching for the fracture function, the team computes predictions across flavors and settings. The predicted correlation varies strongly between those settings, which makes it a sensitive probe of spin-dependent hadronization on both sides of the collision.
arxiv-2510-06203:
Rho, Trinh, Xu, and Ha present Reference-Grounded Skill Discovery for high-dimensional agents in a 2025 reinforcement learning paper. Unsupervised skill discovery struggles as bodies grow complex, because the search space explodes while meaningful skills stay limited. Semantic guidance becomes essential to steer the search toward useful behaviors.

The algorithm first grounds skills in reference motion data. Contrastive pretraining embeds motions on a unit hypersphere, each reference motion getting its own direction. The method then imitates reference behaviors while exploring related variations around them. On a simulated SMPL humanoid, the method imitated walking, running, punching, and sidestepping. It also found offshoots of those skills. When later put to use, the learned skills obeyed user-specified style commands closely. Imitation baselines often lost the commanded style, while the grounded skills kept it. Reference grounding gives such agents a diverse, steerable skill set.
arxiv-2510-06303:
Cheng and ten co-authors combine autoregression and diffusion into one paradigm called SDAR in a 2025 machine learning paper. Autoregressive models train efficiently but generate token by token. Diffusion models decode in parallel but cost far more to train.

SDAR converts a trained autoregressive model into a blockwise diffusion model through brief, data-efficient adaptation. At inference, generation proceeds autoregressively across blocks for coherence. Inside each block, discrete diffusion decodes all tokens in parallel. Experiments confirm autoregressive models are far more compute-efficient than masked diffusion models, ideal starting points. SDAR preserved autoregressive-level performance while adding parallel speed. Scaling studies showed larger models tolerate bigger blocks without accuracy loss. Their thirty-billion-parameter MoE model surpassed its autoregressive counterpart on GPQA and ChemBench. Test-time methods like majority voting added further gains.
arxiv-2510-06603:
Andi Gu and Stephen Jordan connect quantum computing with error-correcting codes. Their 2025 paper studies a method called Decoded Quantum Interferometry, which pairs decoding problems with optimization problems. The original version used Reed-Solomon codes, a classic family with a strict length limit. The authors extend the method to a richer family called Hermitian codes.

Hermitian codes reach far longer block lengths using a smaller alphabet. Their matching optimization problem becomes a polynomial regression task on a Hermitian curve. Because the dual of a Hermitian code is another Hermitian code, the problem also reads as approximate list recovery. The authors compare their method against Prange's algorithm, simulated annealing, and algebraic list recovery. Across a large range of settings, the quantum method finds better approximate answers efficiently. The work widens the kinds of codes that quantum interferometry can exploit.
arxiv-2510-06703:
Zafrin Nikita leads a student team in Bangladesh that built a working spectrometer on a shoestring budget. Their 2025 paper describes an optical instrument that splits light into its wavelengths. Spectrometers are vital lab tools, but commercial units cost far more than many schools can pay. The team aimed for accuracy and ease of use at minimal cost.

Their device pairs a webcam with a grating cut from a DVD. A black box housing blocks stray light that would spoil readings. Free Python software processes the camera images into spectra. Calibration came from a professional Red Tide spectrometer, used as the reference standard. The team measured many light sources, from colored LEDs to a green laser. Peak wavelengths and line widths closely matched the professional instrument. Deviations stayed minimal across the sources tested. The design shows that careful engineering can put a real lab instrument within reach of low-budget classrooms.
arxiv-2510-07103:
Pullisseri and Unnikrishnan propose one field that could play two cosmic roles at once. Their 2025 paper asks whether dark matter and dark energy might share a single source. Both are unseen, yet together they shape how the universe grows. The authors extend an older theory that links gravity to a moving scalar field. Their version gives that field a less standard form of motion.

The team solves for how a flat universe would expand under their model. With no matter present, the field alone drives a steady pattern of growth. For strong enough settings, the expansion mimics an era ruled by cold dark matter. That match is the core claim for a unified picture. A single field acting as both dark parts would simplify cosmology. The model now needs checks against real sky data to earn wider trust.
arxiv-2510-07203:
Akera, Ouma, Yiga, and Walukagga introduce Sunflower, a family of language models built for Uganda's many languages. Their 2025 paper notes that Africa holds over two thousand living languages. Leading models serve only the largest few well. Uganda, with its rich mix of languages, is their test case. They release the models openly for public use.

Sunflower comes in two sizes, both built on an existing open model family. The larger version posted the best translation scores in most of the Ugandan languages tested. It led in twenty-four of thirty-one languages on average translation quality. The models understand the majority of Ugandan languages at a state-of-the-art level, the authors report. Uses include health, farming, and public services where English-only tools fail people. Regional models like Sunflower offer a template for other rich language areas.
arxiv-2510-07303:
Rieke and co-authors check whether infrared colors can be trusted to find black holes hiding behind dust. Their 2025 paper evaluates how active galactic nuclei are picked out by fitting galaxy light across wavelengths. For massive galaxies, detailed spectra confirmed the fitting method's calls. The main failure mode was a wrong distance estimate fed into the fit, which can fake the glow of a hidden nucleus. Low-mass galaxies pose a different trap: their warm dust alone can mimic that glow.

A fiercely star-forming galaxy named Haro 11 works as a guardrail template for that trap. Watching longer wavelengths near thirteen microns further cleans the sample. The James Webb telescope's mid-infrared instrument supports this recipe for nearby-enough distances. Clean samples of buried black holes are vital for tracing how galaxies grew.
arxiv-2510-07503:
Colominas, Steinerberger, and Wu prove that separating a signal's components in time and frequency is secretly a graph clustering problem. Their 2025 paper studies time-frequency representations, maps showing how a signal's pitch content evolves. Each component traces a ribbon across the map, and sharpening methods make those ribbons thin. The authors show the filtering task can be rephrased exactly: build a graph from the map, then find clusters that are tightly knit inside and sparsely linked outside. Decades of graph clustering research thereby become signal processing tools overnight, suggesting many new filtering algorithms.

Masks drawn from the clusters isolate components, and inverting them retrieves the separated sounds. The method is non-parametric, makes no assumptions about the signal, and works in one global shot. Sequential rivals strip one component at a time and accumulate errors as they go.
arxiv-2510-07703:
Ma, Li, and Weng wrote this 2025 computer vision paper on deep hashing for image search. Hashing turns each image into a short binary code, so similar images sit close together. Pairwise methods learn fine local similarity but miss the global layout. Center-based methods capture global structure yet waste local detail. The authors propose letting the two styles teach each other, in a framework called Mutual Learning for Hashing.

A strong center-based branch and a weaker pairwise branch train together, passing knowledge both ways. The center branch absorbs local similarity cues from its weaker partner. A mixture-of-hash-experts module lets the branches interact more richly. Across several benchmark datasets, the combined system beat leading hashing methods in search quality. The result is notable because the weaker branch holds the missing information. Weak supervision, used well, unlocked a stronger final hash function for large-scale retrieval.
arxiv-2510-07903:
Raźny wrote this 2025 differential geometry paper on a spectral sequence for group actions on manifolds. A compact Lie group can act on a manifold so that every orbit has the same dimension. Such equidimensional actions sit between free actions and fully general ones. Spectral sequences are machines that compute cohomology in stages. Raźny builds a Leray-Serre style sequence for this setting and describes its second page in detail.

The second page ties together three cohomology theories. Basic cohomology describes the orbit space, Lie algebra cohomology describes a typical orbit, and together they converge to the manifold's de Rham cohomology. Special cases simplify, especially for simply connected manifolds. A final section handles non-equidimensional actions by a blow-up process. As an application, he derives an obstruction to certain actions. The paper extends earlier work that only covered locally free actions.
arxiv-2510-08303:
Yannis Belkhiter and co-authors set out a vision for flexible AI in future 6G networks in a 2025 arXiv paper. Network control AI must cope with constant change, as vendors, hardware, and services evolve. New sensors and features appear over time, so models trained once soon go stale. The authors promote Adaptive Random Forests, tree ensembles that update as new data streams in.

They show that repeated training of these forests keeps predictions stable as features are added. Accuracy improved over time in their tests when richer feature sets arrived. They also propose DAFI, a method that explains which features drive model outputs. DAFI uses a drift detector to decide when costly importance checks are worth running. On three data sets, their approach cut runtime by up to two times. It also gave more consistent feature importance values than rivals.
arxiv-2510-08403:
Stacey Jeffery and Galina Pass give a quantum algorithm for directed reachability with a sharp space-time tradeoff in a 2025 arXiv paper. The problem asks whether a directed path leads from vertex s to vertex t in a graph. It is complete for the complexity class NL, making it a benchmark problem. Classical algorithms must choose between using much space or much time.

Their quantum algorithm runs with any space budget S above a modest log-squared threshold. The running time beats the best classical algorithm, up to a quadratic factor, for all sublinear space budgets. Only a small log-squared portion of the space needs to be quantum memory. The rest is ordinary classical storage, which is far cheaper to build. This split means classical space can be traded for quantum time. The result sharpens what quantum speedup means for space-limited computing.
arxiv-2510-08503:
Thomas Schuster, Dominik Kufel, Norman Yao, and Hsin-Yuan Huang prove that telling which phase of matter a quantum state is in can be intractably hard, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Phases of matter, like magnetic or topological phases, are central targets of quantum experiments. Recognizing an unknown state's phase sounds like a basic diagnostic task. They show any recognition algorithm's quantum running time must grow exponentially in the state's correlation range.

For even moderate correlation ranges, that growth makes the task practically infeasible. When correlations grow faster than logarithmically in system size, the time becomes super-polynomial. Results cover symmetry-breaking phases and topological phases protected by symmetry, for every discrete symmetry and every spatial dimension. The proof extends pseudorandom unitaries to symmetric systems, constructing them at very low circuit depth under standard cryptographic conjectures. Hardness also holds for translation-invariant systems and purely classical phases.
arxiv-2510-08803:
Dwivedula and co-authors argue that hand-written rules for computer systems should give way to rules written by code generators, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Policies for tasks like web caching and congestion control have long been crafted by experts for one setting at a time. Those rules turn brittle when workloads or hardware change. The team's framework, PolicySmith, uses large language models to search for rules tuned to a specific instance.

Applied to web caching, which decides what data to keep close for fast access, PolicySmith found rules that beat established baselines on standard public traces. Applied to congestion control, which paces traffic on a network, it produced policies safe enough to run inside the Linux kernel itself. The authors present the two cases as evidence that generated rules can match each deployment instead of forcing one compromise on all.
arxiv-2510-09103:
Zhang, Liu, and Fang cut the memory bill of training language models by storing less momentum, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Momentum, a running average of past update directions, speeds training greatly but doubles the optimizer's memory footprint for every model weight. Their optimizer, AdaPM, observes that most blocks of a network do not need the full treatment. It keeps momentum only where it matters, in a non-uniform pattern across the model.

Skimping on momentum normally biases the updates and costs accuracy, so a bias correction step repairs the estimate. In tests, momentum memory fell by over ninety percent while training quality held. Combined with a trick for the second-order statistics, total optimizer memory fell by up to ninety-five percent. The savings held across model sizes, fine-tuning, and preference training, and cut the graphics processor hours for one large pretraining run by over thirty percent.
arxiv-2510-09303:
Sami Raatikainen, Syksy Rasanen, and Eemeli Tomberg examine primordial black holes in a 2025 arXiv paper on the early universe. These black holes may have formed from dense patches soon after the Big Bang. The team studies stochastic kicks, meaning random jolts during inflation, and asks how the jolts change how many such holes form and how heavy they are.

The authors simulate one hundred million patches of the universe, following tens of thousands of momentum shells in each one. They build each patch profile from first principles and include the effects of critical collapse. The profiles turn out very spiky, and the spikes can raise the black hole count by up to thirty-six orders of magnitude. The mass spread also shifts toward heavier holes and widens a lot, though the authors note that convergence problems remain.
arxiv-2510-09403:
J Ablinger, J Blümlein, A De Freitas, and three further co-authors complete a long calculation in particle physics in a 2025 arXiv paper, circulated as the DESY preprint 25-125. They compute operator matrix elements, quantities that connect quark and gluon descriptions inside fast-moving hadrons. The missing piece was the three-loop contribution involving two different heavy quark masses.

The team uses a semi-analytic approach to get results for a general mass ratio, covering both the unpolarised and the polarised cases. They cross-check the formulas against independently computed Mellin moments, a compressed summary of the results, up to very high orders. The two-mass terms turn out to make up about half of some of the full contributions at this order. With this piece in place, all massive three-loop operator matrix elements, polarised and unpolarised, are now calculated.
arxiv-2510-09803:
Md Tusher Ahmed, Farid Ahmed, and Jianzhi Li simulate spraying tungsten with ultrasound assistance in a 2025 arXiv paper. Tungsten is prized for standing up to heat, for strength, and for rust resistance in military and aerospace uses. Its high melting point and poor room-temperature plasticity, however, block many ways of making it, and ordinary cold spray cannot deform its particles enough to bond.

Cold spray builds coatings by firing particles at high speed so impact deformation welds them. Using atomic-scale dynamics simulations, the authors add ultrasonic shaking to the process. The ultrasound produces acoustic softening and brief temperature spikes at particle contacts. Together these effects markedly improved plastic flow and bonding across a wide range of impact speeds, particle sizes, and ultrasonic settings, compared with plain cold spray. The study also tests whether mixed vanadium-tungsten interfaces can be built this way.
arxiv-2510-09903:
Aharon, Keemin Lee, Karan Sikka, and Selmaan Chettih build an uncertainty-aware framework for animal pose estimation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Multi-view pose estimation tracks an animal's body joints from several cameras at once, a key tool for measuring behavior in the lab. Labeled data for training is scarce, and current methods report poor uncertainty estimates.

The team combines new training and post-processing techniques to work well with few labels. They then distill the result, training a smaller model to copy the full system's behavior. Distillation keeps the gains while making the estimator faster and simpler to run. The framework also reports how unsure it is, so researchers can tell which tracked poses to trust.
arxiv-2510-10303:
Jeanine Van Order gives new proofs of a celebrated formula linking heights of points on elliptic curves to L-functions, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Gross-Zagier formula expresses such heights through central derivative values of Rankin-Selberg L-functions. Her proofs realize those values as sums of automorphic Green's functions, built through regularized theta lifts. One proof brings in arithmetic Hirzebruch-Zagier divisors on a product of modular curves, viewed as a Hilbert modular surface.

She then describes applications to the refined Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture. Through these calculations, she also lays out known and conjectural relations between central derivative values of these L-functions and the Fourier coefficients of certain half integral weight forms. The paper ties together explicit height formulas, deep conjectures about elliptic curves, and the Fourier data of special modular forms.
arxiv-2510-10403:
Alice Lin proves a finiteness theorem about heights of motives in this 2025 arXiv paper. A height is a number that measures the arithmetic complexity of an object. Kato and Koshikawa had extended the classical Faltings height from abelian varieties to motives, which are broader building blocks of algebraic geometry, using integral p-adic Hodge theory. Lin asks how these heights behave across an isogeny class, a family of motives linked by special maps.

Assuming the adelic Mumford-Tate conjecture, a widely believed statement about symmetries of these objects, she proves a finiteness property for these heights. Notably, the motives in the family need not be defined over one shared number field. This widens an earlier theorem by Kisin and Mocz on Faltings heights across isogeny classes of abelian varieties.
arxiv-2510-10503:
Kanishkha Jaisankar and Sunidhi Tandel turn instruction tuned language models into planners for self driving cars, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Planning future motion in complex traffic is a core problem for autonomous driving. Newer methods let large language models reason about driving scenes, but it is unclear whether they capture how humans actually think behind the wheel. The team's framework, Align2Act, aims to make model planning both readable and human aligned.

They derive driving instructions from human reasoning patterns, such as anticipating hazards and yielding near intersections, and from traffic rules like stopping at red lights. A module called Align2ActChain then guides step by step reasoning that produces both an explanation and a trajectory. They test the system on the real world nuPlan closed loop benchmark, in its Test14-random setting. There it improved planning quality and human likeness over prior approaches.
arxiv-2510-10603:
WenTao Liu and three co-authors test whether evolution can replace gradients for training large language models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Standard training uses gradient based optimizers such as Adam. These demand high memory GPUs, and they require every operation in the network to be differentiable, which rules out many designs. The team's method, EA4LLM, instead uses evolutionary algorithms, which improve populations of candidate solutions without gradients.

They report the first check of full parameter optimization by evolution starting from the pretraining stage. Their experiments span models from half a billion to 32 billion parameters. The tests yield key insights into when evolutionary search can optimize neural networks well. The work challenges the common assumption that gradient based training is the only viable route, and it may cut training costs for groups with modest resources.
arxiv-2510-10703:
Xiangyu Wang and three co-authors improve how language models solve logic problems by choosing the right formal language for each one, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A common strategy translates a word problem into a symbolic language, then lets a solver finish the job. Success depends heavily on the translation. Different symbolic languages suit different problems: first order logic handles syllogisms and quantifiers well, while Boolean satisfiability fits constraint problems.

The team claims, and verifies, that each problem has its own optimal symbolic language. Their method lets the language model first select among first order logic, logic programming, and Boolean satisfiability. It then translates the problem and calls the matching solver. On a mixed benchmark dataset, the adaptive method reached 96 percent accuracy, improving by 25 percent over the best single language approach. It significantly beat both fixed language translation and random selection.
arxiv-2510-10903:
Shuanghao Bai and twenty co-authors survey the whole field of robot manipulation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Manipulation, getting robots to handle objects, is a core challenge of embodied intelligence. It demands seamless integration of perception, planning, and control in messy, unstructured environments. The survey covers foundational background and organizes benchmarks and datasets by task. It then proposes a unified taxonomy of existing methods.

The authors widen the usual split between high level planning and low level control. Planning now spans language, code, motion, affordance, and 3D representations. For control, they offer a new taxonomy of learning based methods organized by training paradigm, including input modeling, latent learning, and policy learning. They add the first dedicated taxonomy of bottlenecks, covering data collection, utilization, and generalization. A review of real world applications closes the survey, which aims to serve newcomers as a roadmap and experienced researchers as a structured reference.
arxiv-2510-11503:
Experts plan with deep search, but everyday intelligence shows itself when someone faces a completely new problem and still judges sensibly whether it is fair, fun, or worth attempting. Katherine M. Collins and a large team of collaborators study that first-encounter reasoning in this 2025 arXiv cognitive science paper. Their testbed is novice gameplay: people playing two-player board games they have never seen, or evaluating games they have not yet played at all.

The team explains human behavior with a computational model called the Intuitive Gamer, built on fast, flat, goal-directed simulation: very few stochastic samples, simple goal heuristics, and no deep search. In large studies with over a thousand participants and 121 mostly novel games, the model quantitatively captured human judgments and decisions across experience levels, and it beat compute-intensive expert models. The authors suggest such mechanisms could inform more human-like AI.
arxiv-2510-11703:
Yolanda G. C. Frensch leads a very large team confirming two gas giant planets around small, cool stars. Their 2025 arXiv paper opens the GATOS program, a survey of giant planets crossing low-mass stars first spotted by the TESS space telescope. Such giants are rare outcomes of planet formation, so each well-measured case helps test how planets form. The team combined TESS light curves with precise velocity measurements from the HARPS and NIRPS spectrographs.

One planet, TOI-3288 b, is a hot Jupiter about twice Jupiter's mass. It circles a K-type star in under a day and a half. The second, TOI-4666 b, is a warm Jupiter of roughly seven-tenths of Jupiter's mass. It orbits an M dwarf in just under three days. Looking across the known population, the team also finds that later, smaller stars host lighter giant planets than early M dwarfs do.
arxiv-2510-11903:
Rizal Fathony and six colleagues argue that models of user behavior are missing half the picture. User events come in two kinds: personal events, one person's actions in sequence, and relational events, interactions between two users. Sequence models handle the first kind, graph models the second, and the two camps rarely meet. Their 2025 arXiv paper supplies the missing common ground.

The team releases a collection of public datasets that explicitly contain both event types, together with prediction tasks built on them. They also propose a unified formalization covering sequences and relations in one language. Experiments show that models which use both kinds of events outperform those restricted to one. The results also expose clear headroom: today's methods capture only part of the joint signal. By publishing the data and code, the authors invite the field to close that gap. Applications range from e-commerce and finance to cybersecurity.
arxiv-2510-12203:
Federrath and Offner review recent progress in computer simulations of turbulence and star formation, in a 2025 arXiv astrophysics paper. Turbulent gas flows shape how stars are born inside clouds, but modeling them demands enormous computing power. The review gathers the current state of the field for readers entering the field or comparing methods.

The authors first survey the most widely used simulation codes and what each does well. They then examine how the highest resolution magnetohydrodynamic simulations are achieved, where magnetohydrodynamics is the study of charged fluids in magnetic fields, and discuss limits set by numerical viscosity and resistivity. Later sections cover gravity, star particles, and feedback from jets, winds, heat, ionization, and supernovae. The review closes with radiation hydrodynamics methods and new schemes for cosmic ray transport, which link small scale star formation to galaxy evolution.
arxiv-2510-12303:
Kaposi and Xie define a minimal substitution calculus for type theory and relate it to the standard account, in a 2025 arXiv logic paper. Type theory can be cast as a generalised algebraic theory. That yields a notion of model and presents the syntax as an initial model. Most such accounts, such as categories with families, rest on parallel substitution, where many variables are replaced at once.

Their calculus includes only single substitutions and single weakenings, under eight equations. Four equations say how variables are substituted, and four more on types are needed to typecheck the rest. For a theory with dependent function spaces and a hierarchy of universes, they prove the two syntaxes coincide. They compare this to combinatory calculus versus lambda calculus: the leaner calculus admits more models, yet the syntaxes coincide.
arxiv-2510-12603:
Chen and colleagues let multimodal models reason silently in latent space, mixing visual and textual thought without writing steps out, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Multimodal reasoning improves answers by adding intermediate steps, and recent methods weave images into those steps. But explicit vision text reasoning needs laborious annotations and slows inference down considerably.

Their method represents each reasoning step by two implicit parts: latent text, the model's hidden states from the previous stage, and latent vision, a set of selected picture embeddings. A progressive multi stage training strategy teaches models to perform these latent steps. On two reasoning benchmarks the method raised accuracy by several percent on average over existing approaches. It also ran more than five times faster, since no explicit reasoning text is generated. The authors present latent reasoning as a way to keep the benefits of multimodal thought while dropping its annotation and latency costs.
arxiv-2510-13003:
Xiong and Xie modify a popular fine-tuning method so it stops erasing pretrained knowledge in this 2025 arXiv paper. Low-Rank Adaptation, or LoRA, teaches a language model new tasks through small updates to frozen weights. Those updates can interfere with the dominant singular directions, the weight patterns carrying essential pretrained knowledge. That causes catastrophic forgetting.

Their variant, OPLoRA, decomposes each frozen weight matrix and forces updates to live entirely in the space orthogonal to its top singular directions. It uses projections from both sides. They prove this exactly preserves the leading singular triples, giving a guarantee for knowledge retention, and they add a metric measuring how much any update aligns with dominant directions. Across commonsense reasoning, mathematics, and code generation tests on two open models, OPLoRA significantly reduced forgetting while keeping task performance competitive.
arxiv-2510-13603:
Mahatha and a large collaboration explain a first-order phase transition in the layered material tantalum ditelluride. Their 2025 arXiv paper studies charge order in the 1T-prime phase of this transition metal dichalcogenide. First-order transitions jump sharply, and their microscopic drivers often stay murky. The team finds two rival charge patterns fighting for control.

At high temperature, an incommensurate precursor order appears, its wave pattern slightly off the lattice grid. It competes with fluctuating tantalum trimer bonding states at a different wave pattern. The low-temperature commensurate order, by contrast, seems driven by local chemical bonding between sites. Lattice calculations spot an unstable vibration mode tied to the precursor pattern. Phenomenological theory then frames the sharp transition as a contest between two order parameters. One springs from Fermi surface nesting, the other from local bonding.
arxiv-2510-13803:
Dam and Darwish propose a cheap way to test the equivalence principle on cosmic scales using how galaxies group. Their 2025 arXiv paper exploits consistency relations, exact ties between clustering stats in standard gravity. If the principle fails, different galaxy types would fall differently in the same field of gravity. That failure leaves a telltale mark in squeezed three-point stats.

The authors show the breach equals a sign-flipping wobble in the cross-power spectrum of two tracers. Reading that wobble with quadratic tools is far cheaper than full bispectrum work. They apply the tool to a forecast like the DESI survey. Adding mildly nonlinear scales keeps the method as sharp as the exhaustive approach. The forecast pins down the overall size of any breach of the principle. Surveys already running can adopt the tool without new data. A long-held belief of cosmology thus becomes testable with current surveys.
arxiv-2510-13903:
Rizvi-Martel and co-authors map when talking actually helps teams of language model agents reason, using theory plus controlled experiments. Their 2025 arXiv paper analyses multi-agent systems that split long problems among cooperating models. Chain-of-thought in one model degrades as contexts and complexity grow. Whether extra agents and messages truly add power lacked principled answers.

Their framework measures expressivity for three task families: state tracking, recall, and multi-hop reasoning. Bounds emerge for how many agents exact solutions require at each problem size. Communication quantity and structure get their own trade-off curves against agent count. Some regimes show communication is provably beneficial, others expose hard limits. Starved bandwidth or too few agents makes certain tasks impossible regardless of cleverness. Synthetic benchmark experiments with pretrained models confirm the predicted trade-offs. Designers gain principled guidance for scaling multi-agent reasoning systems.
arxiv-2510-14003:
Maksym Luz and Mikhail Moklyachuk study how to estimate unknown values of a random process when only its past has been observed, in this paper on extrapolation. The process they treat has stationary increments, meaning the statistical pattern of its changes repeats over time even though the process itself wanders. The hosted text is their article from the journal Mathematics and Statistics, circulated here as a 2025 arXiv entry.

The authors consider optimal estimation of quantities built by averaging the process against a chosen weight function. When the spectral density, the fingerprint describing which frequencies carry the process's energy, is known exactly, they give formulas for the error and for the best linear estimator. When the density is not known, they take a robust minimax approach. They identify least favorable densities, the worst cases within allowed families. Estimates then stay reliable even under uncertainty about the true spectrum.
arxiv-2510-14203:
Ryo Masumura and co-authors propose recognizing two personality frameworks together, the classic Big Five and the newer HEXACO model, from video of a person introducing themselves, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Apparent personality recognition, judging how someone comes across rather than who they truly are, has almost always targeted the Big Five. HEXACO's Honesty-Humility trait, linked to vengefulness and social dominance, stayed unstudied in this setting.

Their key advance is joint modeling: a single system optimizes recognition of both frameworks at once, exploiting the relationships between Big Five and HEXACO traits that machine learning had not clarified. Experiments on a self-introduction video data set, using sound, image, and language cues together, show that the method can recognize both the Big Five and HEXACO traits. The authors expect that reading multimodal human behavior improves when the two frameworks' traits are used jointly.
arxiv-2510-14303:
Ziye Xia and Sergei Ospichev use small language models, guided by a knowledge graph, to mine academic papers for the conceptual pathways that lead to innovation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. With publication volumes exploding, scientists struggle to track new findings, and existing databases match papers by similarity without exploring how key concepts connect to one another.

Working from the OpenAlex open knowledge graph, the authors analyze nearly eight thousand open papers from Novosibirsk State University. They discover that the distribution patterns of key concept paths correlate strongly with both innovation points and rare conceptual routes. Their method uses prompt engineering with small language models to extract key concepts and innovation points precisely. It wraps the models in an agent constrained by the knowledge graph to keep the analysis accurate. Fine-tuning Qwen and DeepSeek models on the task brought significant accuracy improvements. The resulting models are publicly available.
arxiv-2510-14503:
Andrejs Sorstkins, Omer Tariq, and Muhammad Bilal propose teaching reinforcement learning agents to avoid irreversible mistakes, in this 2025 arXiv paper. They measure how reversible each action is, and roll back the ones that fail. Value-based agents are vulnerable to overestimating actions, and in irreversible environments a step can end an episode or worse.

Their framework learns a score for each state-action pair. It estimates the likelihood of returning to the state within a fixed horizon. The score folds into the temporal-difference penalty, making the value function reversibility-aware. A rollback operator watches for actions whose return falls below their value beyond a threshold. The agent is then penalized and returned to the preceding state instead of progressing. This interrupts doomed trajectories. Tests in the CliffWalking domain, where one misstep plunges the agent off a cliff, show the method improving safety and stability.
arxiv-2510-15103:
Jessy Lin, working with Luke Zettlemoyer and colleagues at Meta and Berkeley, tackles the problem of teaching language models new facts without erasing old ones. Their 2025 arXiv paper calls this failure catastrophic forgetting, and it happens because ordinary training updates weights shared by every task. The team instead updates only sparsely used memory slots inside special memory layers.

Their method, sparse memory finetuning, changes just the memory slots that a new fact strongly activates compared with pretraining use. On two question answering tests, the approach learned fresh knowledge while forgetting far less than standard methods. Accuracy on earlier questions fell only about 11 percent, against drops of 89 percent for full finetuning and 71 percent for the popular LoRA technique. The authors present sparsity as a promising route toward models that keep learning after deployment.
arxiv-2510-15203:
Mauricio Tejo, Cristian Meza, and Fernando Marmolejo-Ramos connect two traditions for studying how fast people make choices, in this 2025 arXiv paper. One tradition models a decision as a mental quantity drifting until it hits a barrier, which sets the response time. The other uses generalized linear mixed models, a flexible statistical family, but often picks response-time distributions by habit rather than by theory.

The bridge is conditioning: by studying response times separately for each possible answer, the authors show when the drift picture yields two specific distributions, the inverse Gaussian and the gamma. Using those distributions inside the mixed models then lets analysts reason backward from fitted data to the mental process that produced it. Simulations confirmed the link behaves as the theory predicts. The team also applied the method to previously published real choice data and discussed where the approach can be extended.
arxiv-2510-15603:
Mean field games model crowds where each person picks a strategy while watching the whole group. Elisabetta Carlini and Luca Saluzzi published this 2025 arXiv paper on solving such systems in many dimensions. The difficulty is that grid methods grow impossible as dimensions increase, since memory needs explode. The pair build a stepwise scheme that pairs time-stepping tricks with tensor-train decompositions of the solution arrays. Their method cuts memory and computing cost from exponential growth down to polynomial growth in the dimension.

Tests show the scheme reaches its predicted accuracy rates in practice. Memory and running time grow only modestly as dimensions increase. The method also beats plain grid-based versions clearly on accuracy for each second of computing time.
arxiv-2510-15803:
Zahra Arjmandi and Gunho Sohn present a fusion method in a 2025 paper. The method sharpens LiDAR mapping and localisation. This is the SLAM problem behind autonomous navigation. Their module is called INAF. It blends AI with geometric odometry. Odometry tracks movement step by step from laser scans.

INAF adjusts its attention weights as it runs. Feedback from the environment drives the changes. The blend of the two sources adapts to conditions. The team tested the method on the KITTI driving data set. Localisation precision improved. Three-dimensional map quality also improved. The authors say adaptive fusion can strengthen navigation in complex scenes.
arxiv-2511-00003:
Eric Ngondiep offers an unconditionally stable numeric method for a nonlinear Sobolev model with distributed delay, where the delay is spread over a past span rather than fixed at one lag. Time derivatives are approximated by interpolation, while spatial derivatives use finite element approximation, keeping the scheme simple to build. Stability and error estimates are proved in a strong norm equal to the standard energy norm.

Theory shows unconditional stability and fourth-order accuracy in space. Numerical analysis readers get a method whose reliability does not depend on tight step limits. Distributed delay Sobolev models arise in flows with memory, where stability assures are mainly valuable.
arxiv-2511-00103:
Rotem Ezra, Hedi Zisling, and Nimrod Berman introduce FreeSliders, a training-free, modality-agnostic way to steer diffusion models along individual concepts. Concept sliders let users continuously vary one trait, like age or smile, without disturbing other content, but earlier sliders needed per-concept training and architecture-specific tuning. FreeSliders discovers semantic directions through textual contrasts without any training.

Images, audio, and video are all handled by the same approach. Generative media readers get fine-grained control that scales to new concepts and modalities cheaply. Training-free steering matters because the set of traits users want to adjust is open-ended.
arxiv-2511-00603:
Yubo Wang and seven co-authors present EPARA, a framework that squeezes more AI inference out of existing edge hardware. Edge clouds run language models and vision services close to users, but demand keeps rising faster than hardware budgets. EPARA sorts tasks by how sensitive they are to latency and how much GPU power they need, then matches tasks to resources at two levels: per request and per service.

Three parts do the work: an allocator that picks each task's parallel mode, a distributed handler that runs requests, and a state-aware scheduler that refreshes service placement over time. A prototype was tested on edge servers, embedded devices, and microcomputers, running language model and segmentation workloads. Goodput rose to more than double that of prior frameworks on production workloads.
arxiv-2511-00803:
Sohini Guin and a large team report transport measurements on thin films of a copper oxide high temperature superconductor. Such materials host many electronic phases, from the strange pseudogap to the superconducting state itself. The team probes these phases by breaking time reversal symmetry with a magnetic field. The record notes that the paper's central conclusions have since changed greatly.

Without a field, the current and voltage data point to two dimensional superconductivity of a topological kind. With a field applied, a weak antilocalization signal appears before superconductivity, as bound vortex pairs break apart through an intermediate localized phase. In highly disordered films, three dimensional weak localization dominates instead, and superconductivity is fully suppressed.
arxiv-2511-00903:
