louisiana-purchase-treaty-1803:
In 1803 the United States bought the Louisiana Territory from Napoleon's France for fifteen million dollars. The sale covered about 828,000 square miles and doubled the size of the young nation at a stroke. President Jefferson had sent envoys to buy only New Orleans and its port, fearing France might close the Mississippi to American trade.

The treaty text sets out the price, the payment terms, and the rights promised to the people living in the territory. France gave up its great North American colony, and the United States became a continental power. The purchase set the stage for a century of westward expansion, with lasting costs for Native nations.
lucretia-volume-03:
Volume 3 of Lucretia brings Bulwer Lytton's plot near its catastrophe. A chapter called 'The Discovery' shows the schemer Dalibard at work. Lucretia's marriage is near, and her portion must pass from her uncle's executor. Her pride shrinks from meeting the lawyer in her shabby lodging.

Dalibard, her old teacher, has kept back his true designs with masterly art. Now the plot is ripe, and he moves to conduct the fall. A hired carriage, a walk to Primrose Hill, and small plans carry the doom. Lytton tightens the net around his dark heroine. The volume shows evil training bearing its bitter fruit.
margery-gred-a-tale-of-old-nuremberg-vol:
Volume three of Margery turns on a confession to Cousin Maud. Herdegen must be back in Padua before Passion week. The months since worthy Veit Spiesz's burial have been full of meetings. At last Margery tells her cousin all that has happened.

A secret, early, and ill-matched betrothal comes into the light. The worthy lady finds it no light matter to smile on it. Yet she cannot spoil the young folks' present bliss with warnings. Ebers writes the scene with tenderness for all three. Love's mystery, once shared, no longer weighs on their souls. The volume turns the tale toward trial and parting.
marx-theses-feuerbach-1903:
In a Brussels notebook in spring 1845, Marx jotted eleven short theses on the philosopher Feuerbach. Austin Lewis translated them for the 1903 Kerr edition of Engels's book on Feuerbach. The theses run to barely a few pages. Their last line became one of the most quoted sentences in modern thought.

Philosophers, Marx writes, have only interpreted the world; the point is to change it. The other theses attack passive views of human nature and knowledge. Truth, for Marx, proves itself in practice, not in thought alone. These notes mark the birth of his mature outlook. Readers can cross them in minutes and ponder them for years.
maupassant-short-stories-1903:
Guy de Maupassant's Original Short Stories, Volume One gives the McMaster English translations of his early masterpieces. The first volume of the McMaster set opens with Boule de Suif, his debut triumph of 1880. Guy de Maupassant learned his craft under Flaubert, who taught him to find the one exact word.

Boule de Suif, a plump prostitute, shares her food with coach companions who then force her to a Prussian officer. Their gratitude curdles into contempt once she has served their need, in a tale of hypocrisy's anatomy. The Maison Tellier, Two Friends, and Mademoiselle Fifi show his range from brothel comedy to war's quiet horrors in France. Maupassant renders peasants, clerks, and officers with the same cool, exact, and pitying eye for detail throughout. This volume is the right door into the greatest short-story writer of his century.
memoirs-of-napoleon-bonaparte-volume-03:
Volume three of Bourrienne's memoirs holds chapters fifteen to twenty six. The contents page marks the year as 1799 in the main. Chapter fifteen opens in Egypt, with a divan set for each province.

Desaix works in Upper Egypt, and Ibrahim Bey falls at Salehyeh. Disaster at Aboukir and army grumbles fill the chapter heads. Bonaparte's plan for Egypt and a thrust at England stand there too. His scorn for the Directory shows through the intercepted mail he cites. Each province gets seven men to watch its interests, by that order. Crime, village feuds, and news for the chief fall to them.
metchnikoff-nature-man-mitchell-1903:
Elie Metchnikoff was a Russian biologist who won fame for finding phagocytes, the cells that swallow germs in the blood. His Nature of Man, in Mitchell's 1903 translation, turns from microbes to aging, death, and the fear of both. He writes as a scientist facing the end of life.

Metchnikoff argues that old age, as most people live it, is a kind of disease rather than a natural close. He blames harmful microbes in the gut and urges habits that might delay decay. His frank talk about death helped start the modern science of aging. He writes without flinching, and without false comfort.
michelson-light-waves-uses-1903:
Albert Michelson was an American physicist who measured the speed of light with unmatched care. His 1903 book, Light Waves and Their Uses, grew out of public lectures. Michelson later became the first American to win a Nobel Prize in science.

He shows how light waves can measure lengths far too small for any ruler. His interferometer, a tool that splits and rejoins a light beam, could detect shifts of a fraction of a wave. Michelson also reports the famous test that found no 'ether wind,' a result that helped open the way to relativity.
mitchell-history-greenbacks-1903:
Mitchell's History of the Greenbacks, published in 1903, began as his doctoral study at Chicago. The greenbacks were the paper dollars the Union printed to pay for the Civil War, money not backed by gold. Mitchell asked what that experiment did to prices, wages, and the worth of the currency itself.

He tracks the greenback's fall and recovery against gold, and weighs who gained and who lost as its value swung. Farmers, creditors, soldiers, and shopkeepers all felt the swings in different ways. The young scholar's first book became the classic on its subject and is still cited in debates over paper money. It shows monetary history at its most instructive, with a war's finance laid out in hard numbers.
monsieur-madame-and-be-be-volume-03: The third volume completes Gustave Droz's Monsieur, Madame, et Bébé in this English edition. The Project Gutenberg header lists it twelfth in the French Immortals series. Droz's domestic sketches end with the family's story fully told across three volumes. The hosted sample, however, preserves no readable content from the volume itself. It contains only the Gutenberg header, with title, author, and series information. Readers get the volume's identity and set place, but none of its scenes.
montaigne-essays-florio-1603:
Michel de Montaigne wrote his essays in French in the late 1500s, and John Florio made them English in 1603. Florio's was the first English Montaigne, the one Shakespeare read. Montaigne had quit law to write, in his tower, about himself.

He asks, in short pieces, what do I know, and tests each claim. Custom, fear, books, thumbs, and coaches all get his cool gaze. He doubts bold claims and trusts lived trials more than rules. Florio's lush prose gave England a new form, the essay itself. He coined the motto that he himself was his study.
moore-principia-ethica-1903:
G. E. Moore published Principia Ethica in 1903, a work that remade moral philosophy in English. Moore asks what the word good itself means. He argues that good is simple and indefinable, like the color yellow. Defining good by any natural trait, such as pleasure, commits what he calls the naturalistic fallacy.

Moore holds that we know some goods by direct intuition. Friendship and the love of beauty rank highest among them. The book influenced the Bloomsbury circle as well as academic ethics. Its demand for clarity changed how philosophers write. Students still meet its open question argument early in ethics courses.
my-novel-volume-03:
Edward Bulwer-Lytton's third book opens by telling how the tale got its name. Mr. Caxton grants that the novel pleases him so far. His praise stops short at a sermon in the text. The ladies rush to defend Parson Dale at once.

Captain Roland urges Pisistratus to leave quiet Hazeldean behind. Open service in the wide world must come, he says. Pisistratus promises a long view of English life in time. Hall and parsonage form the front scene for now. The volume mixes family talk, satire, and a young author's pride in his growing canvas.
myers-human-personality-1903:
Frederic Myers left his crown work to be printed past his death in Human Personality, out in 1903. Myers was a poet and a chief of the new study of ghosts. He holds that the self we know is just the tip of a vast hid self. That hid part, he claims, can act in trance, dreams, and past the grave.

Years of cases fill two tomes in proof of his scheme. His words for the hid self still shape how we speak of the mind. The book is the most cited text of its field. Its scope awes.
myers-human-personality-vol1-1903:
Frederic W H Myers died before Human Personality and Its Survival of Bodily Death appeared in 1903, and Volume 1 came out after his death. Myers, a founder of the Society for Psychical Research, spent years gathering reports of trance, genius, dreams, and ghosts. He built a large theory from them.

Myers proposed a subliminal self, a hidden part of the mind below normal waking thought. From it, he said, came dreams, automatic writing, and some ghost sightings. Volume 1 sets out that theory and the first body of evidence. The book shaped later study of the unconscious and of whether the mind survives death.
myers-human-personality-vol2-1903:
Volume 2 of Myers's Human Personality and Its Survival of Bodily Death appeared in 1903, after his death. The first volume had set out his theory of the subliminal self. The second volume brought the heaviest evidence: reports of ghosts, trance speech, and messages said to come from the dead.

Chapters sort cases of phantasms of the living and the dead, along with sittings and automatic scripts. Myers argued that some cases pointed past telepathy among the living to survival after death. Critics disputed that leap, but the mass of recorded cases made the book a central text of psychical research for decades.
mysteries-of-paris-volume-03:
Eugene Sue opens his third volume in a notary's office at night. He calls Paris the brain and heart of the land. Its nerves and arteries carry passions, horrors, and loves. This part, called Night, traces threads deep into the city's maze.

One thread starts in 1819 with Sarah Seyton, a widowed countess. Her brother Tom helps her scheme to wed a sovereign. Such plots drive the tale's high and low worlds together. Prince Rodolphe still hunts wrongs in disguise. V1 notes the serial invented the urban mystery and made Sue the most-read novelist of his day.
norris-pit-1903:
Frank Norris died at thirty-two in 1902, and The Pit appeared the next year, in 1903. It completes the arc of his wheat trilogy: The Octopus grew the wheat in California, and The Pit sells it in Chicago. Norris researched the Chicago Board of Trade like a reporter, watching the trading floor for months.

Speculator Curtis Jadwin tries to corner the wheat market, buying until prices bend to his will. The strain invades his marriage to Laura Dearborn, who feels the pit's excitement pulling her husband away. Norris renders the trading floor's roar, panic, and collapse in famous set pieces. The Pit is the great American novel of finance from the age of the trusts.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
The third volume of Penzer's Ocean of Story, issued from 1924, carries Tawney's Kathasaritsagara further into its eighteen books. Somadeva's ocean now runs deep with sorcerers, cursed princes, and cities of the Gandharvas. The tales delight in disguise and recognition, loss and restoration, told at a storyteller's pace.

Penzer, a folklorist, loads the margins with parallels from the Nights, the Panchatantra, and European collections. His edition turned a translation into a comparative treasury of world tale. Tawney's plain, steady English lets the Sanskrit invention shine without strain. Sanskritists and story lovers alike keep the set in use. Volume three is mid-ocean: the shores of the frame are distant, and the stories rule.
openalex-w2055077703:
Manuel Hetzel, Gibson Gideon, Namarola Lote and colleagues checked mosquito net ownership in Papua New Guinea. Their paper appeared in Malaria Journal in 2012. The country ran a huge free net campaign. Two million treated nets were handed out. The goal was high ownership and use.

A national household survey followed the campaign. It covered most provinces of the country. About two thirds of households owned a treated net. Overall use of nets stayed much lower. Children and pregnant women used nets more than others. Village access was the key factor in ownership. People without a net at home almost never used one. Too few nets reached some areas, the authors conclude.
openalex-w2100036903:
Keith Hunley, Michael Dunn, Eva Lindstrom and colleagues tested how genes and languages evolved together in Melanesia. Their paper appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2008. Northern Island Melanesia holds striking diversity of both kinds. Two models could explain matching patterns. One stresses early splits and isolation. The other stresses ongoing exchange between neighbours.

The team gathered gene markers from thirty-three populations. They also coded over a hundred language features. Simulations tested each model's predictions. Exchange had erased clear signs of early splitting. The wider region did not fit simple distance patterns either. One large island's interior fit them strongly, though. Language features crossed group borders less easily than genes.
openalex-w2170677203:
Beth Payne, Jennifer Hutcheon, J. Mark Ansermino, and colleagues published this study in PLoS Medicine in 2014. They built miniPIERS, a simple risk prediction model for pregnant women with high blood pressure disorders in low-resource settings. Pre-eclampsia kills many mothers in poorer countries, and staff need a quick way to spot who is in danger.

Data were gathered prospectively on over two thousand admitted women in five low- and middle-income countries. Signs collected within a day of admission fed a model predicting severe outcomes within two days. The model was checked by resampling its own data and then validated on a separate large cohort from a sister study.
openalex-w2515998503:
Diego Juffe-Bignoli, Thomas M. Brooks, and Stuart H. M. Butchart led a large team behind this 2016 PLoS ONE study. It asks a plain money question: what does global conservation knowledge cost? Groups maintain shared products like the IUCN Red List to guide policy and practice. Yet nobody had documented what building and running them actually costs.

The team costed four products, including the Red List of Threatened Species and Protected Planet. Together they absorbed about one hundred sixty million dollars between 1979 and 2013, plus large amounts of volunteer time. Philanthropy supplied over half the money, and staff costs took nearly three-quarters. Keeping three products running costs about six and a half million dollars a year. The authors estimate far more funding is still needed to complete this knowledge base.
openalex-w2766358903:
Luke Thompson, Jon G. Sanders, and Daniel T. McDonald lead the Earth Microbiome Project Consortium in this 2017 Nature paper. It presents a shared catalogue of microbial life sampled across the whole planet. The project, founded in 2010, pools about one hundred studies using standardized methods. Crowdsourced, open science was the design from the start.

Standard sampling and analysis cut the technical noise that normally swamps biological patterns between studies. The combined dataset dwarfs earlier meta-analyses about a hundredfold in sampling and sequencing depth. With it, the team maps how microbial communities are organized across environments and continents. The catalogue is built as a resource others can keep exploring. It gives microbial ecology a common yardstick, much as reference genomes did for genetics. Questions about diversity that no single study could answer become tractable at this scale.
openalex-w2805924003:
Josiane Fukami, Paula Cerezini, and Mariangela Hungría reviewed the bacterium Azospirillum in AMB Express in 2018. It lives near plant roots and promotes their growth. Its fame began with nitrogen fixation, turning air nitrogen into plant food. It also makes plant hormones, above all an auxin that spurs root growth.

Recent studies credit it with shielding plants from drought, salt, and disease as well. Hormones act as the signals coordinating many of those protections. Disease tolerance runs through induced resistance pathways inside the plant. Stress tolerance, a separate induced path, uses antioxidants and osmotic adjustment. The mini-review gathers these mechanisms under one roof. Knowing them helps farmers use bacterial inoculants for greener farming.
openalex-w3035700103:
Tony Bates, Cristóbal Cobo, Olga Mariño, and Steve Wheeler wrote this editorial in the International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education in 2020. It introduces a special collection asking whether artificial intelligence can transform higher education. The four editors frame the debate for the papers that follow.

Priority went to studies with real evidence on results and practice, rather than pure speculation. The editors also welcomed work on the social and ethical issues that AI in universities raises or could raise. Such issues include fairness, privacy, and the changing role of teachers. The editorial sets out why the question matters now: AI tools are entering classrooms and administration faster than the evidence about their effects can grow.
openalex-w3126160703:
Daniel Taliun, Daniel Harris, Michael Kessler, and colleagues published this study in Nature in 2021. It reports whole-genome sequencing of more than fifty-three thousand people through the TOPMed program in the United States. TOPMed seeks the genetic roots of heart, lung, blood, and sleep disorders.

The program joins more than eighty studies and about a thousand investigators. Its participants are diverse in ethnicity and ancestry, a deliberate contrast to older genome collections. Rare variants make up most human genetic variation and often carry the strongest effects on health. By reading them at this scale, the team built a reference that sharpens the search for disease genes in every population, not only the best studied ones.
openalex-w3206015903:
Jad Adrian Washif, Abdulaziz Farooq, Isabel Krug, and colleagues surveyed athletes about training during COVID-19 lockdowns. Their study appeared in Sports Medicine in 2022. More than twelve thousand athletes, from recreational to world class, answered an online survey in mid-2020. They came from one hundred forty-two countries across six continents, all facing closed gyms and cancelled events.

Most athletes wanted to keep training, and higher-level athletes felt this most strongly. Six in ten judged remote coaching good enough to guide them. Yet fewer than four in ten managed to keep up sport-specific training, such as endurance work or weightlifting. The results show how deeply lockdowns disrupted preparation, even among the most committed athletes.
openalex-w4391925503:
Ken Suzuki, Konstantinos Hatzikotoulas, Lorraine Southam, and colleagues map the genetic drivers of type 2 diabetes in Nature in 2024. The disease develops through many different processes in the body, so patients differ widely. The team combined genome-wide studies covering more than two and a half million people. Over four hundred thousand of them had type 2 diabetes, and about two fifths were not of European ancestry.

By joining the genetic data with single-cell evidence from relevant tissues, the authors separated the disease's routes. They built ancestry-aware risk scores for distinct biological processes. Those scores were then tested against blood vessel complications and disease progression. The work shows how one diagnosis can hide several diseases that may need different prevention and care.
openalex-w7128495003:
Moe Hein, Win Lae Lae Aung, Eaindra Myat Thu, and Ashraful Huda report a difficult muscle-disease case. Their case report appeared in the Juntendo Medical Journal in 2026. A seventy-seven-year-old woman developed progressive weakness in both legs. She also struggled to swallow and lost much weight.

Doctors first suspected statin damage, given her recent muscle breakdown episode. Yet she kept weakening after the statin stopped. Her muscle enzyme levels stayed very high. An antibody linked to autoimmune muscle disease tested positive. Scans showed widespread muscle changes. The case illustrates the overlap problem between polymyositis and inclusion body myositis. Telling them apart matters, because their treatments and outlooks differ greatly.
openalex-w7208836903:
Francisco Bastos Cavalcante Sobrinho leads a team that tests the safe use of potassium sorbate, a food keep-fresh salt. They test it pure, and in shop goods that bear it. By world test rules, they gauged short and long harm in rats and mice. They checked shop mixes for harm to genes, blood, and guts, with eyes on the liver and the reins, and on blood traits.

Pure, the salt brought no deaths and no true shift in weight at the lots tried. Its kill lot sits past the range tried. The shop goods showed no gene harm in cell and beast tests. Some flags rose, though: falls in some blood cell counts, shifts in liver work, and a rise in a mark men watch for rein strain. Shifts in rein flesh came too. The study splits the keep salt from the mixes that bear it.
openalex-w7212174803:
Beatriz Borges Brambilla leads a team on the children who watch violence at home, and are too often missed. When a man beats a woman in a home with kids, the young are called side victims, or not named at all. The team reads the theme through a feminist lens. Age, they argue, is a mark of rank in the home, much as sex is. They test laws, plans, and short tales told by the young.

To watch such harm, they hold, is to live a breach of one's rights. It is not a soft or side event. The child takes in fear, guilt, and pain that shape a life. Yet aid plans and courts treat the child as a prop in the mother's case. The authors call for care that hears the young as full selves, caught in the same web as the mother.
openalex-w7212183003:
Marco Antonio Franco Cancado leads a team that asks if low vitamin D feeds a grave jaw disease tied to some drugs. The disease kills jaw bone in people on drugs that slow bone loss or block blood growth. Vitamin D steers bone change and the immune reply. A lack of it can slow the mouth's skin seal and heal rate. The team ran a full search of four databases for past work.

Nine studies fed the final take. People with low blood levels of the vitamin faced more risk of poor bone heal. They also faced more risk that the jaw disease would start or grow worse. The link is not proof of cause, the authors grant. But the tests are cheap and the stakes are high. A quick check of vitamin D may earn a place in the care plan for those on such drugs.
openalex-w7213416303:
Bruna Emily Faustino Baptista and co-authors review how reading and writing can be rebuilt in grades three to five. Their 2026 review searches the SciELO Brazil collection for 2016 to 2026. It follows PRISMA guidance and includes sixteen studies on healing, reinforcement, and intervention.

Most interventions targeted reading comprehension and fluency. Structured classroom programmes and separate recovery sessions both showed in the published work. Diagnosis stood out as the proper starting point for any plan. Recovery, the authors conclude, does not mean repeating earlier teaching. It means reorganizing learning around each pupil's specific gaps, with follow-up and monitoring.
openalex-w7213416903:
Sara Galvão Vieira Pegorário and co-authors review the link between family life and anxiety in teenagers. Their 2026 narrative review draws on psychology and mental health literature. Adolescence, they note, brings intense physical, emotional, and social change that can raise vulnerability to anxiety.

Poor communication, frequent conflict, and excessive psychological control appear as risk factors. So does low family cohesion. By contrast, emotional support, open dialogue, and strong affectionate bonds protect young people's mental health. The authors avoid simple cause-and-effect claims and treat the family as a complex system. Understanding that system, they argue, should guide prevention and clinical help for teenagers.
openalex-w7213493203:
Evandro Pinheiro Almeida Rios and co-authors weigh stopping versus continuing beta-blocker drugs after a heart attack. Their 2026 integrative review covers patients whose heart pumping function was preserved or only mildly reduced. Searches in August 2026 covered PubMed, Embase, and a trials register.

Five studies formed the synthesis: two randomized trials and three observational studies. Observational work found no rise in death or major combined outcomes after stopping. Trial results disagreed with each other, partly for method reasons. A possible rise in ischaemic events after one heart attack type was flagged in exploratory work. No consistent rise in death was seen, supporting decisions tailored to each patient.
openalex-w7213529703: Ana Beatriz Nunes Santos e Silva Barroso leads a team on dental implants in patients with diabetes. Their 2026 article, in a Brazilian journal, notes that diabetes can harm bone metabolism, immune response, and the bonding of an implant to bone, above all when blood sugar control is poor. Small regulatory molecules called microRNAs are examined as candidate markers of that bonding process, known as osseointegration. The sample supports the subject and rationale only, so this summary stays at that level.
openalex-w7213533703:
Lauane Lourenço da Silva and colleagues reflect on falling childhood vaccination coverage in Brazil. Their 2026 experience report comes from a nursing student's practice in a family health unit in inland Minas Gerais, in June 2025. Vaccine hesitation, misinformation, and science denial frame the account.

During a collective health course placement, the student found a child behind on vaccines. The team planned an active search and made a home visit to update the schedule. Reception, health education, and record keeping were done jointly with the unit team. The authors call for stronger education on immunization and note the nurse's leading role in managing such work.
openalex-w7213790703:
Filipe Ribas de Aguiar and co-authors trace continuing teacher schooling policy in Porto Alegre, Brazil. Their 2026 documentary study covers the current municipal administration, 2025 to 2026. Sources include legal and institutional documents, public statements, social media, and press reports, read through the policy cycle approach.

Public actors, third-sector groups, think tanks, and advocacy movements push ideas of efficiency, innovation, and results-based management, the authors find. Those ideas reappear in new training initiatives run by the city. Responsibility for teacher formation is being recentralized after a dispersed period. Qualification investment arrives joined to managerial accountability and tighter regulation of teaching work, a pairing the authors treat critically.
openalex-w7214050803:
Beatriz Barbosa Montanher leads a study, in English in its catalog title, of smoking among dental students in central-western Paraná, Brazil. Their 2026 cross-sectional study used a structured questionnaire and a periodontal clinical exam. One hundred twenty-one students at one university took part.

About a quarter reported current tobacco or nicotine use. Among those users, electronic smoking devices predominated heavily. Smoking tied significantly to bad breath, and longer smoking history tracked deeper gum probing, above all in lower front teeth. Gum changes appeared in half of those examined, mostly localized gum inflammation. Students knew smoking risks well, especially oral cancer, a knowledge-behaviour gap the authors leave visible.
openalex-w7214092903:
Suelen Mariana Henk, as the sample byline gives her name, examines when the limitation clock starts in Brazilian civil law. Her single-author 2026 article works through the actio nata theory in its objective and subjective forms. The 2002 Civil Code chose the objective rule: time runs from the violation of the right.

Germany's 2001 reform, mixing short periods, knowability, and an objective ceiling, offers a comparison. Brazil's Superior Court of Justice admits the subjective view only exceptionally, when the holder could not know of the injury, Henk shows. A 2025 bill would write the subjective rule into law for non-contractual liability, with a ten-year outer limit.
openalex-w7214223603:
Marcelene Alves Duarte and four fellow educators described a school project on Black Consciousness in Anchieta, Brazil, in a 2026 article. Working with young elementary students in five rural schools, the team built lessons around Afro-Brazilian culture, identity, and respect for racial diversity. Their action-research project aimed to start anti-racist education in the earliest school years.

Activities mixed story reading, music, games, art, and group conversation, with children as active participants rather than an audience. The project also matched global goals on inclusive education and reduced inequality. The authors report that this work helped build a school culture where children felt represented, respected, and valued in their identities, and where racism could be named and opposed.
openalex-w7220980603:
João Leonir Mantovani and Rozineide Iraci Pereira da Silva report a school project in Brusque, Santa Catarina, where games carried a geography course on climate. In 2025, twenty seventh- and eighth-grade students joined a Weather Observers Club at their municipal school, and the teachers later wrote up the experience for a 2026 article.

Students gathered weather data, built climate charts and models, and interviewed professionals, then designed their own educational games as the final task. The authors observed more student initiative, creativity, teamwork, and engagement once pupils became game makers. They conclude that games can serve geography teaching well, provided teachers plan carefully and guide the play rather than leaving it as free time.
original-short-stories-volume-03:
Thirteen tales fill volume three of Maupassant's Original Short Stories in English translation, among them The Parricide, Bertha, The Patron, A Sale, and The Relic. The subjects swing from crime and inheritance to the small humiliations of provincial life, in the compressed style that made Maupassant the master of the form.

Miss Harriet, the opening tale, begins with seven travelers in a carriage climbing the cliff road from Étretat at daybreak, bound for the ruins of Tancarville. Half asleep in the autumn dawn, the women nod over the stubble fields while larks sing above them. The red sun rises and the country wakes — a quiet, painterly start before Maupassant turns the party's attention to the English spinster of the title.
paul-clifford-volume-03:
Volume 3 of Paul Clifford opens at chapter twelve with a moonlit ambush. Ten miles from Warlock, two masked horsemen wait among dark trees, one priming a great pistol. The highwaymen Augustus and Ned grumble and joke while they watch for travellers, and Tomlinson moralizes over the night's work.

The scene has the colour of the old road, foam on the bit and a drinking song hummed too loud. Paul's career on the highway runs through these chapters. Lytton mixes adventure with satire, letting his robbers talk like philosophers between robberies.
paulus-aegineta-seven-books-adams-vol-03:
Francis Adams closed his English Paul of Aegina with this third volume in 1847. Paul of Aegina, the seventh-century Greek doctor, ends his Seven Books with the part that made him famous: surgery. Tables of weights and measures and a general index complete the Adams edition.

Paul describes operations for stones, hernias, cataracts, and war wounds, with the tools each one needs. His surgical book was the best of the ancient world and was mined by Arabic and European surgeons for centuries. With this volume the whole medical encyclopedia stands in English. It is the bridge by which Greek medicine reached the schools of Islam and of the West.
pelham-volume-03:
Volume 3 of Pelham opens on the hero's last evening in Paris. Pelham attends a small party at the house of the Duchesse de B—, where most of the company is royal. A prince remembers his presentation of a month before and converses with him in excellent English, with grace and singular fascination.

Pelham studies the great man's dignity, soft eyes, and slight figure, judging how he would strike as a private person. The chapters show the hero moving easily at the summit of French society. Beneath the compliments, the novel keeps measuring rank against real worth.
plaw-108-1-2003: Public Law 108-1 is the first law of the 108th Congress, and it is about unemployment checks. It extends the Temporary Extended Unemployment Compensation Act of 2002 for five months, letting agreements under that program cover weeks of unemployment ending before June 1, 2003. It also gives a transition period to people still drawing benefits when the program ends.
plaw-108-10-2003: The Do-Not-Call Implementation Act (Public Law 108-10) pays for the national do-not-call registry. It authorizes the Federal Trade Commission to set and collect fees, enough to run and enforce the registry under its Telemarketing Sales Rule, for fiscal years 2003 through 2007. Telemarketers' fees, in other words, fund the list that lets households refuse telemarketers' calls.
plaw-108-100-2003:
The Check Clearing for the 21st Century Act (Public Law 108-100), known as Check 21, changed how American banks handle paper checks. Its purpose is to let banks truncate checks, stopping the paper early, by authorizing substitute checks, printed paper copies that carry the legal weight of the original.

The act protects the people on the receiving end. It sets warranties and indemnities for substitute checks and gives consumers and banks expedited recredit procedures when something goes wrong. It encourages electronic innovation in the check system without forcing anyone to accept checks in electronic form.
plaw-108-101-2003:
Public Law 108-101 awards a congressional gold medal, after his death, to Jackie Robinson, and expresses the sense of Congress that the nation should keep a day in his honor. The medal recognizes his many contributions to the country.

The findings trace his life. He was born on January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia, the youngest of five children. At UCLA he starred in football, basketball, baseball, and track. In 1947 the Brooklyn Dodgers signed him. He became the first Black player in Major League Baseball. Congress calls his signing one of the most significant moments in American sports history.
plaw-108-102-2003: Public Law 108-102 is a small shift inside the Government Printing Office. It amends title 44 to transfer authority over the people who prepare the indexes of the Congressional Record to the Public Printer, the head of the printing office. The Congressional Record is Congress's daily journal, and its indexes make the record searchable.
plaw-108-103-2003: Public Law 108-103 redesignates the post office at 48 South Broadway in Nyack, New York. Its new name tells a story: the Edward O'Grady, Waverly Brown, Peter Paige Post Office Building. The three men were a Nyack police sergeant, an officer, and a Brink's guard killed in the 1981 Brink's robbery in Nyack. The renaming was approved in October 2003.
plaw-108-104-2003: Public Law 108-104 is a continuing appropriations resolution for fiscal year 2004. Approved October 31, 2003, it amends the earlier stopgap, Public Law 108-84, by moving its end date to November 7, 2003. Its second section makes further changes to that law, keeping agencies funded while the year's spending bills were finished. It was one in a chain of stopgaps that fall.
plaw-108-105-2003:
The Partial-Birth Abortion Ban Act of 2003 (Public Law 108-105) prohibits the procedure commonly known as partial-birth abortion. It was the first federal law to ban a specific abortion procedure, and Congress built its case in a long findings section.

Congress declares that a moral, medical, and ethical consensus exists against the practice. The findings define the procedure in detail, describing a delivery carried out until the child's head or trunk has passed a stated point, followed by an act meant to kill the child. Supporters and opponents argued over those findings in court for years afterward.
plaw-108-106-2003:
Public Law 108-106 is the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act for Defense and for the Reconstruction of Iraq and Afghanistan, 2004. Passed in November 2003, months after the invasion of Iraq, it pays war costs outside the regular budget for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004.

Title I, National Security, opens with military personnel accounts. The Army alone receives an additional twelve point nine billion dollars for personnel, with further sums for the Navy, Marine Corps, and the other services. The act's second great subject, named in its title, is reconstruction money for Iraq and Afghanistan.
plaw-108-107-2003: Public Law 108-107 is a continuing appropriations resolution for fiscal year 2004. Approved November 7, 2003, it amends the stopgap law, Public Law 108-84, by moving its end date to November 21, 2003. It also moves a matching deadline in the 2003 defense appropriations act to the same date. It is one of several such extensions passed that fall.
plaw-108-108-2003:
The Department of the Interior and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2004 (Public Law 108-108) funds the Interior Department and related agencies for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004. Title I opens, as the year before, with the Bureau of Land Management.

The Bureau's management of lands and resources account pays for protection, use, improvement, surveying, and maintenance across the public lands. The act follows the same course as the 2002 law in this set, working through the department's bureaus and the related agencies that share its bill each year. It passed in November 2003, after the usual fall stopgaps.
plaw-108-109-2003:
The National Cemetery Expansion Act of 2003 (Public Law 108-109) orders the Secretary of Veterans Affairs to set up six new national cemeteries within four years. National cemeteries are the burial grounds where veterans may be laid to rest with public honor. The older ones were filling up.

The act names the areas for the new cemeteries. The first named is the southeast of Pennsylvania. The sites were ones the Secretary had picked as the most fitting. The act works under chapter 24 of title 38, the law for the National Cemetery Administration. The six sites were meant to serve veterans for decades to come.
plaw-108-11-2003:
The Emergency Wartime Supplemental Appropriations Act, 2003 (Public Law 108-11) was Congress's first big war funding bill of the Iraq War, approved April 16, 2003, as the invasion unfolded. It provides emergency money for the fiscal year ending September 30, 2003, outside the regular appropriations cycle.

Title I is labeled War-Related Appropriations, and its first chapter reaches even the Agriculture Department, adding one hundred ten million dollars for buildings and facilities and funding food aid grants. Later chapters carry the main military costs of the war's opening phase and its immediate aftermath. Supplemental bills like this one are how wars get paid for mid-year.
plaw-108-110-2003: Public Law 108-110 redesignates the post office at 120 East Ritchie Avenue in Marceline, Missouri, as the Walt Disney Post Office Building. Marceline was Disney's boyhood hometown, the small town he later said shaped his imagination. The redesignation was approved in November 2003, and the name is now the facility's official one. The act is two sections long.
plaw-108-111-2003: Public Law 108-111 designates the Postal Service facility at 440 South Orange Blossom Trail in Orlando, Florida, as the Arthur 'Pappy' Kennedy Post Office. Kennedy was an Orlando civil rights leader and city commissioner. The naming, approved in November 2003, makes his name the official one in federal laws, maps, and records. The act runs to two sections.
plaw-108-112-2003: Under Public Law 108-112, the post office at 1905 West Blue Heron Boulevard in West Palm Beach, Florida, is designated the Judge Edward Rodgers Post Office Building. Rodgers was a Palm Beach County judge and a local civil rights figure. Congress approved the naming in November 2003. The act follows the usual two-section form for postal namings.
plaw-108-113-2003: Public Law 108-113 names the Postal Service facility at 1101 Colorado Street in Boulder City, Nevada, the Bruce Woodbury Post Office Building. Woodbury was a longtime Clark County commissioner from Boulder City. The designation was approved in November 2003 and binds all federal references to the building. The short act holds the designation and a references section.
plaw-108-114-2003: Public Law 108-114 designates the post office at 2300 Redondo Avenue in Long Beach, California, as the Stephen Horn Post Office Building. Horn was the congressman who had represented the Long Beach area through the 1990s. The naming was approved in November 2003, shortly after his time in office ended. The act follows the standard two-part form.
plaw-108-115-2003: In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, the Postal Service facility at 2001 East Willard Street became the Robert A. Borski Post Office Building under Public Law 108-115. Borski had represented Northeast Philadelphia in Congress for twenty years. The designation, approved in November 2003, fixes his name on the facility in federal records. The law's references section carries the name into later records.
plaw-108-116-2003: Public Law 108-116 names the post office at 1210 Highland Avenue in Duarte, California, the Francisco A. Martinez Flores Post Office. The designation was approved in November 2003. As with the other postal laws, a references section makes the name the one used in federal laws, maps, and records. It changes the facility's name only, nothing about its service.
plaw-108-117-2003: Public Law 108-117 designates the facility at 339 Hicksville Road in Bethpage, New York, as the Brian C. Hickey Post Office Building. Hickey was a New York City firefighter from Bethpage who died in the September 11, 2001 attacks. Congress approved the naming in November 2003. The act pairs the designation with the standard references rule.
plaw-108-118-2003: Public Law 108-118 names the Postal Service facility at 10701 Abercorn Street in Savannah, Georgia, the J.C. Lewis, Jr. Post Office Building. The designation was approved in November 2003. Its references section makes the Lewis name official wherever federal laws, maps, or records mention the facility. Like its sister namings, it runs to two short sections.
plaw-108-119-2003: Public Law 108-119 designates the post office at 141 Weston Street in Hartford, Connecticut, as the Barbara B. Kennelly Post Office Building. Kennelly had represented Hartford in Congress for nearly two decades. The naming was approved in November 2003, and federal records now use her name for the building. The two-section law pairs the designation with a references rule.
plaw-108-12-2003: Public Law 108-12 rescues a stalled power project in Illinois. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission license for project number 11214 had been surrendered, and the deadline to start construction had run out. The act lets the Commission reinstate the license as of the surrender date and extend the start-of-construction period, if the builder shows good faith and due diligence.
plaw-108-120-2003: Public Law 108-120 names the post office at 135 East Olive Avenue in Burbank, California, the Bob Hope Post Office Building. Hope, the comedian who entertained troops for decades, had died that July at age one hundred, and Burbank was his longtime home base. The designation was approved in November 2003. The act is two sections long.
plaw-108-121-2003:
The Military Family Tax Relief Act of 2003 (Public Law 108-121) gives tax breaks aimed at service members and their families during the Iraq War. It amends both title 10 and the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.

Its opening title works on tax equity for military personnel, including excluding gain on the sale of a principal home by members of the uniformed services and the Foreign Service. The act also raises the death gratuity paid when a service member dies and excludes that gratuity from gross income, so grieving families are not taxed on it.
plaw-108-122-2003:
Public Law 108-122 is a joint resolution recognizing the Dr. Samuel D. Harris National Museum of Dentistry in Baltimore, Maryland, an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution, as the official national museum of dentistry in the United States.

Congress found the museum an international resource whose mission is teaching people, especially children, the history of dentistry and the value of good oral care. It calls the museum the most comprehensive of its kind in the nation. It sits on the University of Maryland campus in Baltimore, home of the world's first dental school, founded in 1840.
plaw-108-123-2003: The Federal Employee Student Loan Assistance Act (Public Law 108-123) lets federal agencies help pay off their workers' student loans. It is a recruiting tool for the government. The act raises the yearly cap on such repayments. It goes from six thousand dollars to ten thousand. The lifetime cap per worker rises from forty thousand dollars to sixty thousand.
plaw-108-124-2003: Public Law 108-124 designates the Postal Service facility at 1601-1 Main Street in Jacksonville, Florida, as the Eddie Mae Steward Post Office. Steward was a Jacksonville civil rights leader who had led the local NAACP. The naming was approved in November 2003. The act pairs the designation with a rule that later federal references to the facility use the Steward name.
plaw-108-125-2003: Public Law 108-125 keeps the Martin Luther King, Jr. memorial project alive in Washington, D.C. The authority to build the memorial under the commemorative works law was running out. This act restates the King memorial provision so that the building authority terminates on November 12, 2006 instead, giving the project three more years.
plaw-108-126-2003:
Public Law 108-126 authorizes a visitor center for the Vietnam Veterans Memorial in Washington, D.C. The Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund, the group that built the Wall, may construct the center at or near the memorial on federal land.

The stated purpose is to better inform and educate the public about the memorial and the Vietnam War. The authorization is written into the original 1980 law for the memorial. It comes in as a new section on the visitor center. Detailed rules on its location and design follow in the act's later sections.
plaw-108-127-2003: Public Law 108-127 makes technical corrections to the children's health insurance law. It fixes the definition of qualifying State in title XXI of the Social Security Act, the State Children's Health Insurance Program title. One correction changes a number, striking one hundred eighty-five and inserting one hundred eighty-four. The fixes take effect as if written into the earlier 2003 law.
plaw-108-128-2003: The Black Canyon of the Gunnison Boundary Revision Act of 2003 (Public Law 108-128) enlarges a Colorado national park. It revises the boundary of Black Canyon of the Gunnison National Park to add about two thousand five hundred thirty acres, as drawn on an April 2003 map. The act also transfers administrative jurisdiction over land between agencies to match the new line.
plaw-108-129-2003:
Public Law 108-129, passed by the 108th Congress in 2003, authorizes a land exchange in Alaska. The swap is between the Newtok Native Corporation, a village corporation, and the Department of the Interior. The exchange deals with land tied to a proposed new village site for the community.

The act names about 10,943 acres of federal land marked as the proposed village site on a 2002 map. Against that, Newtok offers roughly 12,101 acres of its own surface land, including ground at Aknerkochik and on Baird Inlet Island. It also defines terms from the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act and sets the terms for handing the land over.
plaw-108-13-2003: Public Law 108-13, enacted by the 108th Congress in 2003, renames a Defense Department school on Guam. The Guam South Elementary/Middle School in Apra Heights becomes the Commander William C. McCool Elementary/Middle School. McCool was a Navy commander and the pilot of the space shuttle Columbia, lost on February 1, 2003. Congress notes that he attended school on Guam as a boy and carried a Guam flag on the Columbia flight. The law says any later reference to the old school name now means the new one.
plaw-108-130-2003:
Fees on animal drugs are the subject of Public Law 108-130, the Animal Drug User Fee Act of 2003. Congress passed it as part of the 108th Congress, amending the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Its findings say fast approval of safe new animal drugs protects both animal health and public health.

Under the law, drug makers pay fees when they submit new animal drugs for review. The money goes to the Food and Drug Administration to add staff and speed up its review work. The fees support reviews of new and added drug applications and of early research submissions, following goals set out in letters from the health secretary to Congress.
plaw-108-131-2003:
Garrett Island, at the mouth of the Susquehanna River in Maryland, is the focus of Public Law 108-131. Congress passed the Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge Expansion Act in 2003. The findings call the island a small sample of the whole region's geology, with hard rock, coastal plain, and volcanic formations side by side.

The law lets the Secretary of the Interior buy the island, about 198 acres, and add it to the Blackwater National Wildlife Refuge. Congress notes it is the only rocky island in the tidal waters of the Chesapeake. Its shores give birds and fish good habitat, and the ground holds old sites that record human history in the area.
plaw-108-132-2003:
Public Law 108-132 is the Military Construction Appropriations Act for 2004, passed in 2003. It pays for building work, family housing, and base closing costs run by the Department of Defense. The money covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004.

The largest early share goes to Army construction, more than 1.4 billion dollars for building, repairs, and equipment at Army posts. Part of that sum is set aside for study, planning, and design work by the Army Corps of Engineers. The act also cancels some unspent money from earlier Army construction laws. Navy and other service building accounts follow in the same pattern.
plaw-108-133-2003:
Retirement credit for past military service is the issue in Public Law 108-133, the District of Columbia Military Retirement Equity Act of 2003. It amends the retirement law for police and firefighters in the nation's capital. The change covers members of the D.C. police and fire departments, the U.S. Park Police, and the Secret Service.

Before this law, past military service could be blocked from counting toward a city retirement pension. The act lets members and former members count that service when they figure their annuities, if they pay a required contribution. It rewrites the rule so the credit applies in most cases, with limits spelled out in the text.
plaw-108-134-2003: Public Law 108-134, passed in 2003, keeps several school lunch and child nutrition programs running a few months longer. It moves end dates in the National School Lunch Act and related laws from the fall of 2003 to March 31, 2004. The programs covered include the child and adult care food program, summer food service for children, and commodity distribution to states. One part also extends a rule that leaves out some military housing allowances when schools decide which children qualify for help.
plaw-108-135-2003: Public Law 108-135 is a short joint resolution from November 2003 that keeps the federal government funded a little longer. It changes one date in an earlier continuing appropriations law, Public Law 108-84, moving the cutoff to January 31, 2004. A second section makes the same date change for a defense spending rule from the year before. Measures like this one bridge the gap while Congress finishes the regular spending bills for fiscal year 2004.
plaw-108-136-2003:
Public Law 108-136, the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004, is the yearly law that sets defense policy and spending limits. Congress passed it in 2003 for the year starting October 1, 2003. It covers the Department of Defense, military construction, and defense work at the Department of Energy.

The act is built in three divisions, one for Defense Department programs, one for military construction, and one for Energy Department security work. Inside, it authorizes money for buying weapons and gear for the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force. It also sets the strength levels for the armed forces, meaning how many people each service may keep on duty.
plaw-108-137-2003:
Energy and water projects across the country are funded by Public Law 108-137, the Energy and Water Development Appropriations Act for 2004. Congress passed it in 2003, covering the fiscal year ending September 30, 2004. It is one of the yearly spending laws that keep federal agencies running.

The first title gives money to the Army Corps of Engineers for its civil works. That work covers rivers and harbors, flood control, shore protection, and restoring damaged water habitats. An early item provides close to 117 million dollars for studies, surveys, and project plans. Later titles fund energy programs and other water projects in the same detailed, line-by-line style.
plaw-108-138-2003: Public Law 108-138, passed in 2003, fixes a map error in the John H. Chafee Coastal Barrier Resources System. It swaps out the official map for Unit T-07 on the Matagorda Peninsula and replaces it with a corrected map dated July 12, 2002. The system marks coastal barriers where federal flood insurance and development aid are limited. The Secretary of the Interior must keep the new map on file so the public can inspect it.
plaw-108-139-2003: Public Law 108-139 is a joint resolution passed in 2003 that honors the federal Inspectors General on the 25th anniversary of their law. The Inspector General Act of 1978 created these watchdogs inside big agencies. The resolution notes that inspectors general now work in the 29 largest agencies and in 28 other federal bodies. Their audits and probes hunt waste, fraud, and abuse, and their reports push agencies and Congress to run programs more cheaply and honestly.
plaw-108-14-2003: Public Law 108-14, passed in April 2003, names a federal office building in New York City for a former congressman. The building at 290 Broadway in Manhattan becomes the Ted Weiss Federal Building. The law is two short sections. The first gives the building its new name, and the second says that any mention of the building in federal laws, maps, or records now means the Ted Weiss Federal Building.
plaw-108-140-2003: Public Law 108-140 is a joint resolution from 2003 marking 50 years of the Agricultural Research Service. That service is the main research arm of the Department of Agriculture. Congress praises its work for farmers, ranchers, food companies, and shoppers. The resolution credits the service with major breakthroughs that keep food safe, protect soil and water, and help American farms compete in world markets. It closes by honoring the service's staff for half a century of work for the nation.
plaw-108-141-2003: Public Law 108-141, approved in December 2003, renames a post office in Brooklyn, New York. The postal facility at 315 Empire Boulevard in Crown Heights becomes the James E. Davis Post Office Building. Like other naming laws, it has one working section and one housekeeping section. The housekeeping part says any reference to the site in federal records now means the James E. Davis Post Office Building.
plaw-108-142-2003: Public Law 108-142, the Kaloko-Honokohau National Historical Park Addition Act of 2003, slightly widens a historic park in Hawaii. It adds two parcels, numbered 1 and 2, that together cover just 2.14 acres. The parcels appear as Tract A on a National Park Service map dated April 2002. The law amends the 1978 statute that set the park's borders and allows money to be appropriated to carry out the change.
plaw-108-143-2003: Public Law 108-143, approved in December 2003, names a post office in Billings, Montana, for a former president. The postal facility at 710 Wicks Lane becomes the Ronald Reagan Post Office Building. The act has the standard two parts used in naming laws. One part gives the building its new designation, and the other says that references to the facility in any federal record now point to the Ronald Reagan Post Office Building.
plaw-108-144-2003: Public Law 108-144, approved in December 2003, names a post office in Prairie Village, Kansas, for a former senator. The facility at 3710 West 73rd Terrace becomes the Senator James B. Pearson Post Office. The law follows the usual naming pattern in two short parts. After the designation, it directs that any reference to the facility in federal laws, maps, or records be read as the new name.
plaw-108-145-2003:
Public Law 108-145, the Adoption Promotion Act of 2003, renews a federal program that pays states bonuses for moving foster children into adoptive homes. Congress first built the bonus program in the Adoption and Safe Families Act of 1997. That earlier law put child safety first and pushed states to find permanent homes faster.

The findings report real gains since 1997, with adoptions up by about two-thirds through 2002. Still, the text notes more than 540,000 children stayed in foster care, and about 126,000 of them were waiting for adoption. The act restarts the incentive payments under the Social Security Act, with extra rewards for adoptions of children with special needs.
plaw-108-146-2003:
Public Law 108-146, the Tornado Shelters Act, lets towns spend housing grant money on storm shelters for manufactured home parks. Congress passed it in 2003, amending the Housing and Community Development Act of 1974. Manufactured homes are among the most dangerous places to be when a tornado hits.

The law adds shelter building to the list of approved uses for Community Development Block Grant funds. Towns can build or improve tornado-safe shelters, or give loans and grants to park owners and nonprofit groups that do the work. A shelter must serve a neighborhood with at least twenty manufactured homes close enough for residents to reach it in time.
plaw-108-147-2003:
Veterans' benefit checks got a cost-of-living raise under Public Law 108-147, passed in 2003. Its short title is the Veterans' Compensation Cost-of-Living Adjustment Act of 2003. The raise took effect on December 1, 2003, and it matches the yearly pattern Congress uses to keep benefits in step with prices.

The Secretary of Veterans Affairs had to raise the dollar rates for disability compensation paid to veterans with service-connected injuries. The same raise covers dependency and indemnity compensation for survivors of disabled veterans who died. It also reaches extra pay for dependents, the clothing allowance, and both the new and old survivor rate tables written in title 38 of the U.S. Code.
plaw-108-148-2003:
Public Law 108-148, the Healthy Forests Restoration Act of 2003, tackles the risk of huge wildfires on federal land. Congress wrote it after severe fire seasons in the West. Its stated aim is to help the Agriculture and Interior secretaries cut hazardous fuels on national forests and Bureau of Land Management land near towns and watersheds.

The act's first title authorizes fuel reduction projects, sets which lands get priority, and creates a special review process for challenges. Later titles work on plant material left after thinning, called biomass. They fund research on using that material, a grant program for putting it to commercial use, and help for rural towns that depend on forestry work.
plaw-108-149-2003: Public Law 108-149, approved in December 2003, names a post office building in Moline, Illinois. The postal facility at 514 17th Street becomes the David Bybee Post Office Building. The text is brief and follows the standard form for these measures. One section makes the designation, and the next says that any reference to the facility in federal records now means the David Bybee Post Office Building.
plaw-108-15-2003:
Public Law 108-15, the American 5-Cent Coin Design Continuity Act of 2003, deals with the nickel. Congress passed it as the country marked two hundred years since the Louisiana Purchase and the Lewis and Clark expedition. The act also creates the Citizens Coinage Advisory Committee to advise on coin designs.

For nickels struck in 2003, 2004, and 2005, the Treasury Secretary may change both sides of the coin. A new front must show Thomas Jefferson, but with a fresh likeness unlike the one used in 2002. That honors his role in the Louisiana Purchase and in sending Lewis and Clark west. The Secretary must consult the new committee and the Commission of Fine Arts first.
plaw-108-150-2003: Public Law 108-150, approved in December 2003, names a post office building in Canton, Ohio. The postal facility at 2650 Cleveland Avenue, NW becomes the Richard D. Watkins Post Office Building. The act is short and follows the standard naming form. Its second section provides that any reference to the facility in a federal law, map, or record now means the Richard D. Watkins Post Office Building.
plaw-108-151-2003: Public Law 108-151, approved in December 2003, names a post office building in Bloomington, Indiana. The postal facility at 3210 East 10th Street becomes the Francis X. McCloskey Post Office Building. The act has two short sections in the usual form. The second section says that any reference to the facility in federal laws, maps, or records now means the Francis X. McCloskey Post Office Building.
plaw-108-152-2003:
Florida national forest land is the subject of Public Law 108-152, passed in 2003. Its title is the Florida National Forest Land Management Act of 2003. The law gives the Secretary of Agriculture power to sell or exchange certain federal parcels inside the state, on terms the Secretary sets.

The listed tracts sit mostly in Santa Rosa County near East Bay, with names like A-942a and A-942b and sizes near 61 and 40 acres. Another small tract lies in Okaloosa County near Fort Walton, at State Road 86 and Mooney Road. Each parcel is described by its survey lines, so buyers and the Forest Service can tell exactly which ground may change hands.
plaw-108-153-2003:
Public Law 108-153, the 21st Century Nanotechnology Research and Development Act, sets up a national program for science at the scale of atoms and molecules. Congress passed it in 2003 to fund nanoscience, nanoengineering, and nanotechnology research. The President must run the program through federal agencies and a coordination office the act creates.

The program must set goals, measures of success, and funding plans for federal nanotechnology work. Its tasks include learning how matter behaves at the nanoscale so it can be controlled and shaped. It gives grants to single researchers and to teams, and it builds a network of advanced user facilities and centers. Agencies must coordinate their work instead of running separate efforts.
plaw-108-154-2003:
Public Law 108-154, passed in 2003, updates federal work on birth defects and developmental disabilities. It revises and extends the Birth Defects Prevention Act of 1998. The law amends the Public Health Service Act section that governs the National Center on Birth Defects and Developmental Disabilities.

The center's duties grow under the act. It must do research on preventing these conditions and on later health problems that people with disabilities often face. The text also backs a National Spina Bifida Program, aimed at the nation's most common permanently disabling birth defect. Other parts direct the center to gather and share data on how often birth defects and disabilities occur.
plaw-108-155-2003:
Drugs given to children are the concern of Public Law 108-155, the Pediatric Research Equity Act of 2003. It amends the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Before this law, many medicines were tested mainly in adults, then used in children with little direct study.

The act lets the Food and Drug Administration require research into how drugs work in young patients. A company filing for approval of a new drug ingredient, a new use, or a new dosage form must include assessments for children. Those studies must use forms of the drug suited to each age group, so doctors get evidence about safety and dose for kids, not guesses based on adults.
plaw-108-156-2003:
Public Law 108-156, the Basic Pilot Program Extension and Expansion Act of 2003, deals with checking whether new hires may legally work in the United States. The Basic Pilot was a test program under the immigration law of 1996. Employers used it to verify work eligibility against federal records.

The act stretches the program's life from a six-year period to eleven years. It also orders the Secretary of Homeland Security to expand the program to all fifty states by December 1, 2004. Before that, the Secretary must report to the House and Senate Judiciary Committees by June 1, 2004, on how the expansion is going.
plaw-108-157-2003: Public Law 108-157, passed in 2003, lets federal court meet in Plano, Texas. It redraws the divisions of the Eastern District of Texas in title 28 of the U.S. Code. The Sherman division gains Delta, Fannin, Hopkins, and Lamar counties, and court is held at Sherman and Plano. Another division's county list is revised as well, adding Red River County. Cases already pending and juries already serving are not affected by the change.
plaw-108-158-2003:
Public Law 108-158, the Overseas Private Investment Corporation Amendments Act of 2003, renews a federal agency that backs American investment abroad. It amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. The corporation helps U.S. firms invest in poorer countries through loans, loan guarantees, and political risk insurance.

The first change extends the agency's issuing authority, moving its end date from November 1, 2000, to 2007. The rest of the act makes careful fixes to the agency's accounts. It renames the old insurance and guaranty reserves as a single noncredit account revolving fund. It also charges subsidy and administrative costs to the right account and updates how the agency pays off its liabilities.
plaw-108-159-2003:
Credit reports and identity theft are the targets of Public Law 108-159, the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act of 2003. It amends the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Congress wrote it to prevent identity theft, settle consumer disputes faster, and make credit records more accurate.

The act's first title covers identity theft prevention and restoring a victim's credit history. It creates fraud alerts and active duty alerts that consumers can place on their files. It orders card numbers to be cut short on receipts, so full account numbers do not print. Later parts deal with blocking false information that comes from identity theft and with coordinating how agencies and firms handle victims' complaints.
plaw-108-16-2003:
Public Law 108-16, the Nutria Eradication and Control Act of 2003, funds a fight against a marsh-eating rodent. Nutria are large rodents from South America that chew through wetland plants. Congress found they were causing heavy marsh loss in Maryland and Louisiana, on public and private land alike.

Failed trapping and harvest efforts meant the loss was speeding up, the findings say. So the act lets the Secretary of the Interior give money to Maryland and Louisiana for control programs. The states use the aid to remove nutria and to restore marshland the animals damaged. The law builds on a pilot program Congress had authorized in 1998 to find better removal methods.
plaw-108-160-2003:
Public Law 108-160, passed in 2003, renews the United States Institute for Environmental Conflict Resolution. The institute helps federal agencies settle disputes over environmental policy without long court fights. The act's full title calls it the Environmental Policy and Conflict Resolution Advancement Act of 2003.

Its single main section funds the institute's Environmental Dispute Resolution Fund. It authorizes four million dollars a year for fiscal years 2004 through 2008. Three million of that pays the fund's running costs each year. The remaining one million goes to grants that help state, local, and tribal governments, groups, and individuals take part in conflict resolution cases that involve federal agencies.
plaw-108-161-2003:
A shortage of veterinarians in rural areas is the problem behind Public Law 108-161, the National Veterinary Medical Service Act. Congress passed it in 2003. Many farm regions and public agencies cannot find enough vets to care for livestock and watch for animal disease.

The act tells the Secretary of Agriculture to run a loan repayment program. A veterinarian who agrees to work for a set time in a shortage area gets part of school loan principal and interest paid off. Each year of service earns another payment under the agreement. The program also covers vets who agree to serve the federal government during animal health emergencies.
plaw-108-162-2003: Public Law 108-162, passed in 2003, awards a congressional gold medal to Dr. Dorothy Height. Congress calls her one of the leading social and civil rights activists of her time. Born in Richmond, Virginia, in 1912 and raised in Rankin, Pennsylvania, she began civil rights work in the 1930s. The findings praise her work for voter education, interracial schooling, and the standing of women. She advised Eleanor Roosevelt and urged Presidents Eisenhower and Johnson toward equal rights steps. Her public career ran more than 65 years.
plaw-108-163-2003: Public Law 108-163, the Health Care Safety Net Amendments Technical Corrections Act of 2003, does repair work on an earlier health law. It fixes technical and conforming errors in the Health Care Safety Net Amendments of 2002. That 2002 law dealt with community health centers under the Public Health Service Act. The corrections undo a few passages that were enacted by mistake, restore one subsection that was dropped, and move other subsections to their proper places in the text.
plaw-108-164-2003:
Contact lens wearers gained a right under Public Law 108-164, the Fairness to Contact Lens Consumers Act. Congress passed it so patients could shop for lenses beyond the office that wrote their prescription. Eye doctors had often held the prescription unless the patient bought lenses from them.

Once a fitting is complete, the prescriber must hand the patient a copy of the prescription, even if the patient does not ask. The prescriber must also share or verify it for anyone the patient names. The law bars making a lens purchase, an extra fee, or a signed waiver a condition of giving the prescription out. Later sections cover when payment for the exam may be demanded at once.
plaw-108-165-2003: Public Law 108-165, approved in December 2003, names a post office building in Tappan, New York. The postal facility at 57 Old Tappan Road becomes the John G. Dow Post Office Building. The measure is short and uses the standard two-section form. The first section makes the designation, and the second says references to the facility in federal records now mean the John G. Dow Post Office Building.
plaw-108-166-2003: Public Law 108-166, approved in December 2003, names a post office building in Nashua, New Hampshire. The postal facility at 38 Spring Street becomes the Hugh Gregg Post Office Building. The law is brief, with the designation in its first section. A references section follows, directing that mentions of the facility in any federal law, map, or record be read as the Hugh Gregg Post Office Building.
plaw-108-167-2003: Public Law 108-167, approved in December 2003, is a one-section law about federal judges' pay. It authorizes salary adjustments for Justices and judges of the United States during fiscal year 2004. The raise follows the adjustment method in section 461 of title 28 of the U.S. Code. A 1981 law required Congress to approve these adjustments year by year, which is why such a short act was needed at all.
plaw-108-168-2003:
Public Law 108-168 renews the National Transportation Safety Board, the agency that investigates major crashes. Its title is the National Transportation Safety Board Reauthorization Act of 2003. The board probes air, rail, highway, and pipeline accidents and issues safety advice.

The act sets the board's funding levels for fiscal years 2003 through 2006. The yearly amounts rise from about 73 million dollars to about 88 million dollars. It also keeps an emergency fund topped up at no more than four million dollars for sudden major investigations. Separate money goes to the board's training academy, which teaches accident investigation skills.
plaw-108-169-2003:
Public Law 108-169 renews the United States Fire Administration, the federal office that supports fire services nationwide. Congress passed it in 2003. Title I keeps the agency's leader in place, stating that a Homeland Security Act rule does not remove the Fire Administrator's post or change how the Administrator is appointed and paid.

The act sets funding for the agency for fiscal years 2005 through 2008. The yearly amount starts at about 63 million dollars and climbs to about 69 million dollars. A small part of each year's money is marked for one named program section. The law's heading also joins the renewal to better coordination of firefighting research, a task carried in its later title.
plaw-108-17-2003: Public Law 108-17, approved in April 2003, names a post office in Charlotte, North Carolina. The postal facility at 2127 Beatties Ford Road becomes the Jim Richardson Post Office. The act follows the standard short form for facility names. Its references section says any mention of the facility in a federal law, map, or record now counts as a reference to the Jim Richardson Post Office.
plaw-108-170-2003:
Public Law 108-170, the Veterans Health Care, Capital Asset, and Business Improvement Act of 2003, is a broad package for the Department of Veterans Affairs. It amends title 38 of the U.S. Code. One title deals with health care rights and related matters for veterans.

The health title improves benefits for former prisoners of war. It gives care to veterans who took part in Defense Department chemical and biological warfare testing. It also opens VA health care to certain Filipino World War II veterans living in the United States. Other parts expand rehabilitation services and the department's power to arrange nursing home and adult day care. Later titles cover big building projects and staff rules.
plaw-108-171-2003: Public Law 108-171, despite being called the National Flood Insurance Program Reauthorization Act of 2004, is a short extension passed in December 2003. It moves the flood insurance program's end date from December 31, 2003, to March 31, 2004. The change covers the power to sign insurance contracts, borrowing authority, emergency program rules, and money for studies. The act says the changes count as if they took effect on December 31, 2003, so coverage never lapsed.
plaw-108-172-2003: Public Law 108-172, approved in December 2003, keeps small business programs alive for a few more months. Any program under the Small Business Act or the Small Business Investment Act of 1958 stays authorized through March 15, 2004. That covers programs set to expire between September 30, 2003, and March 15, 2004. The terms stay the same as they were on September 30, 2003. One exception raises a fee rate in the investment act from 1.38 percent to 1.46 percent.
plaw-108-173-2003:
Public Law 108-173, the Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003, is the law that added drug coverage to Medicare. It amends title XVIII of the Social Security Act. Before it, Medicare paid for hospital and doctor care but not most medicines people took at home.

The act creates a voluntary program for prescription drug coverage under Medicare. It also modernizes other parts of Medicare. Away from the Social Security Act, it changes the tax code to allow deductions for money put into health savings accounts. It further deals with unused health benefits left in cafeteria plans and flexible spending arrangements, where workers set aside pay for care.
plaw-108-174-2003: Public Law 108-174, approved in December 2003, keeps the federal ban on undetectable firearms in force. The Undetectable Firearms Act of 1988 barred guns that metal detectors and X-ray machines cannot spot. This law changes the number 15 in that act to 25, stretching the ban's life by ten years. It also makes matching fixes to penalty and exception sections of the gun laws so the ban still lines up with the rest of title 18.
plaw-108-175-2003:
Public Law 108-175, the Syria Accountability and Lebanese Sovereignty Restoration Act of 2003, presses Syria on terrorism, Lebanon, and weapons programs. Congress states its aims plainly in the opening lines. The law seeks to halt Syrian support for terrorism, end its occupation of Lebanon, and stop its work on weapons of mass destruction.

The findings recall that President Bush told Syria in June 2002 to close terrorist camps and expel terrorist groups. They also cite a United Nations resolution that orders all states to deny safe haven to terrorists. The act notes that Syria already cannot receive United States aid because the Secretary of State has found it backs international terrorism.
plaw-108-176-2003:
Public Law 108-176, called Vision 100, renews the Federal Aviation Administration. Its formal name is the Century of Aviation Reauthorization Act, and Congress passed it in 2003. It amends title 49 of the U.S. Code, the part that governs transportation.

The first title funds airport and airway improvements. It covers airport planning and building, noise programs near airports, air navigation gear, and the FAA's own operations. Another part deals with passenger facility fees, the charges airports add to tickets. That part covers low-emission airport vehicles, use of fees to pay debts, and simpler fee paperwork. Later titles take up safety, research, and airline matters.
plaw-108-177-2003:
Public Law 108-177, the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2004, approves spending for the nation's spy agencies. Congress passes one of these acts each year. Much of the money stays classified, so the public text sets rules and structure more than dollar figures.

The first title authorizes funds for intelligence work across the government and for the account that manages the whole intelligence community.
