David Freire and colleagues present a 2026 geospatial dataset of oil wells and social risk marks in a coastal city in Ecuador. Oil well data aid study of how old hydrocarbon work shapes risk for people near by. In the coastal canton of Salinas, city growth has pushed homes, salt works, roads and fishing ports close to old wells. About two hundred twenty eight wells were drilled there since the early twentieth century.

The dataset joins well sites and technical traits with population, nature and city service data. Wells spread across urban and rural sectors of the coast. Past sets that join well and social data for coastal cities were scarce. With the join, analysts can map where old wells and weak services overlap. Town leaders can then rank clean up, health checks and land use rules by true exposure.
pmc-13280803:
Hao Cheng and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a very rare womb cancer. The cancer, called a yolk sac tumor, grows more often in the ovaries. Fewer than forty cases in the womb lining have been written up in English. Their patient was a sixty-six-year-old woman in China. She had bleeding for about two weeks and doctors found a mass in her womb.

Blood tests showed a very high level of a protein that this tumor sheds. Scans showed a mass about seven centimeters wide. Surgeons removed the womb, ovaries, and part of a fatty sheet in the belly. Lab checks confirmed the rare tumor, at an advanced stage. The blood marker fell sharply after surgery. The authors say full surgery plus drug care may give the best chance.
pmc-13281403:
Mohammad Basheer Alameer and colleagues surveyed vape use among Syrian university students in a 2026 study. Vapes are sold as a safer, cleaner swap for smoking. Little was known about their use in Syria. The team shared a web survey on social media with twenty-six questions. More than fifteen hundred students replied. Questions covered what students know, how they feel, and whether they vape.

About one in four students vaped only, and about one in ten vaped and smoked. Friends were the top source of facts about vapes, ahead of media. Good taste was the top draw, then fun. Knowledge scores were low on the whole. Being male, having a parent who smokes, and a lax view of vaping each raised the odds of use. The authors call for awareness drives on campus.
pmc-13281703:
Wencke Walter and colleagues checked a claimed new subtype of blood cancer in a 2026 letter. The cancer is a fast leukemia of young white blood cells. A recent study had named a subtype marked by high levels of a gene called TWIST2. That subtype was tied to flaws in cell fuel enzymes. The letter writers searched their own adult records for like cases. They read gene activity in six hundred sixty cases and wider blood disease panels.

Seven of their leukemia cases showed the high gene signal. The signal also popped up in a few cases of three other blood diseases. That spread shows the marker is not unique to one subtype. Gene checks of the seven backed the fuel flaw link from the first study. But the flaw mix was varied, not one neat pattern. The authors say the subtype is real yet more mixed than first drawn.
pmc-13282003:
Öner Kilinc and colleagues compared camera angles in knee ligament surgery in a 2026 study. Rebuilding a torn front knee ligament works best when its tunnels sit where the old ligament sat. Surgeons view the joint through a slanted camera, most often at thirty degrees. A steeper seventy-degree camera exists too. The team read records of fifty-five patients from 2020 to 2024, all fixed by one surgeon with hamstring grafts. CT scans measured the thigh and shin tunnel spots.

Thigh tunnels in the steep camera group sat further back and lower. That is closer to the natural ligament's root. Shin tunnels did not differ between groups. Knee function scores at six months or later ran higher in the steep group. Thigh tunnel spot alone predicted function in deeper checks. The authors conclude the steep camera aids truer thigh placement. They note records-based work cannot fully rule out other causes.
pmc-13282403:
Elena Repges and co-authors report a 2026 study on a vitamin K recycling protein that shields blood vessel lining cells from a form of cell death. Vitamin K is known for helping blood clot in the liver. Its lesser-known relative protein, VKORC1L1, works in vessel walls. The team tested vitamin K2 in human coronary artery lining cells and in mice fed a vitamin K2-rich diet after artery injury.

Vitamin K2 raised cell survival and cut lipid peroxidation, the fat damage driving ferroptosis, that iron-linked cell death. Mice on the diet healed their artery lining faster without changes in clotting. Silencing VKORC1L1, but not its clotting relative, harmed cell growth and raised oxidative stress and inflammation. Vitamin K2 could not rescue cells lacking it, proving its role. The authors name VKORC1L1 a repair-promoting part of the vessel vitamin K cycle.
pmc-13282803:
Pengfei Luo and co-authors wrote a 2026 review proposing a framework, the neuroautophagic interactome, for how selective cell cleanup shapes brain disease. Selective autophagy is a disposal pathway that targets specific cargo, such as worn-out mitochondria and protein clumps, for breakdown. It keeps nerve cells in balance, and its failure is tied to degenerative disease, brain injury, and inflammation.

The review maps how this cleanup talks to cell death, inflammation, oxidative stress, and blood-brain barrier damage. Cleanup can protect neurons, yet in some settings it drives harm, a dual role the framework is meant to capture. Key molecular players include switches and tag-readers that interpret ubiquitin codes on cargo. The authors also weigh emerging therapies that tune the pathway to limit neuronal damage.
pmc-13283403:
Antibiotics packed into fat bubbles kill resistant gut bacteria better than free drugs, Barani Devi T's formulation team shows in 2026. Resistant Escherichia coli, Klebsiella, and Salmonella strains raise death risk in hospitals. Bubble carriers may push drugs past bacterial defenses more effectively.

Carriers were made by a thin-film method and loaded with three antibiotics. Sizes fell in a narrow nano range, and drug loading varied by compound. The carriers harmed kidney cells little in lab safety tests. They killed resistant strains far better than free drugs in direct tests. Release stayed steady over 24 hours, and imaging showed strong contact with bacteria. Pump-blocking effects were also probed.
pmc-13283903:
What looked like a heart tumor on ultrasound turned out to be a stomach hernia in a 2026 case from Rifah Anjum Samiha and colleagues. Hiatal hernia pushes stomach tissue up through the diaphragm near the heart. It rarely mimics a heart mass, yet location makes confusion possible.

The elderly woman had the finding during routine heart imaging at the clinic. A chest X-ray showed an air-fluid level behind the heart that hinted at hernia. Contrast CT of the chest then settled the diagnosis with clear images. The authors stress hernia as a key alternative when a heart mass appears. Simple X-ray review can prevent misdiagnosis where resources are limited.
pmc-13284303:
How teens feel after comparing upward on social media, not use itself, forecasts depression growth in a 2026 diary study by Andrea Irmer and Florian Schmiedek. Daily negative feelings that spike repeatedly may pile into disorder risk. Two hundred early teens logged experiences for fourteen days.

Ages ran from ten to fourteen years, with about half the sample female. Daily logs captured media use, upward comparisons, mood, and symptom checks. Teens whose mood dipped hardest on comparison days gained depressive symptoms. That path ran through higher average negative mood across the study. Media use coupling showed no such forecast effect. Emotional response matters more than screen time.
pmc-13284503:
Cinthia Jhovanna Perez-Martinez and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, how oxidative stress may disturb a key light-sensing pathway in diabetic eye disease. Nerve damage in the retina can start early in diabetic retinopathy. The cGMP signal helps photoreceptor cells work and survive, and the enzyme PDE6 controls that signal by breaking cGMP down.

The review links reactive oxygen species from mitochondria and other sources to faults in PDE6 handling, including steps tied to AIPL1 and FAT10. Faulty PDE6 could upset ion channels and calcium balance, harming photoreceptor function. The authors frame PDE6 and cGMP as a redox-sensitive hub and a possible target for protecting vision.
pmc-13286003:
Milad Dodangeh, Hamidreza Kanani, and Mohsen Soori describe a scope-based save for a stomach leak that would not close in a 2026 case report. A 33-year-old man arrived with a burst ulcer and belly-wide infection after a deliberate drug overdose. Surgeons patched the hole, yet eating too soon tore the repair and a second patch also failed to seal the leak.

With leaking fluid staying local rather than spreading, doctors threaded a camera into the stomach and placed a small curled drain across the hole. The drain gave fluid a path back into the stomach, letting the tissue heal from inside without a stent or new open surgery. Infection signs cleared within three days, and he left hospital about a month after the first operation. Checks weeks later confirmed full recovery with no return of the leak.
pmc-13286603:
Denise Lautenschleger Fischer and co-authors profile airway inflammation in young cystic fibrosis patients in a 2026 observational study. Twelve patients aged 6 to 18 gave sputum on a single test day alongside breathing tests and a cycling fitness exam. Their marker levels stood against saliva from healthy peers, and the team probed ties to lung function, fitness, and antibiotic use.

Patient sputum bristled with neutrophils and carried far more interleukin-8 than control saliva. A marker of oxidative damage also ran higher in the patient group. One interleukin tracked days spent on antibiotics closely, while interleukin-8 rose as a mid-range airflow measure fell. Fitness scores, notably, showed no link to the inflammatory markers. The pattern ties airway chemistry to lung health and illness burden even in stable patients.
pmc-13287103:
Petra Fikrova and colleagues test which adhesion molecule really drives liver vessel inflammation in a 2026 cell study. Endoglin helps immune cells stick to vessel walls elsewhere in the body, and oxidized cholesterol builds up in fatty liver, so the pair seemed destined to interact in liver sinusoidal cells. Human cells of that type were dosed with an oxidized cholesterol compound while surface proteins and white cell sticking were measured, with blocking antibodies sorting out credit.

The treatment did inflame the cells and sharply raised monocyte sticking. But endoglin fell rather than rose, and blocking it changed nothing about the sticking. The adhesion molecule ICAM-1 climbed steeply, and blocking it alone erased the extra adhesion. VCAM-1 also fell in the pattern. The authors conclude this vessel bed runs its inflammatory sticking through ICAM-1, and warn against importing endoglin's reputation from other vessels.
pmc-13287203:
Jesus Gomez-Escudero and colleagues studied in 2026 how blood vessel cells inside mouse breast tumours change during long treatment with doxorubicin, a widely used chemotherapy drug. Tumours that first shrank and later regrew were examined for shifts in vessel cell types and the signals those cells send.

Regrowing tumours held a vessel cell group with growth and inflammatory signalling switched on. Another new group carried markers tied to clearing drugs and handling oxidative stress, which may blunt treatment and support new vessel growth. The authors argue that vessel adaptation, not only cancer cell change, helps explain why chemotherapy stops working.
pmc-13287403:
Stefanos Karakolias and Artemis Palla surveyed 120 volunteer platelet donors in 2026 across five public hospital units in Attica, Greece, in the first study of its kind there. Donations took place between February and April 2025. Donors rated access, technical care, and how staff treated them.

Overall satisfaction ran high. Staff courtesy, respect, and attention scored best, and hygiene and skill also rated well. Access scored only moderately: donors named staff shortages, short opening hours, and long waits. Repeat donors were slightly happier than first-time donors. The authors recommend fixing hours and staffing to keep donors coming back for a scarce blood product.
pmc-13288603:
Chencha Chebo and colleagues compare two chicken types in Ethiopia in 2026. The study deals with climate fit. It sampled 262 healthy adult birds. Local birds numbered 122 in the set. Sasso birds numbered 140. Three landscapes were covered.

Most blood values did not split by breed. Season and landscape shifted results clearly. Local birds held higher values in most settings. Sasso birds edged ahead in wet highland seasons. They also led in midland wet seasons. Thyroid hormones ran higher in Sasso birds. Highland birds had the top hormone levels. Breed choice should fit place and season, they warn.
pmc-13288703:
Bjorn Zethelius, Mats Talback, and Rickard Ljung pit four comorbidity scores against plain age and sex for predicting death, in a 2026 Swedish register study. Their cohort held 5,010,261 residents born in 1975 or earlier, followed for deaths from 2015 through 2019, with scores built from hospital and prescription records at several look-back lengths.

Age and sex alone beat every index used on its own, including the Nordic Multimorbidity Index, the Charlson index, and the Elixhauser index. Adding the Nordic index to age and sex helped only slightly, while simple counts such as hospital days or filled prescriptions reached similar modest gains. When full history data are missing, those simple counts may serve nearly as well.
pmc-13288903:
Naiyuan Liang, Cheng Huang, and Qiang Pan study a Chinese folic acid program. The 2009 program gave rural women free folic acid. Their 2026 study uses it as a natural test. They track 1,953 children aged 10 to 15. Data came from a 2020 family panel survey.

Girls in high-need areas scored better on memory tests. Their math reasoning was also stronger. They reported fewer signs of low mood. Boys showed no such gains. Mental health gains clustered in richer homes. Brain gains spread more widely. The authors say food aid alone cannot close gaps. Social gaps still shape who gains most.
pmc-13289003:
Cristina Fernandez Turienzo and colleagues report a blood donor project in Sierra Leone. Their 2026 report covers Kono and Kenema districts. Blood is scarce in the nation. Paid and family donors fill most gaps. Past top-down drives failed to build trust.

Local hubs led the new model. Volunteers taught peers and rallied donors. Monthly drives used non-cash rewards. The project ran for eight months. It drew 539 units from 376 donors. Repeat donors made up 43 percent of gifts. Costs per unit fell by 40 percent. Good will and public praise drove most donors.
pmc-13289103:
Rennie Viah, Rashid Ansumana, and Emmanuel Komba Finoh study care choices in Sierra Leone. Their 2026 study ran in Bo District. It drew 500 women at two sites. One site was a city hospital. One was a rural birth facility.

Nearly all women cited push factors for care. Knowledge and awareness led that list. Culture weighed more for rural women. Means to reach care split town and country most. City women had more cover and cash. Rural women leaned on social and language support. Birth problems were common in both groups. How illness swayed choices split by place, though.
pmc-13289303:
Félix K Pham and colleagues published a 2026 study on how melanoma cell states shape immune neighborhoods and response to anti-PD-1 therapy. Nearly half of patients resist these immune drugs, even though melanoma often responds well. Tumor cells can shift form, and that plasticity may help them evade immune attack in distinct ways.

Tumors came from 57 people with stage III disease, sampled before adjuvant anti-PD-1 care and split by relapse within two years. Slides with many stains plus spatial gene mapping in four cases charted tumor patches, T cells, macrophages, dendritic cells, and lymphoid clusters. Groups of like tumor cells formed tight patches. The team defined a plasticity ratio from patch types to link layout with relapse risk and immune layout.
pmc-13289403:
Mannon Geindreau and coauthors report a 2026 mouse study on how combined vessel and immune therapy recruits killer cells into colorectal tumors. Blocking blood vessel growth plus releasing immune brakes helps some cancers, yet early immune steps inside tumors stayed murky. The team tracked the first wave of changes after dual blockade of VEGFR-2 and PD-1 signals.

CD8 T cells reacted early to vessel blockade and released a signal called IL-10 before gaining full killing power. That signal unexpectedly pulled natural killer cells into the tumor mass. Those cells then released a factor that matured macrophages and drew in more CD8 cells, sustaining attack. Cutting IL-10 signaling or killer cell function erased the treatment benefit in mice.
pmc-13289903:
Joseph J Shearer and coauthors test a 2026 question on whether protein risk scores for death in heart failure travel across populations. Heart failure kills many patients, and scores built from hundreds of blood proteins promise sharper prediction than clinical tools alone. Three published scores, each built in a different setting with the same protein platform, were compared in one community cohort for fairness.

Scores correlated moderately with each other and spread similarly across patients in the test cohort. Each step up in any score raised death risk, even after accounting for clinical factors, though gains shrank with adjustment. Accuracy for five-year death and calibration were checked against a clinical model. Scores stayed useful across pumping strength groups.
pmc-13290103:
Rebuilding teaching for one-year medical fellows is the aim of a 2026 educational improvement project led by Romy Yun at Lucile Packard Children's Hospital Stanford. Using pediatric anesthesiology as the test case, the team replaced a traditional syllabus with a holistic curriculum built on adult-learning principles and twelve teaching formats.

Survey results from 58 of 60 fellows across 2014 to 2024 were tracked on a statistical process control chart. Scores for educational content rose after the new curriculum began in 2021-22, and ratings for diversity, equity, and inclusion training also improved, while resources showed no change. Yun and colleagues argue the model can guide other short fellowship programs squeezed by clinical demands and duty-hour limits.
pmc-13290503:
Plant healing compounds ride nanocarriers into diabetic wounds in a 2026 review by Eko Sri Wahyuningsih and colleagues. Diabetic wounds stall because tissue regrowth is weak and inflammation never switches off, while plant chemicals such as flavonoids and polyphenols fight oxidation and swelling but dissolve poorly and break down fast.

The review focuses on two carrier families: silver nanoparticles, prized for killing microbes and available through green synthesis, and chitosan nanoparticles, which are body-friendly and stick to tissue. Both protect their cargo, push it deeper, and release it slowly, strengthening protection, germ-killing, and tissue regrowth in the studies surveyed. Wahyuningsih and colleagues weigh how they work and the steps still needed before such dressings reach routine clinical care.
pmc-13290903:
A young man's leg weakness turned out to be a mycobacterial infection strangling his spinal roots, Rocco Ricciardi and colleagues recount in a case report from 2026. The 36-year-old arrived with progressive gait trouble, left facial paralysis, a month of leg numbness, and new weakness.

Spinal fluid was strikingly abnormal: yellow-tinted, packed with lymphocytes, very low in sugar, and extremely high in protein. MRI showed thickened, clumped, enhancing cauda equina roots and involvement of the facial nerve, and PET lit up in the same places. Yet tuberculosis PCR, cultures, and immune tests all came back negative, and cancer antibodies were absent. Over ten days on broad antibiotics he worsened into complete cauda equina syndrome with paralysis and bladder failure. Follow-up imaging after three months of therapy showed the swollen roots shrinking. The case shows how this infection can mimic tumor or inflammation while standard tests stay silent.
pmc-13291003: Somya Mehra, James M. McCaw, and Peter G. Taylor issued a short correction in 2026 to an earlier mathematical study of Plasmodium vivax malaria and its dormant liver stage. Only the correction notice itself is present here, so the underlying model cannot be judged from this evidence alone. One symbol in Equation (10) was printed wrongly for a mosquito-to-human transmission rate and must be swapped, and Equation (16) is missing a constant that the notice restores. Readers using the formulas should apply both fixes.
pmc-13292303:
Ken Niwa's team reports a 2026 high-pressure experiment using metallocenes as single-source starting materials for exotic metal phases. Ferrocene and ruthenocene pack metal, carbon, and hydrogen into one molecule at atomic scale. The team squeezed them in a laser-heated diamond anvil cell to pressures up to 68 GPa, watching with optics, Raman spectroscopy, and synchrotron X-rays.

Above roughly 20 GPa both compounds turned opaque, which let laser heating couple efficiently. Treatment beyond 30 GPa broke the molecules down and produced a face-centered cubic phase in each case. That structure signals a metallic phase stabilized by light elements drawn from the precursor itself. The authors argue organometallic precursors open a practical route to exploring metal-light element systems at extreme conditions.
pmc-13293403:
Mingqun Lin, Nan Duan, and Yasuko Rikihisa study, in a 2026 paper, how the tick-borne bacterium Anaplasma phagocytophilum escapes from human white blood cells. The germ must live inside cells, growing in sacs before mature forms break out to infect anew.

Near exit points, the cell skeleton protein actin thinned where sacs touched the cell surface. Drugs that broke actin caused early, messy release of less infectious germs. A bacterial protein called AnkA sat with actin and partner proteins that link and trim it. Cutting those partners also sped early release. AnkA thus seems to time release by steering actin.
pmc-13294003:
Jianv Wang and coauthors report a 2026 case of mycosis fungoides occurring together with squamous cell carcinoma in a young man. Mycosis fungoides is the most common skin T-cell lymphoma and usually moves slowly through patch and plaque stages. Second skin cancers in such patients often follow light therapy, radiation, or skin chemotherapy, none of which this patient had received.

The 29-year-old had a 10-year history of itchy red plaques on the trunk, with fast worsening and ulceration over 4 months. One chest ulcer measured about 15 × 15 cm. The authors warn that new growths still need cancer checks even without classic treatment exposures.
pmc-13294103:
Moirangthem Lakshmipriyari Devi and coauthors sequence the transcriptome of Zanthoxylum armatum in a 2026 study of a traditional medicinal shrub. Leaf, stem, and fruit were sampled across seasons to find genes for berberine and sanguinarine production, two isoquinoline alkaloids, plus the transcription factors that control them.

Assemblies yielded tens of thousands of unigenes per tissue, with 5,576 simple sequence repeats found overall. Pathway genes such as BBE and SOMT varied in activity by tissue and season. Large regulator families included AP2/ERF and MYB-related groups. Linking gene activity to metabolite data could guide engineered boosts in target compound output.
pmc-13294803:
Lillian Hung and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for mapping research on screen-based artificial intelligence companions for older adults. Such companions, without a physical robot body, are promoted as answers to loneliness and unmet social needs in later life. Terms and study designs vary widely, leaving the field hard to survey.

Following established scoping review guidance, the team will search major health, psychology, computing, and grey literature sources. Eligible work must involve older adults and companions built mainly for company, conversation, or social support. Two reviewers will select and chart studies independently, with findings summed up through counts and narrative synthesis to expose gaps.
pmc-13294903:
Ancy Michel and co-authors build a maths model for gallium nitride fin transistors in a 2026 article. Vertical FinFET devices made from gallium nitride suit radio-frequency and power uses, but designers need reliable physics-based models. Their model covers a narrow fin channel on a gallium nitride base with a field plate gate.

Starting from a two-dimensional charge equation, the team derived formulas for surface potential, threshold voltage, current, and on-resistance. Results were checked against detailed computer simulations of a stepped gate device. Close agreement, plus strong simulated current values, supports the formulas as a practical aid for tuning future device designs.
pmc-13295003:
Fengkai Yang and co-authors check a new climbing machine for fitness testing in a 2026 study. Measuring maximum oxygen uptake guides training and heart-lung assessment, with treadmills as the usual standard. A vertical climbing device could offer controlled workloads if its readings prove trustworthy.

Thirty-one male sports students, averaging about 20 years old, completed maximal tests on both machines. Oxygen uptake, heart rate, and breathing measures from the climber matched treadmill values closely, with average error under ten percent. Speed control was accurate and repeat results were steady across sessions. The authors present the device as a valid, reliable option for standard metabolic testing.
pmc-13295903:
Laura Cardoso, Rakiya Saidu and Louise Kuhn review, in 2026, single-visit screen-and-treat care for preventing cervical cancer in poorer countries. Most deaths from this preventable cancer occur where multi-visit care loses many women along the way.

Treatment offered on a positive test, ideally the same day, cuts that loss, and the review weighs testing and treatment options for real clinics. Virus testing, including self-taken samples, proved more accurate than visual checks, while portable heat treatment matched older methods without gas supplies. Treating some women needlessly remains a worry, but missing treatment is judged the larger danger.
pmc-13296103:
Kenji K Kojima and co-authors announce, in 2026, that Repbase and Dfam, the two main libraries for recognising jumping genes in DNA, will merge into one fully open resource. Repbase moves to a CC-0 release and its curators join the Dfam team.

For three decades the pair have underpinned genome assembly and gene annotation, one built on expert-curated consensus sequences, the other on statistical family models with stored evidence. The authors say a single open framework should end split curation and access limits. The merger is presented as a foundation for future work on these mobile elements.
pmc-13297003:
Qinyao Sun and co-authors study, in 2026, the fine geometry of brain wiring in behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia, a disease reshaping personality and conduct. Fifty-one patients and matched healthy volunteers were scanned with a new method reading local fibre arrangement, beyond standard diffusion measures.

Some tracts showed more geometric distortion, many front-to-temporal links showed less, and patients lost brain volume while network efficiency shifted. Lower distortion tracked with worse clinical severity scores closely. The geometry measure also sat in the middle of pathways linking brain shrinkage to symptoms. The authors present it as a sensitive new marker.
pmc-13297203:
Mohammad Islamuddin and co-authors watch, in 2026, kidney macrophages regrow after selective wipeout in mice, using a switchable ablation system and gene reading at four time points. Resident macrophages guard kidney health, but how their niche refills was unclear.

Kidney tube cells quickly raised a lure signal that stayed up as macrophages returned. Newcomers shifted from stressed and inflamed toward energy-rich, dividing states steered by a shared gene module. Early chatter between macrophages and tube cells, especially through osteopontin, drove repair. The authors flag the lure, the messenger and metabolic routes as repair targets.
pmc-13298203:
Outlining tumors in breast ultrasound scans demands both the big picture and fine edges, and Shivpratap Singh Kushwah with co-authors built a network for exactly that in 2026. Their model, LTM-UNet, blends a transformer encoder with a state-space decoder inside the familiar U-shaped segmentation design.

Attention-guided skip connections carry fine spatial detail across the network while limiting the mismatch between encoder and decoder features. On benchmark sets the model scored Dice coefficients of 82.41% on BUSI and 86.62% on Dataset B, beating several existing approaches on overlap measures as well. The authors credit the mix of global context and direction-aware decoding for the gains.
pmc-13298603:
Half of multiple sclerosis patients in Saudi Arabia's Qassim region report bladder overactivity, and similar shares report depression or anxiety, found Mohammed Alqwaifly and colleagues in a 2026 cross-sectional study. They surveyed 262 patients at a specialist hospital during 2024.

Depression affected 53.4%, overactive bladder 50%, and anxiety 43.9%; night-time urination was the commonest bladder complaint, and urge incontinence was more frequent in women. Being single and having anxiety raised depression risk, while anxiety tied to being female and to depression itself. For bladder symptoms, anxiety was the only linked factor. The authors press for routine screening and integrated care for these hidden burdens.
pmc-13302803:
Vitamin K2 fed to arthritic rats spared their knee cartilage, Emre Uzun and colleagues report in a 2026 animal experiment. Twenty-four male Sprague Dawley rats split into sham, untreated osteoarthritis, and treatment groups; a chemical injection into the right knee induced joint damage in the latter two. Treated rats received eight micrograms of oral vitamin K2 daily for twenty-eight days before tissue examination.

Cartilage damage scores in treated animals came in at 4.25 against 11.10 in untreated controls, a wide gap. Treated cartilage also kept more type II collagen staining and showed less of the matrix-chewing enzyme MMP-13. The authors read the vitamin as slowing degeneration in this induced model.
pmc-13303103:
Gut germs shift in a set direction when joint disease also scars the lungs, Ran Fan and colleagues report in a 2026 stool study. Samples came from ten patients with rheumatoid arthritis plus lung scarring, twenty with arthritis alone, and eleven healthy people. Deep gene sequencing mapped each gut community, and a learning model hunted for group markers.

Overall variety looked alike across the groups, and no germ passed strict checks between the two arthritis groups. Early signals, though, showed Escherichia and Shigella up while Roseburia and Ruminococcus, both makers of a helpful gut fuel, thinned out. Inflammatory germs tracked how active the disease was. The authors flag these germs as candidate markers needing bigger studies.
pmc-13303603:
Sasha A. Fleary and co-authors describe a 2026 program report on building health literacy skills in community groups during COVID-19. A federal push funded local work to improve prevention habits and vaccination in underserved city neighborhoods.

From March 2022 to June 2024, a university public health school and the New York City health department partnered with four community organizations. The groups served neighborhoods of Black, Indigenous, and other residents of color hit hard by the pandemic. Training aimed to strengthen how clearly each group communicates health guidance and how well it meets cultural and language standards in its daily work.
pmc-13303703:
Yunjuan Ji, Liping Chen, and Xiang Shi track marriage satisfaction and low mood after childbirth in a 2026 longitudinal study. The early weeks at home can strain both a partnership and a new mother's mental health.

A total of 238 women from Nantong First People's Hospital answered standard scales at one, six, and twelve weeks after delivery. Satisfaction with marriage fell steadily while depressive symptoms rose over the same span. Earlier satisfaction predicted lower later depression, but depression did not predict later satisfaction. The protective link ran strongest for women without paid work, with low household income, or after cesarean birth.
pmc-13304103:
Dongyan Zhao and co-authors study a germanium-on-silicon light detector that multiplies signal through avalanche effects in a 2026 device report. Such detectors suit low-cost silicon photonics for sensing and data links.

A layered design separating absorption, charge, and multiplication zones was driven past its normal threshold with ramped gating. A steady dark avalanche current grew in proportion to the gate and heat generation, and straight-line multiplication continued even beyond the usual Geiger point. Traps at the germanium-silicon boundary help explain the behavior. Under infrared pulses the device showed self-quenching effects tied to shifting internal fields.
pmc-13305503:
Qutaibah Oudat leads a 2026 survey of how United States caregivers of preschoolers misjudge child weight and feed accordingly. What adults believe about a child's size may steer how much they restrict or push food at meals.

Caregivers of 139 children aged three to five joined across the Midwest between 2022 and 2023. Fewer than half judged weight correctly, and nearly as many rated their child lighter than charts said. Underrating tied to looser limits on food for health and weight reasons. Overrating leaned toward tighter weight limits instead. Pressing children to eat showed no link to misjudgment.
pmc-13307003:
Franziska Eckert tracked a cell-death marker weekly during combined chemo and radiation for rectal cancer in a 2026 study. Nineteen patients with locally advanced disease gave blood samples across long pre-surgery treatment.

The marker HMGB1 was compared with tumour size on magnetic scans before treatment and at weeks two and five, plus tumour DNA levels in blood. Higher starting marker levels matched larger tumours and higher tumour DNA shares in reported links. Marker paths wobbled during care, with steady rises in four patients who later showed poor tissue response.
pmc-13307103:
Chufan Ren extracted rock outcrops from drone point clouds in a 2026 study of the southern Junggar Basin. Slanted drone photos map scattered, plant-covered outcrops for oil exploration analogues, yet manual picking is slow and rare rock classes get missed.

A cross-scale attention network built on PointNet++ adds stronger data variation, sampling, encoding and loss tuning in the reported design. The test site holds Cretaceous Qingshuihe Formation rocks near Louzhuangzi. Results judge how well the method keeps sharp rock shapes while still finding sparse outcrop patches at field scale.
pmc-13307203:
Yuting Yan followed Chinese blood cancer patients after stopping BTK inhibitor drugs in a 2026 multicentre study. Records covered 37 people with chronic lymphocytic leukemia or its small-cell form who left this common drug class.

Mean age at stopping was 62.67 years, and most patients were male in reported counts at 67.57% of the group. Resistance drove 48.65% of stops and intolerance drove 32.43% in the recorded reasons. Next treatment most often paired an anti-CD20 antibody, and median time without progression on the original drug was 19.09 months. The data may help teams plan next care steps for men and women who stop such drugs.
pmc-13307303:

pmc-13307603:

pmc-13308703:

pmc-13311103:

pmc-13311303:

pmc-13311903:

pmc-13312203:

pmc-13313203:

pmc-13313303:

pmc-13314403:

pmc-13314503:

pmc-13315203:

pmc-13316003:

pmc-13316203:

pmc-13316303:

pmc-13317303:

pmc-13317403:

pmc-13318703:

pmc-13318903:

pmc-13320503:

pmc-13324403:

pmc-13331803:

pmc-13332103:

pmc-13334403:

Active enhancer marks and the P300 enzyme sat at the promoters of CARM1-controlled repair genes. True to that logic, inobrodib, a p300/CBP blocker, teamed with peposertib in AML cells. The pairing exploits an epigenetic dependency from two sides and offers a reasoned pairing for a disease with poor survival, above all after relapse.
pmc-13335403:
Alejandro Herranz Berzosa and co-authors looked at polymer nanoparticles as fillers for battery electrolytes in a 2026 article. Mixed electrolytes usually rely on inorganic particles to gain strength and conductivity, but polymer bits made from dried latexes offer a tunable option.

The review first explains how sulfonamide-functional poly(methyl methacrylate) particles are made by emulsion polymerization, with size held between 20 and 100 nm and surfaces shaped at will. It then shows how these particles build composite electrolytes with better strength, high ionic conductivity, or lithium single-ion conduction. Finally it surveys how those electrolytes perform inside lithium- and sodium-metal batteries. Edges over inorganic fillers include scalable production, low density, and easy mixing into polymer matrices.
pmc-13336403:
Kyosuke Kagami and co-authors showed that a rare placental tumor can absorb genes from the mother carrying it, in a 2026 case series. Cell fusion between cancer and immune cells had been proposed to create wandering hybrids, but genetic proof in human cancer was missing.

The team followed four cases of placental site trophoblastic tumor that, remarkably, produced immunoglobulin. Three recurred and responded well to pembrolizumab. In one daughter-derived tumor that relapsed after treatment, gene profiles over time showed the tumor absorbing DNA from host maternal cells. The DNA included maternal alleles the daughter never inherited, at the immunoglobulin lambda and HLA-DQA2 loci and across wide regions. Immune-related proteins TLR10 and SIGLEC10 rose as incorporation spread, suggesting the graft taught the tumor immune tricks.
pmc-13336903:
Junming Huang and colleagues use a local tumor treatment to widen cell therapy in pancreatic cancer in a 2026 study. Pancreatic tumors carry few clear targets, starving vaccine and T cell approaches. Their ionic liquid, ILvax, injected into the tumor, kills tumor cells in a way that alerts the whole immune system.

Special dendritic cells, cDC1, carry tumor pieces to lymph organs and start a presenting cascade. That spreading taught the immune system more targets, expanded infused TCR-T cells, and shifted their fuel use toward oxygen-based burning. Both the body's own CD8 T cells and infused cells worked better together. A local jab that teaches broadly could make a hard cancer treatable by cell therapy.
pmc-13337503:
Federico d’Oleire Uquillas leads a large 2026 team mapping how the cerebellum ages across 47,000 adults in three imaging studies. This back-brain structure holds most brain neurons and supports thought as well as movement, yet its aging pattern was murky. Volume and tissue-ratio measures, backed by quantitative scans in an independent sample, charted the changes.

Aging proved uneven: association and motor-related regions declined faster with age than other lobules. Bigger cerebellar volume tracked with higher cognitive scores as age rose, suggesting reserve that protects function. In Alzheimer's patients the link held mainly at lower amyloid burden, even in high genetic risk carriers. The cerebellum emerges as an active guardian of late-life cognition, until disease overwhelms it.
pmc-13337703:
Xuqiang Wang and colleagues chart the learning curve for scope surgery to remove bleeding in the basal ganglia in 2026. The minimally invasive method is demanding, and how many cases proficiency takes was not well defined. Their data come from one experienced neurosurgeon.

Records of 120 straight cases were reviewed, with cumulative sum analysis based on operating time. A clear turning point appeared near the 25th case. Operating time fell across phases from 1.77 hours in early cases to about 1.23 hours later, as reported means show. The share of clot removed rose at the same time. Results give training programs a concrete benchmark for skill growth.
pmc-13338603:
Anthony Hauser and co-authors analyze how COVID-19 reshaped causes of death in Switzerland in a 2026 study. Weekly deaths from 2011 to 2021 were split into nine cause groups, with age, sex, and region also tracked. A Bayesian model trained on pre-pandemic years predicted what 2020 and 2021 should have looked like.

Heart deaths peaked during the autumn 2020 wave, yet no cause stayed high across both pandemic years as reported. Among people aged 80 and older, non-COVID breathing deaths fell by 25 percent in the reported estimate, largely offset by COVID deaths. Only a modest overall excess remained. Hidden COVID deaths and shifted timing likely explain part of the pattern.
pmc-13341703:
Kidney failure racing ahead in tuberous sclerosis is reported by Rushuang Yang and colleagues in a 2026 case report. The 28-year-old woman moved from advanced kidney disease to no urine output and end-stage failure within 3 years, far faster than the usual slow course.

During pregnancy she showed heavy protein and blood in the urine, yet scans found no large tumors. Treatment later lapsed for financial reasons, and over about 30 months both kidneys were replaced by diffuse angiomyolipomas. Guidelines trigger preventive drugs mainly at tumor sizes above 3 cm. The authors urge watching urine markers as early alarms and involving multidisciplinary teams sooner.
pmc-13344303:
Xiaoli Zheng and co-authors review lactylation, a newer chemical tag linking lactate to gene control in cancer, in 2026. Tumors rewire sugar burning and flood their surroundings with lactate, once dismissed as waste, and the review traces how genetic and epigenetic switches govern that abnormal lactate handling.

Methylation marks on DNA and RNA, histone changes, and non-coding RNAs all tune the enzymes and transporters of lactate flow. Lactylation itself writes lactate onto proteins, feeding back into growth, immune escape, and drug resistance. Mapping this loop opens treatment ideas aimed at lactate pathways, which the authors present as a promising front against stubborn tumors.
pmc-13346003:
Ibtissem Ben Bayer and co-authors present a 2026 case where freezing a tumor made the impossible operation possible. A 64-year-old woman carried a giant desmoid tumor in her chest front that caused worsening breathlessness and pain, shrugged off two rounds of drug therapy, and was ruled unresectable.

Inside a prospective trial, the team froze the mass through the skin with cryoablation. The tumor shrank markedly and its grip on nearby structures loosened, reopening the surgical door. Removal through a split breastbone achieved clean margins, with under 10 percent living tumor left in the specimen. Eight months on she remained well and recurrence-free, suggesting freezing deserves a downsizing role in selected chest tumors.
pmc-13346603:
Abdullah and co-authors propose a hybrid deep learning system, issued in 2026, for sorting gut diseases from endoscopy images. Their design joins a Vision Transformer with a layered memory network and then adds bagging and stacking ensembles to combine several model outputs.

Training used the Kvasir-v2 set of over 8,000 labelled images across eight disease classes. The held-out test reached up to 99.99 percent accuracy in the reported runs, with a kappa value of 0.994 that signals very strong agreement. The system beat five named baseline models and stayed above 96 percent correct under added noise, blur, and light shifts, though such near-perfect scores merit care in new clinics.
pmc-13346903:
Ji Hyun Kim and colleagues issue joint guidance for Alport syndrome care in Korea, in a statement published in 2026 for two national kidney societies. Alport syndrome is an inherited kidney disorder marked by blood and protein in urine and slow kidney failure, often with hearing and eye problems. So the group reviewed four drug strategies with a formal grading method.

Early blockade of the renin-angiotensin system was strongly backed, since starting at the stage of trace blood or protein in urine delayed kidney failure and improved survival in the reviewed evidence. Support for cyclosporine, mineralocorticoid blockers, and SGLT2 inhibitors stayed weak, resting on small short studies, and cyclosporine carried a clear risk of kidney harm.
pmc-13348403:
Esther M. Johnston and a global team build a shared framework for training family medicine teachers, in a consensus study published in 2026. Family practice shares core ideas worldwide yet training, certification, and standing vary by region, leaving no global guide for preparing its teachers. So experts from many regions answered a modified Delphi survey rounds until views converged.

The final frame holds three domains, covering hands-on teaching skills and knowledge, personal approach with learners, and acting as a professional role model in daily work. Built for bend, the frame can fit local systems while holding a common core, aiming for steady quality in doctors who train the next family physicians.
pmc-13350003:
Vadivel Ganapathy and Yangzom D Bhutia wrote a 2026 commentary on whether blocking STAT3 sits at the heart of how a plant compound, toosendanin, kills cancer cells. The death route in focus is ferroptosis, an iron-driven process distinct from ordinary cell suicide.

Free iron can spark reactions that burn the fatty building blocks of cell membranes, and cells survive by controlling iron levels or mopping up the damage. Toosendanin reportedly triggers ferritin eating, freeing stored iron, through a chain involving STAT3 and the cargo protein NCOA4. The authors weigh that chain and ask whether one signalling hub truly explains the herb compound's cancer effects.
pmc-13351703:
Jiahui Meng and co-authors test whether salidroside can calm vessel lining injury linked to Kawasaki disease, in a 2026 combined computer and lab study. Kawasaki disease is a fever illness in children that can damage heart arteries. Salidroside comes from Rhodiola rosea and is known for anti-inflammatory effects.

Targets were predicted with screening tools and disease databases, then checked by docking models. Human coronary artery cells were stressed with TNF-alpha to mimic injury, and RNA sequencing tracked gene changes after treatment. Cell tests covered survival, movement, and cell death. Results point to NF-kappaB and NLRP3 pathways in the protective effect, though the work stays at lab stage.
pmc-13351903:
Jiawei Chen and co-authors review outcomes of windpipe surgery after pre-treatment in a 2026 cohort study. Whether treatment before surgery changes later results for primary tracheal tumours was unclear. Records from 2019 to 2024 identified 22 patients who had pre-treatment, then tracheal removal and rebuilding.

After pre-treatment, 8 patients, or 36.4 percent, had a good tissue response, including 4 with complete response. Clean removal was achieved in 16 patients, or 72.7 percent. Complications affected 13 patients, and major ones affected 5, while no deaths occurred at 30 or 90 days. Median follow-up was 29.5 months. Join problems arose in 4 patients, so the authors weigh benefit against a real risk at the join.
pmc-13352403:
Christopher D Hamad leads a 2026 cohort study of cannabis and nicotine use around spine fusion surgery. Cannabis use has risen in the United States and is often thought to aid pain control, yet its surgical effects apart from nicotine are unclear. Records from the TriNetX network covered 144,488 adults who had neck or lower back fusion from 2015 to 2022.

Users were grouped by record codes from the prior 2 years as nonusers, nicotine only, cannabis only, or both. Outcomes ran to 2 years and spanned nerve, surgical, and medical problems, plus pain, mental health, opioid use, and care visits. Separating the two substances lets the team judge each one's own link to recovery.
pmc-13352503:
Hsin-Yin Chuang leads a 2026 nanoparticle study aimed at calming inflammation inside atherosclerotic plaques. Fat build-up, chronic inflammation, and cell death make plaques unstable, and lipid drugs alone leave risk behind. The team built dendrimer gel particles carrying rapamycin and guided by a uPA tag toward the uPAR receptor, which is rich in plaques.

Targeted particles entered macrophages 1.3-fold better than untargeted ones and held drug 2.2-fold longer than free drug. In mice lacking the LDL receptor, particles gathered in aortic lesions. Four weeks of treatment cut plaque burden by 52 percent across the aorta and shrank dead cores by 68 percent. Inflammatory signals and cell death also fell sharply.
pmc-13352703:
Katharina Lüthy leads a 2026 mixed-methods study of how German teachers view electromagnetic field risk. No harm is proven below legal limits, yet public worry stays widespread, and teachers pass health knowledge to children and parents. An online survey in 2024 drew 1,400 school and nursery teachers, with focus groups adding 29 more voices.

About a third of each teacher group, at 32 percent and 33 percent, judged exposure below legal limits as risky. Estimates were corrected for non-response, and latent class analysis sorted teachers into perception types. How informed teachers felt and how often field questions arise at work were also mapped. Findings guide health agencies on what information teachers actually need.
pmc-13354403:
Mahnoor Sheikh and co-authors write a 2026 letter on the fast-tracked approval of orforglipron under a new FDA voucher scheme. The Commissioner's National Priority Voucher programme, announced in June 2025, uses team-style review to cut approval times to 1 to 2 months for products serving national health priorities. Standard review takes 10 months and priority review 6 months.

The FDA approved Foundayo, or orforglipron, on April 1, 2026, the first new molecular entity through the scheme and the fastest since 2002. Use pairs the drug with more activity and a lower-calorie diet for lasting weight control in adults with obesity, or overweight with related conditions. The letter marks a regulatory milestone worth scrutiny.
pmc-13355003:
Aanchal Ralhan and co-authors tested in 2025 a low-cost virtual way to teach point-of-care ultrasound to rural trainees in Canada. Rural doctors value bedside ultrasound but often lack local teachers and funds for pricey gear. Their setup used two rooms linked by video calls, webcams, and a cheap capture card to share the ultrasound screen.

Trainees rotated through nine hands-on stations plus one virtual station that covered the core acute care topics. Teacher and learner could each show probe placement and view the other's images. The authors present the model as a cheap, easy way to bring expert ultrasound teaching to remote sites and working rural doctors.
pmc-13355203:
Trung Dat Phan and co-authors share a 2026 dataset from a motor-driven breathing bag device built in Vietnam. The machine squeezes a standard self-inflating bag to push air, as a low-cost stand-in for a ventilator. Sensors track airway pressure, airflow, and air volume a thousand times per second.

Data were gathered on a test lung set to four states: normal, stiff, blocked airway, and an extreme mixed state. Twelve files cover three motion patterns for each state, with motor and control signals logged alongside. The authors offer the data for building models of the device, testing control methods, and making digital copies for design work.
pmc-13359003:
Zhaoquan Wu and co-authors describe a rare but deadly side effect of targeted lung cancer drugs in a 2026 paper. Drugs that block the ALK gene can inflame and scar the lungs, a condition called interstitial lung disease. The team gathered published cases to chart how it starts, how it looks, and how patients fare.

They found 50 patients, with lung trouble starting a median of 50 days after treatment began. Breathlessness, low oxygen, and cough were the top signs, and scans mostly showed hazy patches. After stopping the drug and giving steroids, nine in ten patients improved, but one in ten died. The paper warns doctors to act fast on new breathlessness.
pmc-13361103:
Jaemin Lee and co-authors compare two anesthesia types for double knee replacement in a 2026 study. The patients had both knees replaced one week apart, so they faced two rounds of anesthesia in quick succession. Spinal anesthesia numbs the lower body, while general anesthesia puts the patient fully to sleep. The team reviewed 207 patients and 414 surgeries at one center.

They compared kidney injury and blood transfusion rates between the two strategies. Many planned spinal cases switch to general midway, so the team sorted cases by the first plan and then double-checked with a second sorting. Results from single knee surgery may not carry over to this harder setting, where patients are older and stress adds up. The study gives surgeons and anesthetists direct proof for planning.
pmc-13361603:
Marzhan Nurbekova and co-authors review a class of magnetic oxide materials in a 2026 paper. Perovskite manganites mix a flexible crystal frame with manganese in several charge states. That mix gives tunable electronic behavior and many useful traits at once. The review covers how these materials are made, sorted, measured, and used.

Making methods range from solid-state firing to gels, water-based routes, and microwave heating. Each route changes purity, grain shape and size, and oxygen content. The authors survey magnetic, optical, electrical, and catalytic behavior across simple, double, layered, and thin forms of the material. Such oxides interest engineers for sensors, memory, and energy devices. The review gives newcomers a single map of a crowded field.
pmc-13364503:
Abdullah Jalal and co-workers tell a 2026 case of a six year old girl with a smooth brain birth flaw, hard seizures, and a strict fat based diet plan. Care teams cut the band that links the brain halves and swapped a nerve stim unit to calm her fits.

Care after surgery brought a rough patch: more fits at first, then a sick spell with low blood sugar, low salts, and a sky high fat burn mark. Fluids, sugar aid, and a diet shift steadied her. A gut drug then let tube feeds run smooth. The case shows the close watch such mixed care needs.
pmc-13364903:
Yiyao Liu and co-workers find in 2026 a pond mud germ that eats a harsh crab germ and may guard farmed mitten crabs. The harsh germ sickens crab farms and few safe guards exist. The team fished the hunter germ from farm mud, use the crab germ as bait, then mapped its full gene set.

The hunter held tools for move and wall break, no harm genes, and no ill effect in crabs at high dose. It slowed the target germ near to nil in glass tests and raised crab life in live tests. It also hit three more farm germs. A green farm guard may be at hand.
pmc-13365303:
Xue Yang and co-workers ask in 2026 if skill at find and judge web health facts guards Hong Kong college youth from game ill. Too much game play can harm mind health, yet few seek help. The team polls 370 students on game signs, health web skill, and help will.

Near three in ten met the bar for like game ill, but near one in ten said they had it. High web health skill tied to few game signs. It also fed help will through faith that care works. Teaching web health skill could cut game harm and lift help use.
pmc-13366203:
Emily Tilstra-Ferrell and co-workers read in 2026 the write ups made in a joint care plan for fresh sex attack harm and drink ill. The plan blends write out care for stress ill with skills for drink use, in five web calls. Ten adults in the plan gave the write ups.

Themes sort into five groups, from sense and mind bits to how write work felt. Folks wrote rich sense bits, named feels, and thought out the harm, with high step true rates. Self and group ties loom large in their tales. Early write care can work for this group, the team holds.
pmc-13371503:
Yin Yen Mun and co-authors share an eye case from 2026 on a shift in sight after lens surgery. A man aged 29 with a flat iris and long-term eye pressure trouble had his clear lens removed and tiny drains placed. Five weeks later his sight blurred and he saw double.

Careful checks found scar bands that pulled the new lens out of place and tilted it. A short second surgery freed the bands and let the lens slip back. His sight cleared and the blur went away. The case warns that scar bands can cause such shifts, and that they can be fixed if found in time.
pmc-13373603:
Paul S. Appelbaum and co-authors asked study members what they want back from gene tests in a 2026 survey. The 149 people had taken part in a large gene study that gave back risk scores for eight common ills. Most were white, well schooled, and at ease in English.

Most said that to get their own results would weigh a lot in a choice to join a next study. Two in three gave that point the top mark. They wanted the facts to guard their own health and their kin's. Fear of harm was low, and most would share the facts. The replies can help teams plan fair returns of results.
pmc-13374203:
Pedro Henrique Takata and co-authors set lab and live tests of germ-eating viruses side by side in a 2026 study. The target germ is a tough lung and wound germ that shrugs off many drugs. Such viruses, called phages, kill one germ type and spare the rest.

Three strict phages were bred and tried on 15 ward germ strains and three stock strains. Dish tests logged how well each phage cleared its host. Live model tests then checked the same pairs. Past work rarely links the two read types. A firm link would let labs screen phages in dishes with more trust in what will work in the body.
pmc-13375603:
Phuong Nguyen and co-authors give a cheap way to light up many proteins in tissue in a 2026 paper. Glow tags let staff see where each protein sits in a slice. Old two-step ways are slow and picky on host type, and one-step ways are dim and fixed.

The new way packs the space with crowd stuff to push tags on with more force. It works with tag pairs past tools could not mix, and needs no dear rigs or rare parts. Strong, cheap, host-free glow work could put fine tissue maps in reach of small labs, not just rich hubs.
pmc-13377903:
Katijah Khoza-Shangase maps risks in ear and speech care in South Africa in a 2026 study. Care there runs in a thin, split health world: state wards with few tools, and paid rooms with cash strain. A total of 92 staff gave their tales in 2025.

Four risk sets came out of the talks and counts. State staff told of more cure slips and late care, most of all in far zones. Staff lack and kit breaks hit them more too. Paid staff fret more on cash swings. One risk plan can't fit both worlds, the study holds: each needs its own guard stack.
pmc-13380103:
Zhanghao Chen and colleagues present a 2026 study on capsule traps for PFAS, the long-lasting chemicals that pollute water worldwide. Inspired by cell membranes, which let only certain substances through, the team built capsules about a millimetre wide. Each has a powdery core rich in nitrogen groups and a porous plastic shell.

Tests and computer models showed the shell lets PFAS pass while keeping out other material in the water. The core then pulls the chemicals inside. By tuning the core, the team also captured short-chain forms, which are usually harder to trap. The capsules caught a wide range of these chemicals, offering a selective tool for cleaning polluted water.
pmc-13380203:
Anmar Al-Taie, Ahmed Shaheen Abdullah, and Oritsetimeyin Arueyingho wrote a 2026 scoping review of artificial intelligence in clinical pharmacy services. Such tools promise to make medicine management safer and more efficient in hospitals and community pharmacies. The review maps what has actually been tried and reported.

Following standard guidance for scoping reviews, the authors searched major databases for studies from 2010 to 2025 and included 36 publications. The largest group used these tools to detect harmful drug interactions and side effects. Other uses covered tasks across the medicine-use process. The map shows where evidence is concentrated and where pharmacy practice has yet to test these tools properly.
pmc-13382503:
Taylor and colleagues review strategies for keeping arteriovenous fistulas open, in 2026 vascular research for dialysis patients. A fistula, a joined artery and vein in the arm, is the preferred dialysis access, yet it often narrows and fails. The chief culprit is neointimal hyperplasia, inward wall thickening driven by needle sticks, shear stress, and the inflammatory chemistry of kidney failure. The authors note it contributes to over 60 percent of dysfunctional fistulas in the literature.

Balloon angioplasty, first used for stenosis in 1982, remains the first-line rescue, forcibly dilating the narrowed segment to remodel it outward. The review weighs drug-coated balloons, stents, surgical revision, and surveillance for catching stenosis before thrombosis closes the vessel, plus the biology that makes each succeed or fail. Taylor argues durable patency needs both mechanical fixes and control of the wall's fibrotic response, since dilation alone invites the hyperplasia to return at the site.
pmc-13383403:
Hanxiao Zhou and colleagues build a single-cell atlas of aging-linked markers in melanoma in 2026 work. Aging reshapes how this skin cancer grows and how well immune therapy works, but the cell-level picture was unclear. The team joined mutation, gene activity, and other data layers to find age-driving factors.

One factor, named a RevitalAge Marker, tied to younger profiles and better survival. Cells carrying the marker aided anti-tumor roles, while cells without it showed spread and immune evasion traits, especially in patients over 65. A five-gene signature predicted therapy response well, and one gene's product bound two candidate drugs strongly in docking tests.
pmc-13385903:
Romina Roozbeh, Narjes Keramati, and Mehdi Mousavi Kamazani test an amine-tuned framework material for clearing tetracycline from water in 2026 work. Their material, NH2-ZIF-11, adds amine groups to a porous crystal to grip the antibiotic more strongly. Structure checks confirmed the framework stayed intact after the change.

Under best settings, removal reached about 91 percent within an hour of contact in their tests. Capacity more than doubled compared with the unmodified parent material, a gain credited to charge, stacking, and hydrogen bond forces working together. The material kept working across three reuse cycles and the process was heat-absorbing and spontaneous.
pmc-13386203:
Hai Xuan Nguyen and co-authors isolate two new plant compounds that block the pigment enzyme tyrosinase in 2026 work. Such blockers are sought as skin-whitening agents for pigment disorders. Chemical analysis of Streblus ilicifolius stems yielded the pair, named strebluses A and B, with structures solved by spectra and light-based methods.

Both compounds beat the standard control kojic acid in lab potency tests. Computer docking placed them snugly at the enzyme's active site, touching the same key residues as the control. Stability runs backed the docking picture, and the authors offer the pair as blueprints for future cosmetic development.
pmc-13389603:
Yaping Chen and co-authors present, in 2026, a highly unusual case of tuberculosis affecting several genital sites at once in a woman past menopause in Guangzhou, China. Lesions were confirmed on the vulva and cervix, with suspected spread to the womb lining.

The authors stress that genital tuberculosis belongs on the list of causes when a postmenopausal woman bleeds, even with no past lung tuberculosis. Sampling with acid-fast staining and culture confirmed the vulvar and cervical disease and allowed prompt cure, while suspected womb involvement still needs tissue and germ proof. Gynaecologists gain a reminder that this infection can mimic cancer and that targeted sampling settles the question faster than imaging alone.
pmc-13390903:
Natalia Gattass-Ferreira and colleagues follow, in 2026, pregnant women whose early blood sugar was only mildly raised, asking whether that small rise truly signals diabetes risk. Mild fasting glucose elevation in the first trimester is sometimes labelled early gestational diabetes, which triggers treatment and monitoring.

The prospective study included 114 women whose first-trimester fasting glucose stayed below a set ceiling. Those in the mildly raised band had the test repeated after three to four weeks. Women whose repeat value fell back below the threshold formed a comparison group. That group received no treatment. Obstetric readers gain evidence on whether a mild, non-persistent rise predicts later diabetes or poor outcomes, or mainly creates needless alarm.
pmc-13393603:
Nathan Muci Aguiar and six colleagues publish the protocol for a systematic review asking how exercise affects pain in breast cancer survivors during chemotherapy. The review separates the immediate sting from the long-term gain. Exercise is considered safe during treatment and broadly recommended, yet a session may flare pain acutely while training over weeks could ease it. The protocol, registered in advance, follows standard reporting rules for review plans.

Searches will span five major databases for randomised trials of set exercise in adults on chemotherapy that measured pain by objective or subjective means. Two bias and certainty schemes will grade each trial and the overall body of evidence. Because studies will differ in exercise type and timing, the team pre-plans subgroup and sensitivity analyses plus structured handling of heterogeneity. The finished review aims to guide pain care during treatment.
pmc-13394403:
Taihei Fujimori and co-authors track, in 2026, how single cells lock genes off for good. They pulled a silencer called KRAB to one test gene and watched the DNA fibre in three dimensions. Silencing left a mark named H3K9me3 and packed the fibre tight over long stretches. A second route, which strips small chemical tags, turned the gene off without such packing.

Only the packed state stayed off weeks after the silencer was removed. Over time the first mark faded while DNA methylation took its place. Models suggest packing helps marks copy themselves along the fibre. The authors saw like packing at real genes as cells took on new fates.
pmc-13394903:
Sianga Mutola and co-authors follow, in 2026, women in Zambia as they rejoin daily life after fistula surgery. Fistula, a childbirth injury, leaves women leaking and often shunned. The study tracked 2,172 women repaired at eight hospitals between 2017 and 2023. Scores blended five parts of social life, from family ties to work.

Most women left hospital dry, and dryness was the strongest driver of social recovery. Scores jumped most in the first three months, then held steady. Women still leaking gained ground too, and the gap slowly narrowed. The authors urge strong surgery plus early follow-up visits. Social support, they say, is part of the cure.
pmc-13395503:
Daniel Lowe and co-authors tell, in 2026, of stubborn belly fluid after a liver transplant that traced to a thieving spleen artery. A 65-year-old man got a new liver for alcohol-linked scarring. Fluid kept pooling, and scans showed the spleen artery drawing blood away from the liver graft. Bile ducts inside the graft also suffered from poor flow.

Two attempts to block the spleen artery from inside failed. Removing the spleen ended the fluid build-up and the bile trouble. The syndrome hides among more common causes of post-transplant fluid. The authors say surgery is a sound backup when artery blocking fails. Early scans of artery balance can speed the hunt.
pmc-13397103:
Marlon Rodriguez Valladares writes a 2026 viewpoint arguing that treating appendicitis with antibiotics alone, rather than surgery, cannot simply be imported into Honduras. Trials in rich countries found the drug route fails for roughly a quarter to a third of patients within a year, yet even those results rest on supports his setting lacks.

The trials assumed early arrival, dependable imaging, a steady antibiotic supply, planned follow-up, and a surgical team on standby. At one Honduran referral center, up to 54 percent of patients arrive with dead or burst appendixes, which removes them from the antibiotic option at once. Local habits, such as abdominal massage, add further delay, he notes.
pmc-13398103:
Josephine D Kahn and co-authors engineer an immune signal that switches on only inside tumours. Their 2026 study tackles interleukin-12, a potent immune activator whose body-wide action causes heavy side effects that have blocked its use against solid cancers. The design keeps IL-12 tied up until the protein meets a matrix marker found across tumours, fibronectin EDB.

A two-armed antibody holds the signal in a competitive grip; crowding at the tumour marker pries it open. Computer modelling first set the binding strengths needed, then phage screening and library design produced switches with the right grip. Lab tests confirmed activation depended on the tumour marker, a step toward strong immune therapy with a wider safety margin.
pmc-13398303:
Lauren R Sastre and colleagues evaluate Fresh Start, a food-as-medicine programme for rural North Carolina adults with type 2 diabetes and thin insurance cover. Their 2026 report covers the 2021 to 2024 rollout across 15 eastern counties. The 20-week scheme handed participants 5 to 7 pounds of produce at each of nine group classes, plus phone coaching one to one.

Programme records measured whether delivery worked as planned, while surveys and interviews captured how participants received it. Before-and-after questionnaires tracked knowledge, skills and habits, and chart review followed blood sugar control through HbA1c readings. The mixed verdict (reach, response and early health shifts) aims to show funders what a produce prescription can and cannot do.
pmc-13399103:
Ji and co-authors review, in 2026, prime editing as a route to treating neuropsychiatric disorders at their genetic roots. The technology fuses a reverse transcriptase to a modified Cas9 and reads its instructions from a guide RNA template. That lets it install base substitutions, small insertions, and deletions without double-strand DNA breaks. That precision suits brain diseases caused by single-letter mutations or small indels, which often produce severe, early-onset symptoms.

Studies in cells and animals have corrected pathogenic alleles and rescued function in monogenic neurodevelopmental disorders, proof of concept. The barriers to clinic are substantial: low editing efficiency in non-dividing neurons, guide design, reverse transcription errors, vector payload limits, and crossing the blood-brain barrier. They survey fixes, including split virus delivery systems, lipid nanoparticles, peptides, and compact Cas variants, and argue translation hinges on neuron-targeted, transient delivery plus genome-wide safety checks.
pmc-13399403:
Qiongyu Zhou and colleagues compared five large language models on oncology nursing decision support tasks, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. pmc-13399503:
Esther Omuseni and colleagues tracked COVID-19 infection and immunity across a rural community in western Kenya through six surveys, reporting in 2026. The authors say the pattern fits widespread natural exposure, while cautioning that unmeasured factors prevent crediting antibodies alone for the decline.
pmc-13399703:

The original work, by Inoguchi and colleagues, found that a higher percentage of oxidized albumin, HNA%, and lower bilirubin each predicted decline in activities of daily living. In an elderly diabetic cohort, death prevents the disability outcome rather than merely censoring it, and a standard Cox model can overstate the risk when deaths are simply censored. pmc-13399803:

pmc-13399903:

The unexpected electrophoresis band led to full genetic testing. The second change, IVS-I-6, is a beta-thalassemia variant that reduces how much beta-globin is made.

The authors stress that because the rare variant can mimic common patterns like HbC, only DNA analysis settles the identity.
pmc-13400603:

Vitamin D pathways may help control viral load, vitamin C can push infected cells toward death in lab work, and B vitamins have improved nerve symptoms in patients. The authors map what is known in both viruses and flag gaps for future work.
pmc-13400903:
Dsouza and colleagues wire a ten step assembly line that turns glucose into isobutanol, a fuel and feedstock, while recycling its helper molecules instead of washing them away. Cell free cascades beat fermentation on control, but redox steps burn through nicotinamide cofactors. In flow reactors they drain off. Their 2026 study fuses the redox enzymes into pairs linked by peptide straps. Each strap carries one attachment point where a tagged cofactor is locked on permanently.

The machines kept working and made isobutanol in both batch and continuous flow runs with no free cofactor added. pmc-13401403:
Gregoire Zerr, David Eichler, Pierre Imbert, and Christian Lutz contributed a 2026 technical note on a combined knee operation. A known weakness of band-based techniques is a thinner graft than hamstring alternatives.

Their modification folds a detached distal strip of the band back over the graft's central portion. This thickens the part inside the joint without harvesting any extra tendon, and it keeps the graft's natural continuity. Other teams had solved the size problem by adding a gracilis tendon graft, which the authors note is reliable but debatable. The note lays out the self-augmenting method step by step so other surgeons can reproduce it.
pmc-13401703:

Equations are displayed for transparency, results export to PDF and Excel, and a glossary links to regulator resources. The tool was validated against a commercial interaction calculator under the same guidance conditions.
pmc-13402003:
Muhammad Zulqarnain and Ilyas Mukhtar recount a 60-year-old man found unresponsive in his garden on a hot summer day, with a core temperature above 42.2 degrees Celsius on first measurement by responders. Cooling and supportive care woke him quickly. Blood tests then showed raised high-sensitivity troponin T, a heart injury marker, yet his heart tracing showed no clear heart attack pattern.

Because he had heart risk factors and no clear cause for the collapse, doctors treated him as a non-ST-elevation heart attack case. A heart ultrasound showed one wall segment moving poorly, and an angiogram found tight narrowing in the proximal left anterior descending artery, treated with a stent procedure. The case warns that heat stroke can raise heart markers while real artery disease hides underneath, so both need checking.
pmc-13402103:
Xiao and colleagues mine a loneliness survey to test a theory of ageing. How older people judge their loneliness, and what meaning they make of it, decides whether age brings more of it. They softened how strongly loneliness struck, though not length. Nothing appeared in the younger group. The text split into two themes, limited social function and unsatisfying relationships, weighted differently by age. Uniform interventions, the authors argue, will miss what changes with age.
pmc-13402703:

Hard tasks build resilience to distribution shifts, but ranking task difficulty requires expensive testing through environment trials or model passes. Their method uses a small generative model that predicts each task's adaptation risk and ranks tasks from that.

The method ranks task difficulty while spreading the testing cost. It plugs into zero-shot, few-shot, and supervised fine-tuning pipelines for foundation models and general policies. Across experiments in pattern recognition with foundation models and in sequential decisions, the approach improved adaptation strength on tail-risk and out-of-distribution tasks. pmc-13403603:
Masao Shioda led a 2026 case of repeated neck bleeding in a man with a genetic disorder that weakens blood vessels. The 67-year-old arrived with sudden neck swelling and no injury at all. Scans showed a large blood pocket pushing his windpipe aside and an active leak from a small artery branch.

Doctors sealed the leak from inside the vessel with a medical glue. Bleeding returned the next day from two other artery branches, so a second sealing session was done. No more bleeding followed, and he recovered with basic support care. Early close watch after the first fix is the core lesson.
pmc-13403803:
Jahnelle Jackson and Jonathan S. Berg argued in 2026 that smart gene screening policy needs solid records of how rare single-gene diseases unfold over a life. Gene reading keeps getting cheaper and faster, yet knowing a variant is not the same as knowing when illness starts. Onset age, reach, and severity vary a lot between conditions.

Such natural history facts decide what to screen for and when screening can help or harm. Rare diseases hit few people each, yet together they affect about 300 million people worldwide. Half show signs early in life, often before age five. Careful records of disease course can sharpen both screening plans and bedside choices.
pmc-13404003:
Saif Ali Malik headed a 2026 case of a woman who developed a runaway immune storm after a liver transplant, then a fatal fungal invasion. The 30-year-old received a new liver for sudden liver failure of unknown cause. Fever, low blood counts, and a faltering graft are warning signs of the storm state, called HLH.

Such signs have many causes after transplant, which makes the call hard. Standard scoring tools can speed the diagnosis when used early. pmc-13404303:

A general engagement factor explained about 85 percent of shared answer spread in both forms. The three named parts kept almost no reliable spread of their own once the general factor was counted. The long form also wobbled in tests, with one model failing to settle. A single total score from the short nine-item form looks most defensible for campus well-being checks.
pmc-13405003:
