Poor micronutrient intake in pregnancy harms mothers and babies, yet local levels were not well documented. The study ran in public clinics from January to March 2024.

About 420 women aged 18 and older who attended antenatal care took part. Each woman recalled everything she ate and drank in the previous 24 hours. Nutrient values were computed with Ethiopian and world food tables, then scored with adequacy ratios. Statistical modelling searched for predictors of inadequate intake, giving local planners a picture of which women need dietary support most.
pmc-13407403:
Lan Sun and co-authors, in 2026, watched how three kinds of carbon nanoparticle get inside cervical cancer cells grown in dishes. Activated carbon particles interest the group as possible drug carriers. The team compared them with carbon nanotubes and quantum dots. Entry routes, cell damage, and final particle locations were all tracked.

All three slowed cell growth more as dose and time rose. Under microscopes, treated cells shrank, lost grip on the surface, and showed membrane damage that differed by particle type. Flow tests and DNA assays found raised cell death and DNA injury across the board. Electron images caught carbon particles crossing into the cytoplasm and even the nucleus. pmc-13408203:

The authors recast the prediction problem in terms of distances between atoms instead of fixed coordinates.

Their generative flow model learns to evolve a starting guess along a transport-inspired path toward chemically sensible structures, using a two-branch network. On benchmark reaction sets it produced starting structures closer to the true transition state than coordinate-based rivals, sped up later refinement, and handled reactions it had not seen in training. Chemists gain a faster front end for reaction modelling and catalyst design work.
pmc-13408403:

In dishes they slashed colon cancer cell survival at the highest dose while sparing normal fibroblasts more, halted several staphylococcus species, and showed modest antioxidant activity. pmc-13410603:

One member, labeled 4h, stood out, clearing wide zones against two bacterial species. Computer docking placed that compound neatly into a bacterial enzyme pocket with the best binding score of the set. Its fat-liking balance also looked drug-like on paper.
pmc-13410803:

Blocking the signal or dissolving the traps eased injury in mice, pointing to fresh drug targets.
pmc-13411103:

pmc-13412603:

Broad intravenous antibiotics alone did not settle her severe pain, prompting a camera inspection of the abdomen. pmc-13413803:

pmc-13416903:

The group held 892 women from the Capital Region of Denmark, scanned up to 28 years after the affected pregnancy. One marker, placental growth factor, ran higher in women with artery plaque, though the link weakened after adjustment. Other marker levels did not differ. The authors treat the result as a lead for more work.
pmc-13418503:

pmc-13418603:

pmc-13418703:

pmc-13420303:

pmc-13420603:

pmc-13421303:

pmc-13421603:

pmc-13421803:

pmc-13422303:

pmc-13422703:

pmc-13422803:

pmc-13423803:

The authors present the waste stream as a way to support circular farming.
pmc-13424403:

pmc-13424603:

pmc-13424803:

pmc-13425403:

pmc-13425503:

pmc-13425603:

pmc-13425903:

pmc-13427603:
Tuna Aras and co-authors reply, in 2026, to commentary on their case of an unusual aortic arch, the big artery leaving the heart. pmc-13430203:

pmc-13431703:

pmc-13432903:

pmc-13433803:

pmc-13434003:

pmc-13434403:

pmc-13434503:

pmc-13434603:

pmc-13435003:

pmc-13435903:

pmc-13437203:

pmc-13438203:

pmc-13438303:

pmc-13439203:

pmc-13439303:

pmc-13440703:

pmc-13440803:

pmc-13442403:

pmc-13443303:

pmc-13444103:

pmc-13445503:

pmc-13446203:

pmc-13446303:

pmc-13447103:

pmc-13447503:

pmc-13447903:

pmc-13449003:

pmc-13449303:

pmc-13449703:

pmc-13450503:

pmc-13451503:

pmc-13451603:

pmc-13451803:

pmc-13452203:

pmc-13453003:

Tests showed the curves followed complex patterns without overfitting and flagged true deviations reliably. The authors offer the tool for first-pass screening of fresh registry data.
pmc-13453503:
Prapaporn Suprasert, Sopita Prasertpakdi, Tip Pongsuvareeyakul, and Surapan Khunamornpong review a rare muscle tumor of the cervix seen in adults, adding one harsh case of their own. The tumor, embryonal rhabdomyosarcoma, usually strikes children, and adult cases leave doctors with thin guidance. Their 2026 review gathers 41 adult cases from reports between 2015 and 2026.

Their own patient, a 50 year old woman with odd vaginal bleeding, had her womb and ovaries removed, then a three drug course. Despite full treatment, the tumor swept back in her pelvis and she died 13 months after diagnosis. The wider set tells a kinder story on the whole: median age 38, most cases caught early, and surgery plus drugs the norm. The authors flag gene changes in DICER1 as a clue that may sort mild cases from deadly ones.
pmc-13454703:
Lopez-Valdivia and co-authors simulate maize roots to find which traits suit many soils at once. Their 2026 study phenotyped roots of 96 maize landraces from the Americas, originally grown in glasshouse chambers, inside a functional-structural model that grows virtual plants in their native soil conditions. The question was which root features adapt a landrace to its home soil, and which travel well.

Landraces from low-phosphorus regions had shallow-angled roots with more nodal roots, a pattern suited to foraging the topsoil where phosphorus sits. Machine learning singled out two anatomical states as most important for stability across environments: large cortical cells and slimmer roots at two upper nodes. Anatomy that cheapens soil exploration, rather than architecture, carried broad adaptation. Slimming roots by cutting cortical cell files alone boosted simulated shoot growth strongly under drought, low nitrogen, and low phosphorus alike.
pmc-13455103:
An and colleagues reinvent a classic chemistry concept for computer materials design in this 2026 study. Electronegativity, a single number describing how strongly an atom attracts electrons, is too crude to capture the varied chemical neighborhoods inside real materials. The team built richer descriptors. Most elements got multi-number vectors, optimized against the energy gained when materials form. Complex-valued versions encoded two classic definitions at once.

They fed these descriptors into crystal graph neural networks, including a complex-valued variant, which model materials as networks of atoms and bonds. The new representations captured local atomic interactions more accurately and made the networks converge better during training in the experiments reported. The authors present the approach as a promising route to faster, more reliable discovery of new materials by computation rather than trial and error in the lab.
pmc-13455503:
Hui Li and six colleagues show, in a 2026 study, that not all strains of a celebrated gut bacterium calm bowel inflammation equally. Pasteurized Akkermansia muciniphila, killed by heat for safety, has drawn interest for ulcerative colitis. The team screened 39 heat-treated strains in a cell inflammation test, then tried the hopefuls in mice with chemically induced colitis.

Strain strength varied widely. One strain, labeled AKK2645 in the study, won in both the dish and the mouse. It rebalanced colon immune cells toward calm types, lowered a suite of inflammatory messages, and raised soothing ones. Gut sequencing showed helpful genera growing under the strain while suspect genera shrank. The authors stress that benefits here are strain-specific property, not a species-wide promise, and they nominate AKK2645 for development as a colitis aid.
pmc-13455603:
Fanhao Kong and Zhong-Shuai Wu lay out, in a 2026 perspective, a cell design that makes chemicals and electricity at the same time, with no power input. Ordinary batteries draw energy from their electrode materials. These electrocatalytic galvanic cells instead run on outside feedstocks, with each electrode acting as a catalyst for one half of a paired reaction.

The voltage gap between a willing oxidation at one side and a willing reduction at the other pushes electrons through the circuit on their own. Candidate inputs include farm biomass, industrial waste, pollutants, air, and water. Outputs can be fuels, commodity chemicals, or useful intermediates, plus usable current. The authors trace two construction strategies and sketch what scale-up would demand, from power density to product purity. They pitch the design as a green complement to fossil-based chemical plants.
pmc-13457203: A drug called bestatin slows skin melanoma by dialing down a protein named LTA4H. Pan Luo, Mingyi Yang, Yani Su, and others uncover the mechanism. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is melanoma pharmacology. It shows bestatin inhibiting cutaneous melanoma development through LTA4H suppression, pointing to a possible new angle against the deadliest skin cancer.
pmc-13457703: An oral GLP-1 pill — orforglipron — may protect kidneys through several workings. Prerana Ramadurgum, Joel Shah, and others review them. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is renal drug research. It explores promise nephroprotective workings of the oral non-peptide GLP-1 agonist in detail.
pmc-13458403:
Trojnar and colleagues turned in 2026 a cancer drug's worst side mark, skin burn in light, into its mode of attack. The drug hugs a knot form of DNA found at gene starts and strand caps. In bare brew it makes both kinds of harsh air bits when lit. Bound to the knots, its light math flips: one kind fades, and free rad sparks take the lead. The team read the sparks, then dosed cancer cells and mice.

Lit drug killed cancer cells at up to a hundredth the dark dose. Harm marks stacked in the cell's code, and the knots them selves came loose. In mice, lit doses shrank tumors and stretched life. Dead cells wailed in ways that wake guard cells, a plus for joint care. The team pitches light aim at tumors as the path to use a known drug anew.
pmc-13458903:
Jin and colleagues argue that a thickened heart wall, found on ultrasound, should start a diagnosis hunt rather than end one. Left ventricular hypertrophy means a wall thicker than set cutoffs. It most often comes from high blood pressure. But it can also signal inherited muscle disease, amyloid deposits, or Fabry disease, a storage disorder. Their 2026 article warns that wall thickness alone cannot tell these apart, yet the right label matters, since each cause now has its own therapy.

Delays are long: amyloid heart disease takes five to six years to name, and Fabry disease more than thirteen years, by the authors' figures. They propose a two step pathway guided by the pattern of clues. Frontline care gathers family history, body signs, heart tracings, and imaging red flags. These split plain pressure effects from suspect cases. Specialist centers then confirm the cause so treatment can start early.
pmc-13459203:
Mohd Aizuddin Mohd Zulastri and co-authors report a 54 year old Malaysian woman whose hidden lung cancer first announced itself through fluid squeezing her heart. She arrived with three weeks of productive cough, low fever, and breathlessness on exertion. She was first treated for pneumonia with fluid around one lung. In their 2026 case report, the authors describe how her symptoms persisted despite antibiotics and drainage. A scan then revealed fluid completely surrounding the heart with signs of cardiac tamponade, dangerous pressure on the heart, even though her blood pressure stayed normal.

An urgent needle drainage removed 600 milliliters of blood stained fluid, and lab analysis of that fluid found malignant glandular cancer cells. Body imaging then revealed a right upper lung mass with spread to the chest lining, pericardium, bones, adrenal glands, and skin. The authors stress that early heart ultrasound and fluid testing are essential when effusions remain unexplained.
pmc-13459603:
Yang Niu and co-authors examined how stroke type affects thinking and speech, using artificial intelligence to analyze patients' voices for diagnostic clues. Their 2026 study compared 117 people at a hospital in Anhui, China, in three groups: lacunar infarction, where tiny deep vessels block; larger non-lacunar infarction; and healthy controls. Everyone took a standard cognitive screening test and described a standard picture aloud, generating speech recordings from which acoustic features were extracted.

Both stroke groups scored lower on cognition than controls, and the non-lacunar group performed worst overall. The gap showed clearly in fluency tasks, where the non-lacunar group differed most from controls, and in memory tasks, where both stroke groups lagged. The speech analysis also found acoustic features that differed between the two stroke types themselves. Voice features could help distinguish small deep strokes from larger ones, the authors suggest, cheaply and non-invasively.
pmc-13460103:
Hao Chen and a Beijing team compared in 2026 two strategies for repairing disease of the aortic arch, the curved top of the body's main artery. Hybrid repair reroutes the branches above the arch and then relines the aorta from inside, while the frozen elephant trunk operation replaces the arch in open surgery. Records for 785 patients treated at Beijing Anzhen Hospital from 2015 to 2023 were analyzed, with statistical weighting to balance the groups.

Hybrid patients were older and carried more diabetes and lipid problems before adjustment. Even so, their operations involved less blood loss and quicker recovery than the open procedure, advantages that persisted after weighting. The study weighs those perioperative gains against later outcomes such as death, stroke, and repeat intervention, informing choices for patients unfit for the bigger operation.
pmc-13460203:
Josefina Principe and Facundo Iriarte review in 2026 an uncommon surgical route for closing bronchopleural fistula, a leaking airway stump left after a lung is removed. Rather than reopening the original chest incision, surgeons approach through the breastbone and the sac around the heart, reaching the central airway from the front. The review gathers case series and technical reports on who qualifies, how the closure is reinforced, and what outcomes follow.

The front route avoids dissecting through an infected, scarred chest cavity, and published series report durable closure with acceptable complication rates in chosen patients. Results vary widely, reflecting differences in patient condition, fistula size, infection, and earlier failed repairs. Bronchoscopy and camera assistance are emerging helpers, yet the research base remains small and retrospective.
pmc-13461503:
Hikmat Abdel-Razeq and colleagues report in 2026 germline genetic findings from 652 Jordanian men diagnosed with cancer at age fifty or younger. Inherited risk is often suspected in this group yet rarely mapped outside Western populations. Every man in the King Hussein Cancer Center program received multigene panel testing of inherited DNA regardless of tumor type, stage, or family history, and results were sorted against standard testing criteria.

Ninety men, about fourteen percent, carried a clearly harmful inherited variant, and a third carried an uncertain one. Yield ran far higher in men meeting standard criteria, and youngest patients, those diagnosed between eighteen and thirty, showed the richest haul at over a quarter testing positive. Colorectal cancer dominated the case mix and the positive findings, with six genes recurring most often.
pmc-13462003:
Lindsey Vilca and co-authors examined the internal structure of the PHQ-4, a four question anxiety and depression screener, across four Latin American countries using network psychometrics. That newer framework treats symptoms as a web of interacting items. Whether the scale forms one dimension or two, anxiety versus depression, has been argued from older methods. In their 2026 study, 1,887 adults aged eighteen to forty from Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru completed the questionnaire. Community detection analysis mapped how the four items cluster in each country.

In all four countries the four items formed a single community with large network loadings, supporting one unified dimension of distress rather than separable clusters. Redundancy analysis confirmed every item contributed uniquely to the network in each national sample. The structure held consistently across countries with different sample sizes. For Latin American screening practice, the authors conclude, the PHQ-4 works best scored as one total.
pmc-13462403:
Cheng and co-authors proposed a 2026 review framing inflammatory bowel disease as a disorder of chemical conversation between gut microbes and the body. Microbes release metabolites, small molecules such as short-chain fatty acids and bile acid products, that shape the gut barrier and immune activity. The authors call the lasting imprint of those signals microbial metabolic memory.

Cheng argues that helpful metabolites dwindle while inflammatory ones build up, breaking immune tolerance and weakening the barrier even during remission. Inflammation then reshapes the gut environment, which pushes microbes to make yet more inflammatory products, locking in a feedback loop. That loop may explain why the disease keeps relapsing after symptoms settle. Treatments discussed include adding back helpful metabolites, blocking harmful signals, engineered probiotics, and diet guided precision care.
pmc-13463503:
Gavin Haines and three co-authors review nitrate poisoning in cattle and other ruminants, in a 2026 paper on farm animal health. Forage can build up nitrate under drought, frost, or heavy fertilizer use. Once eaten, that nitrate can turn to nitrite in the rumen and block the blood from carrying oxygen well.

Guidance for safe intake levels varies a great deal between sources and between states, the authors show. Much of the base research is old, and fresh work since the 1970s has been thin. Their review sorts the factors that drive buildup and risk, then presses for clear, proof-based limits. Ranchers and vets get a plain map of where the rules agree and where they still clash.
pmc-13463603:
Mohammad Faraz Zafeer and a large team study how a distant gene switch controls GDF6, a gene needed to build the cochlea. The cochlea is the snail-shaped hearing part of the inner ear. Switches far from a gene can still turn its activity up or down.

Human ear organoids, small lab-grown ear models, showed the same dependence on the switch. The findings help explain deafness in patients who lack this stretch of DNA.
pmc-13463703:
Ana María Quirós and colleagues profiled the nutrition of a Costa Rican cricket powder to judge its value as human food. The cricket belongs to the genus Gryllus, though its form hints it may differ from described species.

Corrected for shell fibre, the protein content reached about 61.5 grams per 100 grams of dry powder, with fat near 11.7 grams. Essential amino acids made up about 56.5 percent of all amino acids, a strong share, though lysine ran short against world reference patterns. The powder was rich in potassium, phosphorus, and calcium, and its fats were mostly the heart-friendlier unsaturated kinds. Quirós concludes the cricket could complement other proteins in sustainable foods, best paired with lysine-rich partners.
pmc-13464403:
Al-Hatab and colleagues built in 2026 a light computer pipeline that sorts brain MRI scans into four stages of Alzheimer's disease, from no dementia to moderate dementia. Sorting stages accurately helps plan care, but heavy deep-learning systems demand costly hardware. The team wanted a lean method that still scores high.

Their pipeline pulls features from scans with a compact pre-trained network, then shrinks the feature list with principal component analysis, a method that keeps the most informative parts. A hundred kept components held nearly all the signal. Several classifiers were then tested, and a fuzzy neural method called EFMM won, scoring about 97 percent accuracy on held-out scans and about 98 percent across repeated validation folds. The authors present the pipeline as a fast, low-cost aid for staging the disease.
pmc-13466903:
Marta Carnovali and colleagues feed zebrafish a diet laced with PFOA, a persistent industrial chemical. Their 2026 study watches what happens to the fish's bones and to their offspring. Exposed young adult fish grew shorter and lighter than unexposed controls. Their scales, which soak up the chemical into the mineral layer, shrank in area.

Bone-building cells in the scales worked less while bone-eating cells worked harder, especially at the scale's center. The inner skeleton showed malformations across spine, ribs, fins, and jaw structures. Embryos from exposed parents were also checked for viability and development, extending the harm picture across a generation.
pmc-13467003:
Tingting Wen, Bing Xiong, Chengjie Mei, and Shengwen Song present four anesthesia patients who inhaled stomach contents and were treated by washing the airways through a scope, in a 2026 case series. Aspiration during anesthesia can be life-threatening, and whether washing helps or spreads contamination further has long been debated. The four were high-risk patients who had inhaled large amounts of fluid, solid food, or bile.

After washing with a quarter to over two thirds of a liter of saline into the affected lung sections, every patient's oxygen levels improved at once and airway pressures fell. None developed severe pneumonia or lung failure, and follow-up scans showed no spread of contamination. One patient even had pre-existing lung injury from pancreatitis and still recovered well.
pmc-13467103:
Boyi Wei and colleagues designed a foldable honeycomb material studded with resonators that blocks low-frequency waves and softens impacts. The structure builds on the Miura-ori fold pattern, adding tuned vibrating masses inside a polygonal honeycomb.

Analysis and lab tests found two complete bandgaps, frequency ranges no wave can cross, in the low-frequency zone. Widening the resonators merged two narrow gaps into one broader gap, giving designers a tuning knob. Under impact pulses, the material cut peak reaction force by 43.43 percent versus the same honeycomb without resonators. The peak force also arrived 26 milliseconds later, spreading the blow over more time. Eight resonators per cell proved the best balance of performance and light weight, Wei reports.
pmc-13467803:
Li, Lan, and Yao primed a 2026 study of sweet sorghum seed soaked in gibberellic acid, a plant hormone, to harden seedlings against drought. How the leaf cuticle, the waxy skin that seals in water, responds to such priming was unclear. A screening test first picked the dose that helped growth most under dry conditions.

Under drought, primed plants boosted leaf alkanes and primary alcohols sharply, and one waxy compound rose more than four fold. Li found primed plants also lost water from leaves most slowly, matching their heavier cuticle deposits. The work used a single sorghum genotype under controlled conditions, so field confirmation remains open.
pmc-13467903:
Gan and colleagues describe an unusual cancer case in this 2026 report: a palate tumor that returned as neck lymph node metastasis more than a decade after seemingly successful treatment. The tumor type was mucoepidermoid carcinoma, the most common cancer of the salivary glands, in this instance arising in the hard palate of a 47-year-old woman.

Her original, well-differentiated tumor was removed surgically, and she stayed clear for 11 years before lumps appeared in the right side of her neck. Surgeons at Guangxi Medical University removed the neck mass completely along with the surrounding lymph nodes, and pathology confirmed the same carcinoma had spread. Eleven months after the second operation she remained under follow-up. The authors stress that even low-grade palate tumors keep a long tail of metastasis risk, so close surveillance should extend for many years.
pmc-13468003:
Weixuan Liu and colleagues review in 2026 how quantum dots, tiny semiconductor crystals, can push perovskite solar cells closer to their theoretical limits. Perovskite cells already exceed 26 percent certified efficiency, yet they still fall short of the maximum possible and degrade too fast for the market. Quantum dots bring size-tunable energy levels, bright light output, and easy solution processing to that fight.

The review examines four ways of adding the dots: modifying the charge transport layers, doping the active layer, converting ultraviolet light into usable light, and serving as sub-cells in tandem stacks. It compares the mechanisms behind each, from defect repair to slowing ion drift. It also names the open problems, including toxic lead and cadmium in many dots and the lack of standard stability tests. The framework helps cell designers pick the right dot strategy for each layer.
pmc-13468103:
Sakhile T. Dube, Lindelani Q. Qwabe and Holger B. Friedrich published this 2026 review on turning waste glycerol into glycerol carbonate, a useful chemical for solvents and plastics. Glycerol floods the market as a biodiesel by-product, so upgrading it adds value. The route reviewed reacts glycerol with alkyl carbonates, helped by catalysts made from mixed metal oxides. The authors examine how these catalysts work, aided by computer modelling.

Catalysts pairing metals such as magnesium with aluminium, iron, zirconium or barium converted over 90 percent of the glycerol fed in. Of the product, 90 to 96 percent was the carbonate, often without solvents. Modelling showed the secret is teamwork between basic sites, which strip a proton from glycerol, and acidic sites, which activate the carbonate partner. The review also covers microwave and ultrasound heating to speed the process. The authors map what blocks scale-up, including catalyst fouling and metal loss.
pmc-13469303:
Ya-Nan Zhang and co-authors build in a 2026 letter a safer screening system for hunting drugs against Mayaro virus. The mosquito-borne alphavirus causes fever, headache, joint pain, and rash much like chikungunya. The virus is classed at biosafety level 3, which makes live-virus drug screening slow and restricted, and no approved vaccine or specific treatment exists. Their solution is a replicon: a stripped viral genome that copies itself inside cells without producing infectious virus.

The replicon carries a drug-resistance marker and a light-producing reporter gene, and it was installed in a stable hamster cell line kept under puromycin selection. Compound activity then reads out as fading light, enabling high-throughput screening in ordinary containment. A screening platform that removes the dangerous virus from the assay lets many more laboratories join the search for Mayaro antivirals.
pmc-13471303:
Xiang and an international team showed in 2026 how black soldier fly larvae staff their gut with microbes to digest tough plant waste they cannot break down alone. Larvae raised germ-free barely degraded the fiber at all, while larvae with gut microbes degraded about a third. The team mapped immune activity and sugar-coating genes along the gut, profiling microbe communities in each section.

The gut runs a dismissing-then-recruiting strategy: the front midgut bristles with antimicrobial weapons, a selective barrier killing most arrivals. The rear midgut lowers its immune guard and ramps up genes coating surfaces with sugars, a four-to-fivefold rise. Those sugars feed exactly the symbionts thriving there, microbes armed with fiber-cutting enzymes. The rear gut thus farms its workforce rather than tolerating it. The authors say the principle could improve industrial waste conversion with these larvae, already farmed for protein and waste processing.
pmc-13471403:
Wang and co-authors searched for a way to make kidney tumors that resist PARP inhibitors, a class of DNA-repair-blocking drugs, vulnerable to them. Tumors with normal BRCA genes, usually unmoved by these inhibitors, were the specific target.

The effect depended on SLFN11, a protein missing in about 45% of cancer cells, which marked which tumors responded. Combinations shrank tumors in mouse xenografts and in patient-derived tumor grafts, and every drug involved is already approved for cancer treatment.
pmc-13471503:
Han and co-authors pooled trials of online advance care planning decision aids, websites that help cancer patients record future care wishes. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis gathered 12 studies, including 10 randomized trials, mostly from the United States, searching the literature through March 10, 2026.

The programs worked where it matters most administratively: patients using them were about twice as likely to have planning documented, with an odds ratio of 2.06 in the pooled analysis, and engagement scores rose by 0.28 points on average. But completing an advance directive itself did not significantly improve, with an odds ratio of 1.37 whose interval crossed no effect. Satisfaction, decisional conflict, and anxiety also showed no clear change.
pmc-13471603:
Feyissa and colleagues asked new mothers in Adama town, Ethiopia, whether they could recognize the warning signs that a newborn needs urgent care. Their 2026 cross-sectional study interviewed 426 postpartum women at public facilities during April 2022, testing recognition of nine World Health Organization danger signs with prompted yes-or-no items.

Three quarters scored well: 75.5% of mothers showed good knowledge by the study's cutoff, far above the 20.3 to 67.1% range reported in earlier Ethiopian studies. Education drove the gap, with college-educated mothers at 4.83 times the adjusted odds of good knowledge and secondary schooling at 3.10 times the odds. Caesarean delivery, at 2.47 times the odds, and having given birth before also helped, which the authors link to longer contact with health staff.
pmc-13472003:
Baptiste Ganachaud and colleagues review in 2026 how gut microbes and the gut own nervous system interact in the digestive troubles that shadow autism. The enteric nervous system, the nerve web governing gut movement, sits exactly between those microbes and gut function.

Serotonin related and metabolite pathways feature heavily in that traffic. The authors suggest the gut nerve interface may also feed back on behavioral severity, making it a therapeutic target worth testing rather than a curiosity.
pmc-13472803:
Ren and colleagues present a 2026 comprehensive review of blood-based monitoring of ESR1 mutations in advanced breast cancer that is hormone-sensitive and HER2-negative. First-line treatment pairs hormone therapy with CDK4/6 inhibitors, but resistance grows, and mutations in the estrogen receptor gene ESR1 are a central escape route. Tumor DNA circulating in blood lets doctors track these mutations without repeat biopsies.

The review weighs the value of ESR1 mutations found before treatment and during it: they forecast worse outcomes on standard therapy and can signal when to switch to newer receptor-targeted drugs. Because mutation levels rise and fall with treatment, they act as moving decision points rather than fixed labels.
pmc-13473003:
Ladányi and colleagues report a 2026 study of tumor-infiltrating immune cells as predictors in melanoma patients given PD-1 inhibitor drugs after surgery. A tumor's immune mix at surgery thus carries information about whether adjuvant therapy will hold.  Such markers are urgent because the drugs are costly and can cause lasting side effects.
pmc-13473503:
Hafsa Khan and colleagues put forward a neural network method in 2026 for equations with memory and delay effects. It uses a smooth memory kernel that avoids sharp faults found in older forms.

Four test problems checked the method, from delayed growth rules to circuit models. Error levels stayed very low across the tests, near the floor set for the runs. Charts of error over training backed up the headline scores. The work gives modelers a flexible solver for systems where the past shapes the present.
pmc-13473703:
Erdoğmuş and colleagues in Türkiye tested in 2026 whether a folk herb, Anchusa azurea, can speed wound healing when packed in tiny fat bubbles. Wounds shrank faster, and tissue checks showed more collagen, more new blood paths, and quicker new skin. The alcohol brew and its bubble form led the pack. The team backs them for wound care goods.
pmc-13473803: Correction notice: Sylvain Rama, Thomas P. Jensen and Dmitri A. Rusakov correct Figure 2 of their 2026 article on glutamate imaging in the giant mossy fiber boutons of the brain's CA3 region. The figure appeared heavily distorted in the online version, and the notice supplies the corrected version, which also appears in the PDF. The figure shows distinct glutamate release sites inside single large boutons, with line-scan traces capturing releases that are not synchronised between sites, including spontaneous events. The original article has been updated.
pmc-13474003:
Phillips and co-workers in Australia read in 2026 the files of a state body that runs a new web of help hubs for the families of people with mental ills. Its meets gave a far flung new workforce a place to swap craft and feel one team. The authors set out steps that like bodies can use to name their own work values.
pmc-13474703:
Xuhao Liu, Minfeng Chen, and Yi Cai test chatbots as teaching aids in 2026 for prostate cancer training of urology residents. Three leading models answered a forty-item question bank and were graded blind by experts. The top scorer then joined a small randomized teaching trial with thirty-four residents. Both trial groups got the same lectures, with one group allowed model help for study questions.

One model, DeepSeek R1, ranked first, with an edge on higher-order and creative questions. The aided group scored about ten points higher on a closed-book exam. Gains concentrated in choice questions and research items, not in team case review. Teachers and students both rated the aid well, which supports careful classroom use.
pmc-13474803:
Song and co-authors studied in 2026 which psoriasis patients test positive on the interferon-gamma release assay, a blood test for latent tuberculosis that guidelines recommend before starting biologic therapy. A positive result can delay treatment, yet the factors behind positivity in this population were poorly characterized. The team reviewed records from a single dermatology center and built a statistical model of the associations.

Older age, pulmonary nodules, and a higher eosinophil percentage each independently raised the odds of positivity, while prior biologic exposure lowered them, likely through selection effects. The eight-variable model discriminated acceptably. The authors say it adds context but must not replace standard tuberculosis assessment.
pmc-13475703:
Chunming Tan and seven colleagues published this 2026 food science study on how vacuum-packed marinated silver carp, a popular Chinese freshwater fish product, spoils over 60 days of storage. The team tracked appearance and taste acceptance, spoilage markers, flavour compounds and the bacteria living on the fish, tying the threads of spoilage into one story.

Protein and fat oxidation advanced together, shown by rising spoilage nitrogen and fat breakdown values, falling protective sulfhydryl groups and rising carbonyls. The authors offer the combined picture as a basis for keeping fish fresh.
pmc-13475803:
Lin Chen and seven colleagues published this 2026 case report of one patient, a 64-year-old man whose heart artery procedure caused a tear that spread into the aorta. During treatment of his right coronary artery, the tear began as a Dunning class II dissection. It resisted the rescue attempt: standard drug-eluting stents failed to seal the backward tear into the aortic root, and it progressed to class III.

The operators then placed a covered stent at the artery's opening, halting the dissection's advance. Strict blood pressure control and a surgical team on standby backed the rescue. The case is presented as the first report of this percutaneous strategy for this complication. The authors argue covered stents deserve a defined bailout role when standard stents cannot seal tears, avoiding emergency open-heart surgery in stable patients.
pmc-13476703:
