Treated T cells resisted IL-10 damping and fired up more strongly than with either part alone. Helper immune cells also shifted toward a mature, active state. Killer T cell activation beat checkpoint care alone and beat the loose mix of parts. Dual targeting may rescue patients whom single checkpoints fail.
pmc-13476903:
Kai Tsugaru and colleagues studied d-serine, a mirror-form amino acid, as a hidden brake on the immune attack against stomach tumours. Amino acids are the building blocks of proteins, and the d-form is the flipped twin of the usual l-form.

In mouse tumours, d-serine weakened killer T cells and boosted suppressive macrophages, the immune cells that calm attacks down. Blood, urine, and stool levels of d-serine ran higher in stomach cancer patients than in 87 healthy controls. Higher blood levels tracked later disease stages across the patient groups studied. Patients with high levels also answered poorly to a standard immune therapy drug, marking d-serine as a warning sign.
pmc-13478603:
Kefan Chen and colleagues report a 2026 climate study reconstructing the Atlantic overturning circulation across the last preindustrial millennium. This circulation moves heat northward and shapes climate worldwide, yet its past behavior and causes stayed disputed. The team combined indirect natural records, several climate models, and a data assimilation method that merges both.

Their reconstruction shows the circulation slowly weakening from the year 850 into the Little Ice Age, losing roughly 0.7 sverdrups, about four percent of its flow. Explosive volcanic eruptions emerge as the main cause. Each eruption briefly strengthened the circulation, then left a century-scale weakening as cold stored in the deep Atlantic fed back on surface climate. The work offers a physical explanation for a long-debated trend.
pmc-13479203:
Dalibor Procházka and coauthors published a 2026 computer-model study of driverless ground craft for battlefield medical rescue runs. Speed from the point of injury to a casualty pickup point strongly shapes survival, and combat units now handle this leg with one armored vehicle per pickup point under current doctrine. The team modeled a possible fleet of robot craft.

Data on injury timing and place came from computer-aided drills, and the test used agent-based models mixed with discrete event models. Spread-out unmanned transport worked better because the wounded could be served by injury class first rather than in simple order. The authors stress the idea stays on paper for now. Benefits depend on AI support plus live data on each wounded soldier's state from body sensors.
pmc-13479503:
Mika P. Nadvornik and colleagues published a 2026 protocol for comparing antiseptic irrigation fluids in patients with abdominal abscesses drained through the skin. Drainage is the standard treatment, and saline rinsing cleans mechanically but kills no germs. Hypochlorous acid, an antiseptic the body itself produces, offers broad germ killing with good tissue tolerance.

The study exploits a hospital practice switch on the first of December 2025, comparing patients treated before and after in one center. Main questions are whether the antiseptic shortens drain time and the course of systemic antibiotics. The ambispective design combines records already collected with prospective follow-up. The authors pre-register their methods so the eventual results can be judged against a fixed plan.
pmc-13479703:
Angelika Lahnsteiner and coauthors published a 2026 analysis of how metabolic disease gene variants may act by breaking tiny folded DNA structures called G-quadruplexes. These four-stranded knots sit in gene control regions and tune how strongly genes are read. Genome studies have tied thousands of variants to metabolic diseases, yet most have no known mechanism.

Between about one and two percent of metabolic disease variants fell inside predicted quadruplex motifs, depending on the prediction method. The team tested how those variants change the structures' stability and shape, and whether they sit in alternative promoters also seen in cancer. A variant that collapses a quadruplex could raise or lower a gene's output, offering a concrete mechanism for otherwise mysterious statistical associations.
pmc-13480103:
Aman Shrestha and co-authors offer a 2026 pooled review of elder abuse among older adults living at home in South Asia. The team searched six databases plus grey sources and kept 33 studies from five countries, with most from India and Nepal. Adults aged sixty and above counted, and abuse within family or community settings formed the focus.

Across studies, about thirty-two percent of older adults reported abuse, though results varied so widely that the pooled figure needs care. Nepal showed the highest share near fifty percent, while India sat near twenty-six percent. Women faced abuse more often than men. Neglect by caregivers and emotional abuse were the most common forms, each near twenty percent. Three countries in the region had no usable studies at all. The authors call for country-level research and for community programs that fit local family norms.
pmc-13480203:
Yue-Loong Hsin and Min-Fei Chuang report a 2026 study of frailty among older adults admitted to hospital with epilepsy. The team drew on a national United States inpatient database spanning 2005 to 2022. Adults aged sixty and above with epilepsy as the main diagnosis numbered near 177,000 stays, and a standard frailty index sorted patients into frail and non-frail groups.

Nearly fifty-eight percent of stays counted as frail. After matching patients on other traits, frailty linked to more major complications, more urinary infections, longer stays, and more discharges to care settings rather than home, plus higher hospital costs. Oddly, frail patients showed lower death rates during the stay, which the authors tie to discharge patterns rather than protection. Spotting frailty early may help teams plan support and discharge for this group.
pmc-13481403:
Muyang Liu and Xiaojun Shen report a 2026 study of a stitch that may cut fluid build-up after keyhole groin hernia repair. Large hernia rings leave a pocket where fluid gathers after surgery. The team reviewed 162 patients with wide rings at one Chinese hospital across a year, half with the inner ring stitched shut during repair and half without.

Fluid pockets at one week struck under nine percent of the stitched group against over twenty-eight percent of the rest. At one month the gap held, near two percent against fourteen percent. By three months both groups matched. Surgery ran about three minutes longer with the stitch, while pain, other side issues, and early hernia return matched across groups. Closing the ring seems a cheap win against early fluid trouble.
pmc-13482303:
Abdullahi and colleagues propose a faster solver in 2026 for large systems of nonlinear equations, the kind that arise when cleaning up signals and restoring damaged images. Their method blends four existing conjugate gradient algorithms, a family of step-by-step solvers prized for low memory use, into one hybrid with a restart rule. Whenever progress slows, the search direction resets instead of dragging old information forward into the next step.

The hybrid inherits the strengths of its parents while keeping two safety properties, a guaranteed downhill direction at each step and bounded step sizes throughout the run. Under standard assumptions the authors prove the method converges globally and estimate how fast that convergence should be for large problems. On benchmark problems it reached solutions faster and more accurately than the existing methods it was compared against, and the paper points it at signal processing and image recovery tasks.
pmc-13482403:
Xiao and Zheng build an automated simulation system in 2026 for incremental launching, the method that slides a bridge into place segment by segment over its supports. Curved city bridges launched in linked sections strain older analysis tools, which miss working conditions and distort the geometry. Their system pairs quick one-dimensional models with detailed three-dimensional mapping and writes the simulation commands itself through a Python program.

They validated the approach on the Guangzhou-Shenzhen Expressway reconstruction, running 771 distinct working conditions across the whole launching sequence for the project. The system extracted support reactions, hinge shear forces, displacements, and stresses at each stage, and measured how deck curvature and twisting change those forces during the slide. The authors say the automated pipeline fixes the efficiency and coverage gaps of hand-built models and gives engineers a safer basis for launching bridges in tight urban sites.
pmc-13483603:
Liu and co-authors built a two-step deep-learning system that finds and labels each vertebra in chest and abdomen CT scans. Accurate labels matter for planning spine surgery, yet vertebrae look alike and span a long column, which trips up single-step software. Their 2026 framework first outlines the whole spine roughly, then pinpoints each bone's center with a coordinate-predicting module built for three-dimensional images.

The system lifted correct identification from about 81 percent to about 96 percent against the baseline approach compared. Average position error shrank from 7.6 millimeters to about 2 millimeters, a gain that matters when surgeons plan screw placement near nerves. The method beat current rival approaches on the test data used. Liu presents the two-stage design as a robust aid for spinal diagnosis and surgical planning.
pmc-13483903:
Ahmadullah and co-authors calculated how desert dust changes the right size for a home solar-plus-battery system in Saudi Arabia. Dust films steal sunlight, so a system sized for clean panels under-delivers once panels dirty. Their 2026 study examined real dust under microscopes, measured how it dims glass at three coating levels, then ran an economic model for a typical household that must never lose power.

Dust grains averaged about 50 micrometers across and cut glass light transmission to roughly a third at the heaviest coating tested. A clean-condition home system needed 21 panels and five batteries at the lowest electricity cost figure computed. The heaviest dust case demanded double the panels, nine batteries, and raised the cost figure by about 82 percent. Ahmadullah argues planners in arid regions must budget for dust or for cleaning.
pmc-13486103:
Dilson Lobo and co-workers measure each source of error in a diode tool that checks radiation dose inside the body. The dose is given in cobalt-60 brachytherapy, where seeds sit close to a tumor. For this 2026 study, the tool is tuned in plastic models of the body. Straight-line response is checked from 1 to 8 Gray. Slabs like bone, lung, and soft tissue are placed in the beam path.

Repeat reads swung by less than 2 percent across runs. Drift across piled-up doses stayed under 2.5 percent. Response stayed straight across the whole dose span. More results on tissue-like slabs sit in the full text. A bedside check guards patients only if its own error size is known. This work turns a neat tool into a trusted safety net.
pmc-13486803:
Hashii and colleagues report a phase 2 trial of a cancer vaccine for children whose leukaemia returned or resisted treatment. Their 2026 paper tests WT1 peptide vaccines given after a donor stem cell transplant, called allo-HSCT. WT1 is a protein found on leukaemia cells, and the vaccine aims to train the immune system to attack leftover disease without harming healthy tissue.

Children at three Japanese hospitals who had reached remission after transplant received the vaccine into the skin, weekly at first and then less often, for up to three years. Three years after treatment, 70.6 percent of vaccinated patients were alive, a share the authors contrast with about 30 percent in historical comparison patients. They conclude the maintenance vaccine appears both effective and safe in this hard-to-treat group.
pmc-13487303:
Jang and colleagues discovered that a long RNA molecule in liver cells has its own tumor-blocking job, separate from the famous small RNA it was thought merely to precede. The long form, lnc122, was dismissed as a raw intermediate for microRNA-122, a known liver guardian. Their 2026 study silenced the long form in liver cancer cells and mouse livers while leaving the small form's supply intact, then watched cancer-relevant pathways.

Silencing lnc122 let the growth-driving protein MYC accumulate, because lnc122 normally stabilizes the machinery that tags MYC for destruction. That machinery, built around the UBR5 protein, sits beside MYC in the genome and is co-amplified in over forty percent of human cancers. In a mouse liver tumor model driven by MYC, lnc122 held back tumor formation. Jang argues the long RNA deserves study as a cancer actor in its own right.
pmc-13487803:
Willem H Collier and co-workers test a ranked joint score for child cancer support care trials. Such trials juggle many key results at once, which clouds what a result means. A ranked joint score stacks results by clinical weight, so a win on life trumps a win on comfort in one sum. This 2026 work re-runs two large phase three trials from a US child cancer group with that lens.

The ranked score proved more apt to catch true gains than one-result reads. It also gave clear calls when a care step helped on one front yet hurt on the next. Fever bouts, drug use, blood infection, and death show the layers such trials must weigh. The team backs set use of the score when new trials are drawn up, not just in hindsight checks.
pmc-13488203:
Xiaojing Chen leads a large team studying a stress signal protein called GDF-15 in a 2026 analysis of United Kingdom Biobank data. Nearly thirty thousand people with early stages of cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic syndrome, a grouping of linked heart, kidney, and metabolic risks, had the protein measured. The team tracked who developed fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, or atherosclerotic heart and vessel disease, where fatty deposits narrow arteries.

Higher GDF-15 tracked with worse overall syndrome health, most strongly with kidney function measures. Each step up in the protein came with higher risk of both outcomes and of having both together in the reported models. Transitions ran both ways between the diseases. The authors test whether the marker sharpens risk prediction beyond standard factors.
pmc-13488303:
Sarah E. Philo and colleagues trace which bacteria carry antibiotic resistance genes through water reclamation plants in a 2026 study of three sites in North Carolina, Texas, and California. Samples of incoming wastewater, treatment sludge, and cleaned outflow were collected over three spring weeks. A sequencing method called Hi-C links DNA pieces that sit inside the same cell, revealing whether a resistance gene rides on a movable plasmid or sits on the chromosome.

The team found 244 distinct resistance genes, with seven present in every sample. Resistance genes were more often plasmid-borne in incoming water and more often chromosomal in sludge. Seventeen bacterial hosts still carried resistance genes in treated outflow. Four bacterial families accounted for over half of all host links.
pmc-13489703:
Samantha A. Swanson and a large team test copper feeding levels in young and growing pigs in a 2026 study with two experiments. Added copper can boost growth, and the trials used about 150 milligrams per kilogram of feed from different copper sources. The nursery trial followed more than two thousand small pigs for thirty-eight days across feeding phases, while the finishing trial followed a similar number of larger pigs for one hundred ten days.

Nursery pigs gained faster on added copper during the middle phase, yet overall performance did not differ between feeding schedules in the first experiment. Finishing pigs on added copper grew faster in the first half of the second trial, with no advantage later and no difference between copper sources in the reported results.
pmc-13490603:
Korczyńska and team read the gene activity of womb-lining tissue from women with two common benign growths, fibroids and polyps, comparing diseased-looking and normal-looking patches side by side. Both conditions impair fertility, yet their molecular footprints on the lining were unmapped. Their 2026 study sequenced paired samples collected during hysteroscopy from women before and around menopause, then contrasted the patterns statistically.

Normal-looking lining barely differed between the two conditions, with only nine genes separating the groups in that comparison. The lesional tissues diverged sharply instead, with 398 genes differing between fibroid and polyp samples in the reported analysis. Further contrasts within each condition traced how each growth remodels its own neighborhood, with fibroid tissue leaning on matrix and survival genes the authors name. Korczyńska concludes the two growths imprint distinct molecular signatures despite their shared benign label.
pmc-13490903:
Tjampakasari and colleagues profiled the resistance genes behind treatment failure of an antibiotic pairing in urinary E. coli from Indonesian patients, in a 2026 gene study. The drug pairing trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is increasingly defeated by acquired genes named dfr and sul, which bacteria trade between themselves. From 678 urine samples the team got a culture-positive set and studied eleven E. coli isolates in detail, with eight resistant ones.

Tjampakasari used DNA amplification and sequencing and found the resistance genes spread unevenly: some isolates carried dfrA5, one carried dfrA1, several carried sul2. Sul1 appeared unchanged from the version. Sequencing exposed amino-acid changes inside the dfr and sul genes, though no change explained resistance in all of them. One resistant isolate carried none of the targeted genes at all, pointing to other routes. The authors present the survey as gene evidence and call for studies with whole-genome sequencing and tests.
pmc-13491603:
Jessica J Wong and ten colleagues publish a 2026 scoping review on why older adults with low back pain struggle to reach rehabilitation care. Rehabilitation helps people function better despite health problems, yet access depends on far more than clinic availability. The reviewers mapped structural barriers and supports reported in qualitative research on adults aged fifty and older.

From 8,550 citations, sixteen studies qualified, covering low back pain and lumbar spinal stenosis in middle- and high-income countries. Cost and insurance gaps, distance and weak transport, and limited knowledge or stigma around certain treatments came up most often. Some patients met ageism from providers who treated pain as normal aging. Findings shifted with rurality, income, and disability, and no studies came from low-income countries.
pmc-13491703:
Weizhen Liu and seven co-authors introduce in 2026 a method for outlining plant structures inside CT scans without any training data or hand labeling. Standard deep learning approaches demand large sets of painstakingly labeled images for each new species, which slows cross-species research. Their system, DiffPlantCT, borrows visual features from a pretrained image generation model and combines them with the scan's own gray levels.

Each two-dimensional slice is segmented by unsupervised clustering, and the slices are then stacked back into a three-dimensional result. Tests ran on walnut fruit and barley spike datasets plus self-collected wheat and rice material. The method beat the best previous unsupervised approach by a wide margin on overlap scores. The authors present it as the first proof that plant CT segmentation can work with neither annotations nor training.
pmc-13491803:
Natalie Erickson and four colleagues profile in 2026 how a human gene variant linked to schizophrenia and bipolar disorder changes the protein makeup of young brain cells. The variant, an inverted copy of CHRFAM7A carrying a two-letter deletion, dials down a nicotine-responsive receptor. The team grew neural progenitor cells from stem cells that either carried the variant or lacked the gene entirely.

Mass spectrometry compared thousands of proteins between the matched cell lines. Some 129 proteins differed, clustering in pathways that build the matrix around cells, make collagen, and glue cells to their surroundings. Direct adhesion tests confirmed that cells with the variant gripped their matrix differently from gene-free cells. The authors propose that faulty cell anchoring may be one route from this variant to brain disease.
pmc-13493903:
Fei Wei leads an eleven-author team uncovering in 2026 how a little-known surface protein helps liver cancer grow, and how to drug it. The protein, LY6H, sits anchored on cell membranes and appears at abnormally high levels in hepatocellular carcinoma, the dominant liver cancer, where patients carrying more of it die sooner. Laboratory and animal experiments traced its grip on the cell's recycling system, autophagy.

LY6H grabs a key signaling subunit and shields its activated form from destruction, keeping a growth pathway switched on and autophagy humming. Blocking that pathway or silencing LY6H stalled tumor cells, confirming the chain of command. A screening hit, the compound NSC243928, shut down LY6H-driven recycling and tumor promotion in dishes and in animals. Tumors co-expressing the whole axis predicted the worst outcomes, marking both a prognosis tool and a target.
pmc-13494403:
Guglielmelli and colleagues write to the editor in 2026 about an inherited DNA pattern that shapes polycythemia vera, a blood cancer where the marrow overproduces red cells. Most cases carry the JAK2 V617F mutation. A common inherited haplotype called 46/1, a set of neighbouring DNA variants, makes that mutation more likely. Their letter analyses 756 patients with the mutation, asking whether inheriting the haplotype from both parents changes the disease's face or course.

Patients homozygous for the haplotype showed a distinct clinical picture and carried a heavier load of the cancer mutation in their blood. They also faced a higher risk of venous thrombosis, dangerous blood clots. That risk stayed significant even after accounting for the mutation load itself. A nearby immune gene's behaviour offers one possible explanation, since the same haplotype has been linked to higher expression of the PD-L1 checkpoint protein.
pmc-13495203:
Zhenyu Zhu and co-authors report, in a 2026 study, that a gene called ThASR4 helps plants withstand salty soil. ASR genes switch on under stress and during fruit ripening, yet their role in Tamarix hispida, a salt-tough shrub, was little studied. The team cloned six family members from the shrub and found salt switched them on, with ThASR4 answering most strongly in shoots and roots.

Moved into a model plant, ThASR4 raised seed sprouting, root length, and weight gain under salt. Both the model plant and the shrub carrying extra copies held less harmful oxygen waste and less cell damage, while their protective enzymes and a stress amino acid rose. Silencing the gene in the shrub flipped every result. The gene also woke partner genes for waste cleanup and salt defense. The authors frame ThASR4 as a useful lever for breeding salt-tough crops and shrubs.
pmc-13495303:
Sara A Kohlbeck, Jacey M Kant, and Katherine A Quinn explore, in a 2026 study, what they call the school-to-suicide pipeline among Black youth. Suicide in this group has risen, and the authors stress that race itself is no risk factor; social conditions and school settings shape the risk. The team gathered records for county residents who died by suicide across ten years and interviewed school psychologists and social workers.

The records covered 293 deaths, most of them Black residents, and school issues counted as a contributing factor for several. Interviews yielded four themes, with exclusionary discipline, such as suspensions, standing out for its harm to mental health. Staff also described thin resources for supporting Black students. The authors urge trauma-informed, restorative, and non-punitive ways of handling behavior in schools, above all for minoritized students, and frame the change as urgent suicide prevention.
pmc-13495403:
Ayşe Karacalı Tunç and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, silver nanoparticles brewed with an extract of Stachys spectabilis, a mint-family herb, against germs and their biofilms. Biofilms are slimy germ cities that shrug off many drugs. Green brewing uses plant chemistry to form the particles, avoiding harsh reagents. The team made the particles and checked them against four hospital germs.

On agar plates the particles barely spread, so zones stayed tiny. In liquid tests a clear dose pattern emerged: the staph germ was most sensitive, and killing doses sat above stopping doses. The particles also cut biofilm mass sharply in all four germs, by about half in three of them and two fifths in the fourth. The authors conclude the brew works in liquid settings despite its poor spread on plates, and merits work toward wound or surface uses.
pmc-13495903:
Fabricio O Lima leads the RESILIENT investigators asking, in a 2026 analysis, whether age changes who gains from clot removal after a major stroke in Brazil. Trials in rich countries found the catheter treatment helps old and young alike, but proof from poorer health systems is thin. The team reexamined their randomized trial of 221 patients treated in Brazil's public system, splitting patients at seventy and eighty years.

Age itself predicted worse recovery across everyone. The treatment's edge also shrank steeply with age: patients under seventy gained a strong benefit, while those over seventy and over eighty showed little or none. Statistics confirmed the split as real. The authors caution that results from rich systems may not travel to stretched public hospitals, and call for work on why the benefit fades and whether older patients there still gain.
pmc-13500203:
Carlsen and colleagues tested how the brain's quieting of the motor pathway before a movement depends on the task, in a 2026 neuroscience experiment. Before a go signal, magnetic stimulation of the motor cortex evokes a shrinking muscle response. That suppression is thought to stop release of a prepared action or to sharpen signal detection. Participants performed simple, choice, and go/no-go reaction tasks while stimulation probed excitability.

Carlsen found responses shrank toward the go signal in all three tasks. Suppression ran deeper in the simple and go/no-go tasks in the last fifty milliseconds before and at the signal. The timelines diverged in the final stretch, with choice reactions, which cannot be prepared, plateauing earlier. The authors conclude suppression is multifactorial: an early phase shared across tasks likely aids initiation, while a late phase reflects preparation and inhibition tuned to what the task demands.
pmc-13500503:
Shafique Ahmed Memon and co-authors propose in 2026 a method for explaining medical AI predictions through counterfactuals, changes that would flip a prediction, tuned by multi-goal optimisation. Doctors distrust black-box models, and plain explanations rarely show how features combine or offer realistic alternatives. Their two-phase method first trained a random forest classifier on a chronic kidney disease dataset. Candidate counterfactuals for one patient profile were then generated with an established generator and with their evolutionary algorithm approach.

Both methods produced fully valid counterfactuals, meaning every suggestion changed the model's prediction for that test case. The comparison weighed how few features each method changed against confidence and clinical plausibility, with a kidney specialist judging relevance in a first review. The optimised approach was designed to balance those rival goals better, tackling the problem that many equally valid accounts can conflict with each other.
pmc-13500703:
Shima Tavoosi and colleagues test in 2026 whether infecting leukaemia cells with a harmless bird virus can make them easier targets for the immune system's natural killer cells. Killer cells suit cell therapy because they attack tumours and tolerate donor mismatch, yet acute myeloid leukaemia often evades them. Laboratory lines and fresh patient cells, from new diagnoses and relapsed disease alike, were infected with a non-destroying Newcastle disease virus strain. They were then mixed with killer cells at several ratios while killing and immune signals were measured.

Infected leukaemia cells displayed a viral surface protein that acts as a danger flag for killer cell receptors in the reported experiments. Killer cells responded with stronger specific killing and released more interferon gamma plus the toxic proteins perforin and granzyme B. The authors propose sequencing treatment, virus first to sensitise the cancer, then an infusion of expanded killer cells to finish it.
pmc-13500803:
Yasir Almukhlifi leads a six-author team with a 2026 survey of safety knowledge among emergency medical services students in the Makkah region of Saudi Arabia. The cross-sectional study questioned 96 students at three schools with a structured form covering background, hazard knowledge, safety measures, and where students get their information. Paramedic trainees face physical, biological, chemical, and mental risks during training, yet how far knowledge becomes safe behaviour was unclear.

Students showed moderate to high knowledge overall, strongest for hand hygiene and protective equipment. Physical hazards were recognized by 83.3 percent and chemical hazards by 81.3 percent, while ergonomic risks were spotted by only 26.0 percent. About 63.5 percent had faced aggressive patients at least once a year. Progress through the programme showed no clear link with knowledge, and the link between knowledge and reported safety behaviour was weak.
pmc-13501303:
Peng and colleagues built ViralQC, a quality-control tool for viral genome fragments pulled from metagenomic sequencing, in a 2026 paper. Such samples yield mostly microbial DNA. Would-be viral sequences often carry host material or are partial, so judging their quality is needed before listing new viruses.

Peng combined DNA and protein foundation models, large pretrained neural networks, into an ensemble that flags microbial contamination inside supposed viral sequences. It estimated completeness from how the encoded proteins are arranged. Benchmarked against CheckV, the current standard tool, ViralQC detected contamination more sharply in fragments longer than ten thousand bases while keeping similar accuracy. Its completeness estimates were more accurate for fragments that were more than half complete. The authors offer the tool as a sharper filter for the flood of new viruses from such studies, with source code posted openly.
pmc-13501603:
Yoconda Arias leads a ten-author team with a 2026 feasibility study of combined exercise and brain training at a community aging centre serving a low-income area. Fifty adults over 55, living at home, enrolled after medical and mental health screening, and 46 finished with final testing. Sessions lasted one hour on alternate days for four months, rotating between structured physical exercise and supervised thinking activities. The study's main questions were practical ones of recruitment, retention, adherence, and safety.

Retention reached 92 percent, and no adverse events were blamed on the programme. Average attendance totalled 18.7 hours, though it ranged widely across people. Walking capacity improved strikingly: the six-minute walk distance grew by an average of 140 metres, a large effect, while blood pressure and oxygen responses stayed stable. Global cognitive scores rose modestly. Because the study had no comparison group, the authors treat the gains as early hints.
pmc-13501703:
Weiwei Zou leads a thirteen-author team reporting a 2026 study of spinal cord repair that began by watching what transplanted stem cells switch on inside an injured cord. Human umbilical cord mesenchymal stem cells were placed into rats with a cut spinal cord, retrieved, and profiled by RNA sequencing. One gene stood out: Neuroligin 3, a cell adhesion molecule better known from synapses. Screening confirmed it drove much of the transplant benefit, and restoring Neuroligin 3 in neurons alone matched the effect of the cell therapy itself.

Protein fishing experiments showed Neuroligin 3 recruiting two partners, Sar1a and Hspa8, proteins tied to synaptic vesicles. Restoring Neuroligin 3 together with either partner repaired the injury better than any single component, pointing to a noncanonical three-protein complex that tunes synaptic strength. Behavioural tests and motor evoked potentials backed the anatomical gains. The authors propose combination gene targeting of this complex for spinal cord injury.
pmc-13503903:
Nyssa K Krull leads a large team presenting IDBac, a free web platform that names bacteria from their protein fingerprints, in a 2026 paper. The method, mass spectrometry biotyping, is fast and fine-grained, yet it stayed in clinics for lack of a shared public library of fingerprints. IDBac aims to fill that gap.

The platform holds crowd-sourced protein signatures from seven bacterial groups. Users can match an unknown germ against the library, sort how strains in a collection relate, and compare the small molecules each strain makes. Worked examples show each use in action. The team invites labs worldwide to add their data, which would widen the library's reach for research outside hospital walls.
pmc-13505103:
Dongyang Wang leads a team mapping why Chinese teens with alcohol use disorder injure themselves without intent to die, in a 2026 interview study. The two problems often arrive together in adolescence, yet how they feed each other in daily life was little explored. The team traced the journey across home, hospital, and return home.

Eighteen diagnosed teens took part in deep interviews. Three nested themes emerged: a hunt for emotional numbness, a tunnel of narrowed thinking once alcohol loosens control, and a loop kept turning by shame after each episode. The mapped journey showed a hidden build-up before hospital, a stark closed-ward phase, and isolated recovery after. Teens felt most bare of support during late-night crises at home. The authors urge trauma-aware care and digital safety nets.
pmc-13506203:
Arif Khan, Rashmi Prakash, Anshu Arora, and Aishwarya Prasad argue that psychiatry's neuron-only picture of mental illness is too narrow. More than sixty approved drugs exist, yet their benefit over placebo stays modest and side effects are heavy. Surprising mood and reward effects from GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, large molecules once feared to mimic starvation's mental harm, pushed the authors to question synaptic models built on small transmitter molecules.

Psychiatric disorders run in families without following simple inheritance patterns, and symptoms vary widely, which weakens explanations based on DNA sequence alone. Drawing on Alan Turing's chemical-gradient ideas about development, the authors highlight astrocytes, support cells long treated as background. They review astrocyte variety across species and brain regions and propose that neurons and glia work as joined networks whose shared molecules produce mental function. Drug development, they suggest, should target those combined networks and the molecules glia release.
pmc-13507203:
Rinku Sharma Dixit leads a 2026 team that designs an AI-driven security framework for hospital cloud systems that run records, imaging, telemedicine, and live monitoring. Attacks such as ransomware and insider misuse can halt care, so defense must react in milliseconds without blocking clinicians. Their design joins smart threat spotting, probability-based risk scoring, and self-adjusting response control.

Tests used a public network traffic dataset with about two million records across attack types. Scores reached high levels for accuracy and related measures, with response latency near twenty-six milliseconds and few false alarms. Comparisons with current methods favored the new framework on security and service continuity. Scalable defense for round-the-clock clinical clouds is the aim.
pmc-13507303:
Emilia Anna Ossowska leads a 2026 team that profiles chemistry across the Parmelia saxatilis lichen group in Europe and names a new species, P. tobolewskiana. These leafy lichens look nearly identical, so the chemicals they produce carry much of the identification burden. About 600 specimens underwent sensitive liquid chromatography to map their secondary compounds.

Galbinic acid, rarely reported in this group, turned up in all three studied species, most often in P. saxatilis and newly in P. serrana. Fourteen chemical profiles emerged, eight of them first records. Specimens bearing galbinic acid did not cluster together on the family tree, so the trait evolved repeatedly or varies freely. Chemistry alone cannot sort these look-alikes.
pmc-13508403:
Yun Liu and four co-authors report a huge but silent heart tumor growing in both upper chambers of a 75-year-old woman, in a 2026 case report. Such tumors, called myxomas, usually grow in one chamber, and growth in both is extremely rare, with about fifty cases reported in fifty years. Hers surfaced by chance after chest trauma, alongside a rhythm flutter. Detailed heart CT mapping showed the tumor reaching into a great vein and part of the left chamber's back wall. That map guided the surgery plan.

Surgeons removed the tumor on a heart-lung machine, took the left atrial appendage, and rebuilt the vein and chamber wall. She recovered smoothly and left hospital on day ten. The authors suggest CT mapping earns its place when ultrasound leaves the picture unclear. They stress that careful planning of vein access and rebuilding is vital for giant tumors of this kind.
pmc-13508503:
Siriporn Somjit and seven co-authors run a randomized trial comparing two ways to clean the vagina before keyhole womb removal, in 2026 work at a Thai tertiary hospital. No agreement exists on the best prep to prevent wound infection. Patients were assigned to scrub-and-paint cleaning or paint-only cleaning with the same antiseptic. Neither patients' assessors nor outcome checks knew the assignments. Infection risk factors, operation details, and outcomes were tracked for thirty days after surgery.

Among 370 participants, no surgical site infections occurred in either group. That clean sheet limits what the trial can prove. Thirteen patients in the scrub-and-paint group, about seven percent, had light vaginal spotting after surgery, a nuisance the paint-only group avoided. The trial also stopped early, which the authors flag plainly. Their reading is that paint-only prep seems sufficient here, and scrubbing may add minor harm without proven gain.
pmc-13509303:
Ioannis Ogrotis and seven co-authors review biopsy-proven kidney inflammation cases tied to cancer immune therapy at one Greek hospital, in 2026 work. Immune checkpoint drugs can inflame the kidney's interstitium, causing sudden kidney injury, yet biopsy-confirmed series are rare. The team searched native kidney biopsies taken from early 2021 through late 2025. Cases counted when immune therapy came before the injury and the treating team blamed the drug on combined clinical and tissue grounds. Fifteen biopsies showed this inflammation pattern, and twelve were tied to the immune drugs.

Kidney function at biopsy was severely reduced, and most patients met the worst injury stage. White cells in urine appeared in every case, with sterile cultures and modest protein loss. All patients got steroids, and none needed dialysis. Recovery was complete in eight, partial in two, and absent in two, with stricter scoring shifting the split.
pmc-13509603:
Yitong Chen, Fengji Geng, Mengyuan Gong, Hui Zhou, and Yuzheng Hu introduce a mouse-tracking task for studying how past rewards pull attention, in 2026 work. In the classic version of this task, people respond while colors tied to earlier rewards appear as distractors, and speed alone is used to judge the pull. The new version records the full path of the hand on a mouse, so bends in the path can reveal attraction or avoidance during a choice.

Two groups of 45 and 59 people completed the task plus scales covering reward sensitivity, impulsivity, self-control, and digital addiction tendency. The path measure matched the classic speed effect and added a sharper signal: path bending toward high-value distractors tracked the personal scales in both groups, while the speed measure did not. The authors offer the method as a finer tool for studying reward-linked habits.
pmc-13511203:
Kylee R. Graham and Sean K. Meehan chart how a brief calming effect on the motor system shifts with muscle state and magnetic stimulation settings, in 2026 work. The effect, called short-latency afferent inhibition, appears when a nerve signal from the hand reaches the brain just before a magnetic pulse over the motor area. Eighteen healthy adults took part in two sessions, at rest and while holding a gentle thumb muscle contraction.

During contraction, the calming window peaked later and spread wider, whatever the pulse direction or length. The depth of calming grew during contraction for one pulse direction yet stayed flat for the other. The authors argue the effect holds several parts with distinct timing and jobs, rather than one fixed response. Mapping the full time course, they say, tells more than a single-interval measure when studying how touch shapes movement.
pmc-13511703:
Deyuan Kong, Jianing Zhao, Haichang Diao, Shuyao Qiu, Yuanyuan Peng, and Tingting Liu review new molecular tests for inherited diseases used before conception and during pregnancy, in 2026 work. The survey covers the past five years across three stages: carrier screening before pregnancy, embryo testing before implantation, and testing during pregnancy itself. Each stage has gained sharper tools.

Modern sequencing now anchors carrier screening, and long-read methods catch complex changes older tools miss. Embryo testing is moving toward non-invasive routes, with computer models helping solve DNA contamination snags. In pregnancy, pairing chromosome micro-tests with whole-exome reading has lifted diagnosis when scans show structural problems, while blood-based screening widens toward small deletions and single-gene diseases. Positive screens still need invasive confirmation. The authors see future gains in blending technologies and data types under cost and ethics limits.
pmc-13512103:
Yong Shi, Jiejun Liu, Lei Ren, Chen Feng, and Yuan Liu assemble the full chloroplast genome of a fig variety, in 2026 work. They test where the variety truly belongs on the family tree. The plant is classed as a variety of one fig species by its looks. No complete plastid genome evidence had been available for checking that placement.

The genome runs about 160,000 letters in the usual four-part layout and holds 110 unique genes. Its repeats and codon tastes match an AT-rich plastid genome, and several variable spots could serve as markers for later fig work. In every family tree built, from whole genome to split data sets, the variety grouped with a climbing fig species at full statistical support. Formal tests rejected the looks-based grouping in each set. The authors say plastid evidence and visible form tell different stories here.
pmc-13512303:
Giulia Pianigiani and nine co-authors widen the known picture of a syndrome tied to the gene PPP1R12A by reporting a patient with hearing loss and inner ear malformations, in 2026 work. The syndrome was known for brain and urinary tract malformations, and neither hearing feature had been reported before. The patient, aged twelve and a half, had profound hearing loss in both ears with inner ear defects plus urinary and brain findings.

Gene reading of the child and parents found a new single-copy change near a splice site in the gene. Lab tests on the patient's RNA and a minigene assay proved the change makes the cell skip a whole segment, shifting the reading frame and cutting the protein short. A literature sweep found no tidy link between variant type and symptoms so far. The authors argue hearing checks belong in this syndrome's care.
pmc-13514803:
Ecem Güler and colleagues report a prognostic study, published in 2026. They built a simple early risk score. It targets acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding. This is bleeding from the stomach or upper gut. It brings patients to emergency care. Existing scores can be impractical. The new score is called HOLD-B. It uses routine emergency measures taken before endoscopy.

The team used records from 312 adults. All had confirmed non-variceal bleeding at one hospital. The score combined several signs. They covered blood loss severity and metabolic response. Circulation instability was also included. The score separated high-risk patients well. It compared favourably with several common scores. Including transfusion in the outcome may flatter it, the authors note. Broader testing is still needed.
pmc-13515603:
Nishiza and colleagues published a 2026 study on cleaning tiny holes drilled through glass plates. Through-glass vias carry signals in advanced chip packaging stacks. Grime inside the holes blocks cleaning fluids and spoils later metal coating. The team asked whether lowering a cleaner's surface tension helps it penetrate.

Outside the holes, all cleaners left the glass equally wettable afterward. Inside the holes, lower surface tension clearly improved the cleaning result. Two stronger mixtures brought the inner wetting angle down to near flat. With the strongest cleaner, later copper coating formed fewer voids inside holes. Film thickness inside the holes also varied less after that cleaning. Cleaner holes should raise yields in advanced packaging lines overall.
pmc-13517203:
Qadeer and colleagues published a 2026 review of brucellosis, a bacterial infection that passes from livestock to people and ruins animal breeding. Infected herds suffer abortions and stillbirths, and farmers lose heavily, yet outcomes vary widely between animals. The review gathers genetic evidence from both host animals and the Brucella bacteria themselves.

Qadeer highlights gene markers that could, after independent checks, guide breeding of naturally resistant cattle, goats, sheep, and buffalo. Gene activity signatures may also sharpen diagnosis and staging of the disease in practice. Drug resistance in Brucella seems to arise through regulatory and metabolic routes that standard resistance gene databases miss. The authors close by ranking research gaps for vets working at the animal and human health boundary.
pmc-13518603:
Maria Claudia Rodríguez Duplat and four colleagues report a throat tumour slowly strangling a teenager's airway in a 2026 case study. The fifteen-year-old girl had carried a palatal mass since early childhood. It grew until breathing trouble, painful swallowing, and a lump-in-throat feeling brought her in. Scoping showed a wide purple vascular mass partly blocking the upper airway, and contrast scans agreed on a probable hemangioma with no bone involvement.

Size and position ruled out removal surgery. After team review she started oral propranolol, the blood-vessel drug borrowed from infant birthmark care. Over six months her breathing symptoms cleared, no side effects appeared, and the lesion visibly improved. Rodríguez Duplat's team stresses the work-up's breadth and the tailor-made plan: for deep airway vascular lesions, a medicine-first route can succeed where the knife cannot safely go.
pmc-13518903:
Nicholas D. Kathman, Aaron J. Lanz, Jacob D. Freed, and Katherine I. Nagel locate working memory in a fruit fly's brain in 2026 during odor-guided navigation. Following a scent plume means adding up scattered whiffs and holding a heading when the odor vanishes. Theory predicted both abilities, yet no neuron group had been tied to them.

While flies navigated a virtual plume, a bump of activity in a small set of local neurons in the navigation center grew with each odor encounter and lingered after odor loss. During the linger, flies kept their chosen heading, and silencing those neurons broke that persistence. Simulations showed the observed memory duration suits turbulent plume tracking near the ground.
pmc-13519003:
Zehua Zhang, Ning Shen, and Xingfen Wang tackle a factory dilemma in 2026: spare bearing stock and predictive maintenance are usually planned separately, wasting money both ways. Worse, standard learning agents treat remaining-life forecasts as exact, so they keep no buffer when forecasts are shaky. Bearings are cheap parts whose sudden failure stops costly machines.

Their uncertainty-aware strategy estimates both a bearing's remaining life and the forecast's variance using Monte Carlo dropout sampling. A risk-sensitive training reward, with penalties reshaped between practice and scoring, teaches the agent to hold safety stock when confidence is low. Simulations under heavy noise cut total costs by 40.3 percent versus deterministic baselines.
pmc-13520303:
Mehmet Aksan, Ozgur Genc Sen and Elif Bastug Guven assess in 2026 how well preclinical dental students filled root canals in extracted teeth. Their review covers work by 120 third-year students between 2019 and 2021, judged on X-rays for length, evenness and taper.

Of 1,050 fillings, about two thirds met the set standard for good quality. Lower premolars scored highest, while lower molars scored lowest on every measure. Single-rooted teeth did better than teeth with several roots. For teachers, the pattern pinpoints where extra practice is needed before students treat patients, namely curved and multi-rooted molar canals.
pmc-13520403:
Shawn L. Hanlon and colleagues pilot in 2026 a twelve-week exercise and activity plan for young people with Sever disease, a common cause of heel pain in active youth. Standard care has no firm consensus, so the team first checks whether a fuller trial is practical.

Thirteen patients aged 7 to 17 years did daily Achilles loading exercises, adjusted activity by pain levels, and received education, logging adherence in diaries. Recruitment reached about two thirds of target, with similar retention, while activity adherence averaged high. Symptoms, function, mood factors and ultrasound findings were tracked to guide outcome choices for a future definitive trial.
pmc-13520503:
Tuncer Karpuz and colleagues compare in 2026 two official testing sequences for syphilis that start from a reactive screening result, one from United States guidance and one from European guidance. Wording differences can change whether a case counts as confirmed at first visit.

Stored samples numbered 82, all reactive on the initial automated test at one university hospital. Overall agreement between sequences was high, at just over 96 percent, although statistical uncertainty was wide due to few disagreements. Three samples met one pathway yet stalled in the other, with follow-up clarifying two cases. Labs gain a concrete view of where guidance wording matters.
pmc-13521103:
Glynn and colleagues describe a 2026 surgical technique that corrects gynaecomastia, the growth of gland tissue in the male chest, while also building up the chest muscle contour. Their case involved a 35-year-old man with severe bilateral gynaecomastia and loose skin after major weight loss.

Instead of discarding the extra skin, the surgeons shaped it into a dermal flap and used the man's own tissue to enhance his pectoral outline during the same operation. This avoided implants and any second donor site on the body. The authors report a pleasing cosmetic result. They also review other published options for chest enhancement, and they stress that removing gland tissue alone can leave a flat or hollow look that this flap approach helps prevent.
pmc-13521903:
Yumiao Yuan and colleagues track in 2026 ecological quality across Shanxi Province from 2000 to 2025 using a satellite-based index, in a coal-heavy region where dry climate and mining strain the landscape. Trend tools and persistence checks map where quality rose, fell or held steady.

Average index values climbed by roughly nine percent overall, with improvement covering about 42 percent of land and decline about 36 percent. Mountain districts improved most clearly. Future persistence analysis suggests polarisation, with stable land dominant yet stubborn pockets of gain and loss. Human activity outweighed natural drivers, while rainfall details follow in the driver ranking.
pmc-13522003:
Wuhui Sun, Cheng Xiang and Yaqun Wang pinpoint in 2026 a gene called ITM2A that keeps thyroid cancer cells in a mature, better-behaved state. Tumour maturity tracks closely with outlook, yet control switches were poorly understood.

Database mining around progression-linked genes defined two molecular subtypes, with one subtype more mature and longer progression-free. ITM2A emerged as the hub gene. Raising ITM2A in cells promoted maturity, curbed aggressive traits and shifted fuel use from sugar burning toward fat burning. The gene also resisted a dedifferentiation signal and strengthened antigen display plus T-cell responses tied to PD-L1, linking maturity with immune visibility.
pmc-13522603:
Vezvaee and colleagues reported in 2026 progress on surface code quantum memory run on IBM superconducting processors whose wiring layout does not match the code's needs. Surface codes protect quantum information by spreading it across many physical qubits, but scaling them up on mismatched hardware is a central hurdle. The team co-designed the code layout and its control, folding the code onto the chip with swap operations and using helper qubits as bridges.

Vezvaee stretched the code unevenly, from distance 3 to mixed distances of 3 and 5, and gained stronger protection for each type of logical state in turn. Noise control pulses during idle gaps suppressed cross-talk between qubits and removed false claims of good scaling. Their analysis showed a noise cut of about a third would allow full distance-5 scaling on this layout. A new fidelity measure also exposed flaws in common one-number summaries of code performance.
pmc-13522803:
Nguema, Lévy, and Godot reviewed in 2026 a rare class of immune cells that may hold the key to longer lasting vaccines. The cells are CD8 stem cell-like memory T cells, killer T cells that act like stem cells. They can copy themselves for years, spawn many cell types, and spring back fast when a germ returns. Such cells were seen in blood more than 25 years after a yellow fever shot.

The review maps how these cells form. Their growth rests on a tuned signal from the T cell receptor, not too weak and not too strong, a balance the authors name after Goldilocks. Fuel choice inside the cell and cues from lymph tissue also steer the path. The authors argue that shots built to raise this cell pool, for germs and for cancer, could guard health far longer than shots that raise plain memory cells.
pmc-13523203:
Xiangxiang Wang and collaborators catalog nitrate transporter genes in quinoa in a 2026 genome study. Nitrate is the main nitrogen source for plants and also acts as a growth signal, yet its handling in quinoa was little studied. One hundred fourteen genes from one transporter family and fifteen from another were identified, and their uptake ability was tested in a yeast system lacking its own transporter.

Eleven transporters from the first family and three from the second proved able to take up nitrate. One high-affinity transporter rose strongly in roots when nitrate was scarce. A transcription factor was shown to bind its control region and switch it on, and boosting either gene lengthened roots in a model plant. The findings offer targets for improving nitrogen use in quinoa cultivation.
pmc-13523703:
Barney and a team in the United States found in 2026 a light driven way to turn sulfonamides, a vast class of drug like compounds, into fresh goods. Drug firms hold hoards of these sulfur builds, yet most known tricks keep the sulfur group, which caps what can be made. Their method shines light on the build and cuts the sulfur out.

A wide set of ring sulfonamides with choice side groups came out the other side as anilines, a prized drug frame in their own right. Probes of the path point to a rare swap: in the lit state, a ring slides from sulfur to nitrogen as the bond breaks. A twin polar path, through a reshaped form of the start build, runs as a small side road. The authors pitch the find as a key to locked hoards.
pmc-13524003:
Ann Tanyous, Iten Tanyous, and Alaa-Salah Eldin present a 2026 case report built around a fast heart rate that could mean two opposite emergencies. A 57-year-old man with prior triple bypass surgery and peptic ulcer disease arrived vomiting blood while taking low-dose aspirin without stomach protection. Scoping showed inflamed, eroded stomach lining without active bleeding.

Hours after intensive care admission, the man developed tachycardia and tremors. One explanation was renewed bleeding with low blood volume, calling for fluids, while the other was alcohol withdrawal, where a racing heart reflects overactive stress responses needing sedation. A standard withdrawal scale is not validated during acute illness and can mislead. Records showed fifteen years of progression from denied drinking to dependence. The authors propose a bedside framework and urge repeated alcohol screening.
pmc-13524903:
Mahdi Rezaverdinejad, Amir Tukmechi, and Mojtaba Hadian look into drug-resistant Staphylococcus aureus in dogs and cats with outer ear infection in Urmia, Iran. Ear infection is a common reason for veterinary visits and often comes with bacterial trouble. The team looked for resistance genes that defeat standard antibiotics.

The team collected 108 ear swabs from 56 dogs and 52 cats between July 2024 and May 2025. The germ was found in eighteen samples, more often in dogs. Resistance was high in dog samples, notably against penicillin and tetracycline. Over a quarter of them carried the mecA gene behind methicillin resistance, and over half carried a tetracycline resistance gene. Animals older than four years carried resistance genes more often. The authors urge routine drug testing and a One Health response.
pmc-13526803:
Zheng and colleagues combined multi-omics surveys with lab cultivation in 2026 to reveal an overlooked guild of deep-sea bacteria that digest laminarin. This storage sugar from algae makes up about a quarter of marine particulate carbon. The deep sea's microbial world is mostly uncharted. Sampling cold seeps, hydrothermal vents, and seamounts in two years, the team mapped communities by gene surveys, metagenomes, and gene activity.

Communities varied with place, season, and geochemistry, yet the capacity to digest it was widespread. The standout was the PVC superphylum, a bacterial grouping with broad sugar-cutting toolkits. Using laminarin as bait, the team isolated two strains that proved strictly dependent on it, each deploying a distinct family of cutting enzymes found widely across the group. The authors show laminarin is both a real food web currency in the deep sea and a practical hook for isolating its hidden bacteria.
pmc-13527103:
Rubi and colleagues demonstrated in 2026 that a strong magnetic field can bring superconductivity back in infinite-layer nickelate films, materials that lose resistance below about forty degrees above absolute zero. Fields normally kill superconductivity by aligning electron spins and threading it with vortices. Rare materials cheat this rule through the Jaccarino-Peter effect, where an internal magnetic influence cancels the applied field at a sweet spot.

Measurements across very high fields showed the nickelate films superconduct at low field, lose the state as the field climbs, then regain it at still higher fields, a reentrant pattern. Both the low- and high-field states fit the compensation picture, in which exchange coupling to magnetic moments offsets the external field. The authors argue this route could push the working field limits of high-temperature superconductors far beyond current ceilings, a prize for magnets, power, and fusion technology.
pmc-13527903:
Weijie Zhou and nine colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare bacterial infection caused by Cysteiniphilum litorale, a germ that needs the amino acid L-cysteine to grow. Their patient was a 46-year-old man whose left ring finger was punctured by a sea shrimp, after which a severe soft-tissue infection developed.

The report follows the man's course over roughly fifteen days, from a small prick near the nail to a ruptured ulcer with pus, plus further abscess-like lesions spreading up the same arm. Zhou's team explains how the infection was identified in the laboratory and how it was treated. They stress that injuries involving seawater creatures deserve prompt microbiology testing, because uncommon aquatic bacteria can invade deeply and even reach bone.
pmc-13528003:
Ramadhan Karsono and four colleagues test whether changes in the PD-L1 gene predict survival in Indonesian women with advanced breast cancer. The 2026 study analyzed 132 patients treated with chemotherapy or hormone therapy. A lab method counted copies of the gene in tumor samples. Five fibroadenoma samples served as references.

Gene copy changes appeared in twenty-two percent of cancers. Twenty cases had extra copies and nine had lost copies. Losing copies was tied to clearly worse survival. The risk stayed significant after adjustment for other factors. The effect was strongest in hormone receptor positive and HER2-negative tumors. Copy changes were also more common in patients over forty. The authors propose PD-L1 copy loss as a prognostic marker in this population.
pmc-13529603:
Anggoro and colleagues described a staged treatment for a displaced jaw joint disc in a 2026 case report. Their patient, a 21-year-old woman, had a year of pain in front of her right ear, clicking, and intermittent locking of the temporomandibular joint, the hinge connecting jaw to skull. Imaging confirmed the disc had slipped forward, with early joint arthritis, in a condition called internal derangement.

Anggoro first applied eight months of conservative care, including physiotherapy, medication, a bite splint, and diet changes, which widened her mouth opening greatly yet left symptoms in place. The team then washed out the joint in two sessions and injected hyaluronic acid, a natural joint lubricant, followed by a session adding dextrose solution to stimulate healing tissue. At four months her function was restored, pain and clicking had resolved, and opening stayed wide, supporting staged minimally invasive care for stubborn cases.
pmc-13530803:
Hevesi and colleagues present in 2026, as conference paper 35, a matched comparison hunting for what makes medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction fail. The operation is the foundation of treatment for a kneecap that keeps dislocating, yet some reconstructions still give way.

The team identified 34 patients whose reconstruction failed and required revision at one institution between 2004 and 2022, matching each to two successful controls by age and sex. Body mass was clearly higher in the failed group, and joint hypermobility appeared more often, though that gap fell short of statistical certainty. Every standard imaging measure of kneecap alignment, including groove distances and height indexes, looked the same in both groups. So did the mix of extra procedures performed alongside the reconstruction. The authors frame body mass as the standout signal in this comparison.
pmc-13531503:
Froentjes and colleagues ask in 2026 whether opioid painkillers lose their punch the longer they are taken for chronic low back pain or osteoarthritis. Long-term prescribing is common, and opioids can themselves heighten pain sensitivity over time.

The systematic review pooled 27 randomized trials and compared results by treatment length. In trials of four weeks or less, opioid patients were clearly more likely than controls to reach meaningful pain relief. Meaningful relief meant at least a thirty percent improvement on their pain scores in the short trials. In trials running four to twelve weeks, and again in trials past twelve weeks, that advantage disappeared, and the longest trials even leaned slightly toward the control treatments. Average pain score gaps never reached the review's bar for clinical importance at any duration.
pmc-13531803:
Jiapeng Yang and colleagues study in 2026 a small RNA that calms osteoarthritis by restraining a low-oxygen response gene. Blood from patients and healthy controls was measured, and cartilage cells stressed with an inflammatory signal formed the lab model. The RNA ran low in patients and fell further as joint damage grades rose.

Its level sorted patients from controls with strong accuracy and tracked pain and function scores sensibly. Adding the RNA in cells boosted growth, cut cell death and inflammatory release, and shifted the cartilage balance toward building rather than breakdown. Silencing its target gene copied those gains.
pmc-13531903:
Srikanth Thiyagarajan and co-authors report in 2026 a spinal blood-vessel growth that masqueraded as a common nerve tumor. A 66-year-old woman endured a year of back pain and worsening leg weakness until she was bedridden. Imaging showed a dumbbell-shaped mass spanning three chest spine levels with a large component outside the spine.

Surgeons combined back and chest approaches and removed the whole lesion despite heavy bleeding risk heightened by recent heart surgery and blood thinners. Tissue proved a capillary hemangioma, not a schwannoma. She regained bladder control and walked again with support.
pmc-13536703:
Khadijeh Moulaei and co-authors build a shared minimum data set for hip and knee replacement registries in a 2026 methods study. Registries track implants, repeat operations, complications, and patient-reported results, yet differing forms block comparison across hospitals. The team first mined papers, existing registries, and medical records for candidate items. A panel of 17 experts then refined the list through two survey rounds.

Experts kept items that reached strong agreement, narrowing an early list of 154 items to 136 and then to 111 confirmed items. The final set covers care before, during, and after surgery for both hip and knee replacement. The authors present the set as a common base for consistent recording, outcome tracking, and multicenter research on joint replacement.
pmc-13538203:
Rachel Cannon and co-authors demonstrate fast loading of a grating atom trap from a cold-atom beam in a 2026 physics study. Grating traps cool atoms with one beam and a patterned chip, suiting portable quantum sensors, yet vapor loading limits atom flow. Simulations compared side entry with entry along the beam axis. Bench tests then fed atoms from a two-dimensional trap into the grating trap using moving light fields.

Simulations showed uneven diffracted beams push side-entering atoms away from the trap center, tightly limiting side loading. Axial entry drops atoms straight into the trapping space and largely avoids that push. Bench loading reached billions of atoms per second. The authors present axial loading as a sturdy route to high-flow portable cold-atom devices.
pmc-13538303:
Lei Tang and co-authors profile a gene called OSR2 across many cancers in a 2026 combined database study. The gene has been tied to killer T cell exhaustion inside tumors, hinting at a drug target, yet its wider cancer picture was unmapped. Data from tumor, normal tissue, and protein collections supplied expression, survival, gene change, immune, and drug response checks across cancer types.

Expression ran high or low depending on cancer type and stage, with gene copy and chemical tagging changes tracking abnormal levels closely. Survival links flipped direction by cancer type, acting as risk in some cancers and protection in others. Expression also tracked immune cell entry, checkpoint genes, mutation load, and drug sensitivity. The authors propose OSR2 as a candidate marker for immune therapy research.
pmc-13538403:
Zhifang Wang, Quanzhen Huang, and Jianguo Yu propose a fault-tolerant deep learning method for predicting height and weight from finger length in a 2026 study aimed at public security uses. Standard predictors wobble under noise, missing data, and outliers. The design wraps learning updates in an adaptive control loop that limits fault impact during repeated training rounds. Tests used 372 data sets with heavy artificial data loss, judged on similarity, overall accuracy, and rare-class detection.

After long iterative training, height and weight prediction stayed highly accurate under both normal and fault-tolerant modes, with only small drops when faults were forced. Separate left and right hand tests also held strong accuracy with modest fault penalties. The authors note trade-offs among the three judging lenses and limit claims to small and medium tabular data with moderate imbalance.
pmc-13538503:
Hiromi Nyuzuki and colleagues report a post-mortem diagnosis of a severe newborn metabolic disorder in a 2026 case account. The disorder blocks fat burning for energy when a shuttle protein fails, often killing within days. A Japanese newborn girl died suddenly at two days old after being found not breathing, despite prolonged resuscitation. After-death scanning showed a diffusely fatty liver, prompting gene testing of the infant and parents.

Gene analysis found two faulty copies of the shuttle gene in paired form, one known change and one new stop change never reported before. Parents each carried one copy, matching inherited recessive transmission. The authors present after-death gene testing as a decisive tool for explaining sudden newborn death when rapid decline blocks testing during life, with value for family counseling.
pmc-13539703:
Mohamad Abi Nassif and colleagues compare surgery against conservative care for children with a compressed belly artery syndrome in a 2026 chart review. The syndrome squeezes the celiac artery and causes gut symptoms. Among 34 patients aged 7 to 21 years, most had belly pain and nausea, over half also met criteria for gut-brain interaction disorders. Ten received drug and behavioral therapy while twenty-four had decompression surgery.

Long-term outcomes did not differ significantly between groups. About six in ten conservatively treated children improved, as did just over half the surgical group despite a strong early response after surgery when nearly nine in ten felt better or resolved. A notable share of surgical patients worsened long term. The authors call for prospective studies to guide patient selection.
pmc-13540203:
Taraneh Rezaei and four colleagues explore, in a 2026 cell study, how male and female sex hormones affect liver cancer growth, since this cancer strikes men far more often. Two human liver cancer cell lines with different levels of aggression were exposed to estradiol and testosterone.

In the calmer HepG2 line, both hormones lowered division-driving Aurora kinases, raised GATA3, and paused the cell cycle. The aggressive Huh-7 line moved the opposite way, speeding through early division stages. Small regulatory RNAs shifted in matching patterns in both lines. The authors conclude that the cell's character, not the hormone, decides whether the signal restrains or encourages growth.
pmc-13540903:
Nagasundaram Nagarajan and three colleagues combine, in a 2026 study, single-cell gene data with machine learning drug screening to find targets shared by lung cancer and its spread to brain and bone. Non-small cell lung cancer kills largely through such spread, and few drugs work across all sites.

Gene profiles from primary tumors and matched metastases highlighted eight candidate targets. Three proteins, ARPC2, PSMB4, and RAC2, stayed elevated everywhere and sat in key cancer pathways. Prediction models trained on chemical activity data screened millions of compounds per target with strong accuracy. Docking and simulations produced one stable lead pairing for each target, ready for laboratory testing.
pmc-13543503:
Shanza Waseem's team published a 2026 case-based review of placenta accreta spectrum at its most dangerous: a 54-year-old woman with an IVF twin pregnancy and two previous caesarean births. In this disorder the placenta grows too deeply into the womb wall and cannot come away at delivery, risking massive bleeding. Her scans showed the most invasive form, placenta percreta, and she was taken in for a planned birth with a full specialist team.

Acute bleeding forced emergency surgery: a standard caesarean hysterectomy with partial bladder removal, backed by arterial balloon occlusion, clotting drugs, salvaged blood, and a massive transfusion protocol. Blood loss reached four and a half litres, and both twins lived after intensive care. The authors present the case as hypothesis-generating: older age, IVF, and uterine scarring may demand early imaging, delivery at top-level centres, and blood planning from the start.
pmc-13543603:
Qinyuan Yang and colleagues published a 2026 study of treating pelvic floor dysfunction in postmenopausal women at community clinics. The clinics replaced a distant specialist hospital, with a digital service package wrapped around electrical stimulation therapy. Two hundred women took part in a non-randomised comparison lasting one month. The community group received the stimulation locally plus digital support, while controls received standard stimulation at a tertiary hospital. Statistical methods tried to balance the self-selected groups.

Muscle-strength gains in the community group fell within the study's prespecified exploratory margin of the hospital group's, suggesting comparable short-term effect.
